chapters.r: Middle mediastinum, behind the sternum
chapters.b: Right & left coronary arteries (first branches of the aorta)
chapters.n: Cardiac plexus — vagus (slows) + sympathetic T1–T4 (speeds up)
chapters.bl: A four-chambered muscular pump with four valves and its own electrical conduction system.
chapters.sum: The heart is a double pump. Its right side receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae and sends it to the lungs; its left side receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and ejects it into the aorta. The two sides never mix because of the interatrial and interventricular septa, and one-way valves keep blood moving forwards. Contraction is triggered by an electrical impulse that begins in the sinoatrial node and sweeps through the atria, the atrioventricular node, the bundle of His and the Purkinje fibres.

chapters.r: Pleural cavities of the thorax, either side of the mediastinum
chapters.b: Pulmonary arteries (gas exchange) + bronchial arteries (tissue supply)
chapters.n: Pulmonary plexus — vagus (bronchoconstriction) + sympathetic T2–T4
chapters.bl: Two elastic, pleura-lined organs where air and blood come within 0.5 µm of each other.
chapters.sum: Air is conducted from the trachea through progressively dividing bronchi and bronchioles until it reaches the alveoli, where oxygen diffuses into pulmonary capillaries and carbon dioxide diffuses out. The right lung has three lobes separated by oblique and horizontal fissures; the left has two, with a cardiac notch and lingula to accommodate the heart. Each lung is wrapped in visceral pleura, opposed by parietal pleura across a thin fluid-filled cavity whose surface tension keeps the lung expanded.

chapters.r: Cranial cavity, above the brainstem
chapters.b: Internal carotid + vertebral arteries → circle of Willis (15% of cardiac output)
chapters.n: Itself the source of cranial nerves I–XII
chapters.bl: Midsagittal section: cerebrum, diencephalon, brainstem and cerebellum around the ventricular system.
chapters.sum: The brain integrates sensation, generates movement, and supports language, memory and consciousness. It uses about 20% of the body's oxygen and glucose despite being 2% of body weight, and it has almost no energy reserve — four minutes of ischaemia starts to kill neurons. The cerebral cortex is folded into gyri and sulci to pack ~0.15 m² of grey matter into the skull. Beneath it, white-matter tracts such as the corpus callosum connect the hemispheres, while the diencephalon and brainstem handle relay, arousal and the automatic control of breathing, heart rate and blood pressure.

chapters.r: Retroperitoneal, T12–L3 (left slightly higher)
chapters.b: Renal artery from the abdominal aorta — 20–25% of cardiac output
chapters.n: Renal plexus (sympathetic T10–L1) — mainly vasomotor
chapters.bl: Coronal section plus a nephron: filtration, reabsorption, secretion and urine concentration.
chapters.sum: Each kidney filters about 180 litres of plasma a day and returns all but 1–2 litres to the blood. Filtration happens in the renal corpuscle, where glomerular capillaries sit inside Bowman's capsule. The filtrate then passes through the proximal tubule (bulk reabsorption), the loop of Henle (concentration by countercurrent multiplication), the distal tubule (hormone-controlled fine tuning) and the collecting duct (final water handling under vasopressin). Nephrons drain via the papilla into minor and major calyces, the renal pelvis and the ureter.

chapters.r: Right hypochondrium & epigastrium, under the diaphragm
chapters.b: Dual: hepatic artery (25%) + hepatic portal vein (75%)
chapters.n: Hepatic plexus (vagus + sympathetic coeliac fibres)
chapters.bl: The body's chemical plant: metabolism, bile, clotting factors, detoxification and storage.
chapters.sum: The liver receives blood twice over — oxygenated from the hepatic artery and nutrient-rich from the portal vein — and mixes them in the sinusoids between plates of hepatocytes. Each hepatocyte performs hundreds of jobs: making albumin and clotting factors, conjugating bilirubin, storing glycogen and vitamins, and detoxifying drugs through the cytochrome P450 system. Bile, made continuously, is concentrated in the gallbladder and released into the duodenum to emulsify fat. The liver is also the only visceral organ that can regenerate: removing 70% leaves a liver that regrows to full size.

chapters.r: Abdominal cavity, from diaphragm to pelvic floor
chapters.b: Coeliac trunk, superior & inferior mesenteric arteries
chapters.n: Vagus (parasympathetic) + thoracolumbar splanchnic (sympathetic)
chapters.bl: The gastrointestinal tract from oesophagus to rectum, with the villus that does the absorbing.
chapters.sum: Food is stored and acidified in the stomach, where pepsin begins protein digestion and the muscular wall churns it into chyme. The duodenum neutralises acid and receives bile and pancreatic juice; the jejunum and ileum absorb almost all nutrients across a surface amplified by circular folds, villi and microvilli to roughly 250 m². The colon then reclaims water and electrolytes and stores faeces. The gut also carries its own nervous system — the enteric plexuses — with more neurons than the spinal cord.

chapters.r: Orbit, protected by the bony orbital walls
chapters.b: Ophthalmic artery (central retinal + ciliary branches)
chapters.n: Optic (II) · motor III, IV, VI · autonomic for pupil
chapters.bl: Sagittal section: an optical instrument that focuses light onto a neural film.
chapters.sum: Light is refracted mostly at the cornea and finely focused by the lens, whose curvature is changed by the ciliary muscle for near vision. The iris adjusts pupil size to control light entry. The image lands on the retina, where rods (dim light, motion) and cones (colour, detail) convert photons into signals through bipolar cells to ganglion cells, whose axons leave as the optic nerve. The fovea, a pit in the macula with cones only, gives sharp central vision. The retina is neural tissue: it is the only place in the body where the central nervous system can be seen directly.

chapters.r: Temporal bone: external, middle and inner ear
chapters.b: Labyrinthine artery (from basilar or AICA)
chapters.n: Vestibulocochlear (VIII)
chapters.bl: A pressure-wave collector that turns vibration into nerve impulses and doubles as a gyroscope.
chapters.sum: Sound waves are funnelled by the auricle down the external canal to the tympanic membrane. The membrane vibrates the ossicular chain — malleus, incus and stapes, the three smallest bones in the body — which amplifies pressure about 22-fold as it transfers vibration from a large eardrum to the tiny oval window. In the fluid-filled cochlea, the travelling wave bends hair cells on the basilar membrane: high frequencies at the base, low at the apex. Beside it, the vestibule and three semicircular canals sense gravity and angular acceleration for balance.

chapters.r: Retroperitoneal, across L1–L2 behind the stomach
chapters.b: Splenic artery + pancreaticoduodenal arcades
chapters.n: Vagus + splanchnic via coeliac plexus
chapters.bl: A dual gland: digestive enzymes from acini, hormones from the islets of Langerhans.
chapters.sum: The pancreas is both an exocrine and an endocrine organ. Acinar cells package trypsinogen, lipase and amylase into zymogen granules and secrete them into the pancreatic duct, which joins the common bile duct at the hepatopancreatic ampulla; bicarbonate-rich fluid from duct cells neutralises gastric acid. Scattered among the acini, the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin (beta cells), glucagon (alpha), somatostatin (delta) and pancreatic polypeptide directly into blood, minute-to-minute control of glucose.

chapters.r: Left hypochondrium, ribs 9–11, posterior to the stomach
chapters.b: Splenic artery (largest branch of the coeliac trunk)
chapters.n: Coeliac plexus (sympathetic) — mostly vasomotor
chapters.bl: The largest lymphoid organ: a blood filter, immune sentinel and red-cell graveyard.
chapters.sum: Blood enters the spleen through the splenic artery and percolates through two compartments. White pulp — cuffs of lymphocytes around central arterioles — mounts immune responses to blood-borne antigens, making IgM and opsonins. Red pulp is a mesh of sinusoids and cords where old, stiff or antibody-coated red cells are trapped and destroyed by macrophages, and where platelets are stored (a third of the body's pool). In fetal life the spleen makes red cells; after splenectomy the liver and marrow take over, but the loss of opsonisation leaves lifelong risk of encapsulated bacterial sepsis.

chapters.r: Anterior neck, C5–T1, in front of trachea and larynx
chapters.b: Superior & inferior thyroid arteries (± thyroidea ima)
chapters.n: Sympathetic + parasympathetic (vasomotor only; secretion is TSH-driven)
chapters.bl: A butterfly gland of follicles that sets the body's metabolic rate.
chapters.sum: The thyroid is built from follicles — spheres of cuboidal cells filled with colloid, a store of thyroglobulin. Iodide is trapped, oxidised and attached to tyrosine residues to make T3 and T4, released under control of pituitary TSH. These hormones raise basal metabolic rate, oxygen consumption and heat production, and are essential for growth and brain development. Parafollicular C cells secrete calcitonin. Embedded behind the gland, the four parathyroid glands sense calcium and release parathyroid hormone — the minute-to-minute controller of plasma calcium.

chapters.r: Pelvis, behind the pubic symphysis
chapters.b: Superior & inferior vesical arteries (internal iliac)
chapters.n: Parasympathetic S2–S4 (contracts) · sympathetic T11–L2 (stores)
chapters.bl: A detrusor-muscle reservoir with a smooth trigone and a two-stage sphincter.
chapters.sum: The bladder is a muscular sac lined by transitional (urothelial) epithelium that stretches from five cell layers down to two as it fills. The detrusor muscle contracts under parasympathetic control (S2–S4) while the internal sphincter (smooth muscle) and external sphincter (skeletal, pudendal nerve) keep urine in. The trigone — the triangle between the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice — is smooth because it develops from the mesonephric duct, and its oblique ureteric tunnels act as flap valves preventing reflux. Micturition is a spinal reflex under voluntary control from the pons and cortex.

chapters.r: Whole body surface — the largest organ
chapters.b: Dermal plexuses from segmental perforators
chapters.n: Somatic sensory (touch, pain, temperature) + sympathetic
chapters.bl: A layered barrier with hair, glands, receptors and its own immune system.
chapters.sum: The epidermis is a keratinising stratified squamous epithelium renewed from the basal layer every ~4 weeks, with melanocytes, Langerhans cells and Merkel cells among the keratinocytes. Beneath it the dermis gives strength and elasticity (papillary loose, reticular dense connective tissue) and carries the vessels, nerves, hair follicles and glands. The hypodermis is fat that insulates and cushions. Skin makes vitamin D, senses the world, and regulates temperature by sweating and by shunting blood through arteriovenous anastomoses.

chapters.r: Vertebral canal, foramen magnum to L1/L2
chapters.b: Anterior spinal artery + two posterior, reinforced by radicular arteries
chapters.n: 31 pairs of spinal nerves; ascending & descending tracts
chapters.bl: Cross-section: a grey butterfly inside white tracts, wrapped in three meninges.
chapters.sum: In cross-section the cord shows an H- or butterfly-shaped core of grey matter — posterior (sensory) horns, lateral (autonomic) horns in thoracic segments and anterior (motor) horns — around the central canal. White matter surrounds it in funiculi carrying the dorsal column–medial lemniscus (fine touch, proprioception), the spinothalamic tracts (pain, temperature) and the corticospinal tracts (voluntary movement). Dorsal roots carry sensory fibres with their cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion; ventral roots carry motor fibres. Three meninges and the denticulate ligaments suspend the cord in CSF.

chapters.r: Pelvis, perineum and scrotum
chapters.b: Testicular arteries (abdominal aorta, L2)
chapters.n: Sympathetic T10–L2 (emission) · parasympathetic S2–S4 (erection)
chapters.bl: Sperm production in the scrotum, maturation in the epididymis, and a shared exit with urine.
chapters.sum: Spermatogenesis runs for ~74 days in the seminiferous tubules, where Sertoli cells nurse dividing germ cells behind the blood–testis barrier; Leydig cells between tubules make testosterone under LH. Sperm mature and are stored in the epididymis, then travel through the vas deferens, which joins the seminal vesicle duct to form the ejaculatory duct crossing the prostate. Seminal fluid from seminal vesicles (fructose), prostate (citrate, PSA) and bulbourethral glands makes up semen. The scrotum keeps the testis ~2 °C below core temperature.

chapters.r: Pelvis: uterus, tubes, ovaries, vagina
chapters.b: Uterine + ovarian arteries (internal iliac & aorta)
chapters.n: Uterovaginal plexus (T12–L2 sympathetic, S2–S4 parasympathetic)
chapters.bl: A cyclic system: ovulation, fertilisation in the tube, implantation in the endometrium.
chapters.sum: Each cycle, FSH recruits a follicle that secretes oestradiol and builds the endometrium; the LH surge triggers ovulation at a variable cycle day (often about 14 days before the next period), and the corpus luteum then secretes progesterone to make the endometrium secretory. If fertilisation does not occur the corpus luteum regresses, progesterone falls and menstruation follows. Fertilisation normally happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube, and the embryo reaches the uterus after 3–4 days. The cervix, with its mucus plug, and the vaginal microbiome form the defence against ascending infection.

chapters.l: Clitoris · corpora cavernosa et bulbi vestibuli
chapters.r: Anterior perineum; deep to vulvar surface and along ischiopubic rami
chapters.b: Internal pudendal → deep and dorsal clitoral arteries; posterior labial branches
chapters.n: Dorsal nerve of clitoris (pudendal S2–S4); cavernous autonomic fibers via pelvic plexus
chapters.bl: A three-dimensional neurovascular and erectile complex: paired crura, body, glans and closely related vestibular bulbs.
chapters.sum: The visible glans is not the whole clitoris. Two corpora cavernosa join into a body, while proximal crura anchor to the ischiopubic rami. The glans is particularly sensory and is not simply another corpus cavernosum. Paired vestibular bulbs are neighboring erectile tissue flanking the vestibule, anatomically distinguished from the corpora. Arterial inflow, smooth-muscle relaxation and venous outflow restriction contribute to engorgement; somatic sensation travels largely in the dorsal clitoral nerve.

chapters.r: Root, shaft and glans of penis; superficial perineal pouch to external genitalia
chapters.b: Internal pudendal → deep, dorsal and bulbourethral/urethral arteries
chapters.n: Dorsal penile nerve (pudendal S2–S4); cavernous nerves from pelvic plexus
chapters.bl: Two dorsal cavernous bodies and one ventral spongiosum carry arterial, neural and urethral pathways through the penis.
chapters.sum: The paired corpora cavernosa are enveloped by strong tunica albuginea and form the main rigid erectile compartment; the ventral corpus spongiosum surrounds the penile urethra and expands distally as the glans. Deep penile arteries feed cavernous spaces. Parasympathetic-associated cavernous neural signaling relaxes smooth muscle, increasing arterial inflow and restricting subtunical venous outflow. The spongiosum remains comparatively compliant to protect urethral patency.

chapters.r: Whole-body integument; thick glabrous skin of palms/soles differs from thin hairy skin
chapters.b: Dermal superficial and deep vascular plexuses; epidermis is avascular
chapters.n: Cutaneous sensory afferents and sympathetic sudomotor/vasomotor fibers
chapters.bl: The five thick-skin epidermal strata, two dermal zones, hypodermis, receptors and follicle–gland units.
chapters.sum: Epidermis is a stratified keratinizing epithelium nourished by diffusion from vascular dermis. From deep to superficial: basale, spinosum, granulosum, optional lucidum (most evident in thick skin), and corneum. Basement membrane joins epidermis to papillary dermis; reticular dermis provides strength. The hypodermis is adipose-rich subcutis beneath the dermis. Hair, sebaceous glands and most sweat glands are skin appendages; cutaneous receptors relay varied forms of mechanical and thermal input.

chapters.r: Pons → internal acoustic meatus → facial canal → stylomastoid foramen → parotid plexus
chapters.b: AICA/labyrinthine and petrosal branches intracranially; stylomastoid artery distally
chapters.n: CN VII motor, parasympathetic and taste fibers; cutaneous face sensation mainly CN V
chapters.bl: Track facial motor branches, taste, lacrimation and salivation through the temporal bone and parotid gland.
chapters.sum: CN VII contains motor fibers to muscles of facial expression, taste from anterior two-thirds of tongue (via chorda tympani), and parasympathetic pathways for lacrimal, submandibular and sublingual glands. It enters the internal acoustic meatus, bends at geniculate ganglion, traverses the facial canal and exits at stylomastoid foramen. Within the parotid it forms a motor plexus giving temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical branches; it passes through the gland but does not provide its secretomotor supply.

chapters.r: Pons → trigeminal ganglion → orbit, midface and mandible
chapters.b: Brainstem branches and regional meningeal/orbital arterial branches
chapters.n: Main somatic sensory supply of face; V3 also innervates muscles of mastication
chapters.bl: Map facial sensation and masticatory motor fibers without confusing trigeminal CN V with facial CN VII.
chapters.sum: Most facial skin sensation travels by CN V. Ophthalmic V1 supplies forehead and cornea; maxillary V2 supplies the cheek, upper lip and upper teeth; mandibular V3 supplies lower jaw, lower teeth and general anterior tongue sensation and carries motor fibers to mastication muscles. Taste from anterior tongue is carried by facial chorda tympani joining lingual V3, not by trigeminal sensory neurons. Corneal reflex enters by V1 and blink exits by VII.

chapters.r: Orbit; anterior refractive media to posterior neural retina and optic nerve
chapters.b: Ophthalmic artery: central retinal and posterior ciliary branches; aqueous is avascular
chapters.n: II vision; III/IV/VI eye movement; V1 corneal sensation; III parasympathetic pupil/contraction
chapters.bl: Three ocular coats, five classical corneal layers, aqueous route, lens suspension, macula and optic disc.
chapters.sum: The globe has an outer fibrous tunic (cornea and sclera), vascular uvea (iris, ciliary body and choroid) and inner neural tunic (retina). Aqueous from ciliary processes flows posterior chamber → pupil → anterior chamber → trabecular meshwork/Schlemm canal or uveoscleral routes. Corneal epithelium, Bowman layer, stroma, Descemet membrane and endothelium are the classical five-layer teaching scheme; some texts describe an additional pre-Descemet layer. Retina transforms light to neural signals; the optic disc lacks photoreceptors.

chapters.r: Inner posterior globe; photoreceptors interface with pigment epithelium and choroid
chapters.b: Inner retina: central retinal artery; outer retina: choriocapillaris
chapters.n: Ganglion cell axons → optic nerve II; autonomic supply regulates ocular vessels
chapters.bl: Rods, cones, bipolar and ganglion circuits; fovea, optic disc, pigment epithelium and dual blood supply.
chapters.sum: Light traverses inner retinal layers before reaching rods and cones against retinal pigment epithelium (RPE). Neural signaling runs the opposite direction: photoreceptors → bipolar cells → ganglion cells → optic nerve. Horizontal and amacrine cells modify lateral signaling. The foveal center has dense cones and displaced inner layers for acuity, while the optic disc has no photoreceptors. Inner retina is supported mainly by central retinal circulation; photoreceptors and RPE depend strongly on the choriocapillaris.

chapters.r: Renal cortex (corpuscle and convoluted tubules) → medulla (loop and collecting system)
chapters.b: Afferent arteriole → glomerulus → efferent arteriole → peritubular capillaries/vasa recta
chapters.n: Renal sympathetic fibers reach vasculature, juxtaglomerular cells and tubules
chapters.bl: Follow filtration through glomerular barrier, segmented tubules, medullary loop and collecting ducts.
chapters.sum: Each nephron begins with a glomerular capillary tuft inside Bowman capsule; the filtration barrier includes fenestrated endothelium, glomerular basement membrane and podocyte slit diaphragms. Filtrate enters proximal tubule, descends and ascends in the loop of Henle, then passes distal tubule into a collecting duct. Collecting ducts arise from a different embryologic lineage than nephron tubules. Peritubular capillaries and vasa recta reclaim water and solutes; juxtaglomerular apparatus links distal salt sensing to renin secretion.

chapters.r: C5–T1 ventral rami between scalene muscles → behind clavicle → axilla and upper limb
chapters.b: Cords surround axillary artery; regional supply from subclavian/axillary branches
chapters.n: Ventral rami C5–T1, with frequent prefixed/postfixed variation
chapters.bl: Trace the arm nerve network from spinal roots through trunks, divisions and cords to five terminal nerves.
chapters.sum: The brachial plexus usually arises from ventral rami C5–T1. C5–6 form upper trunk, C7 middle trunk and C8–T1 lower trunk. Each trunk divides anteriorly and posteriorly; anterior divisions of upper/middle form lateral cord, lower forms medial cord, all posterior divisions form posterior cord. Cords are named relative to the axillary artery. Musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves reach the limb; several important scapular and pectoral branches leave the plexus before these endpoints.

chapters.l: Cortex cerebri · substantia alba · nuclei basales
chapters.r: Cerebral hemispheres: cortical ribbon, deep white matter, ventricles and diencephalon
chapters.b: Anterior, middle and posterior cerebral arterial territories; perforators supply deep nuclei
chapters.n: Corticospinal, thalamocortical, commissural and association pathways
chapters.bl: Trace cortex, white matter, corpus callosum, basal nuclei and thalamus on a realistic coronal section.
chapters.sum: Most cerebral neocortex has six microscopic layers, but cortical areas and older hippocampal cortex differ. Beneath cortical gray matter, association fibers link areas within a hemisphere, commissural fibers cross hemispheres and projection fibers connect cortex with deeper structures. The internal capsule carries densely packed motor and sensory pathways between thalamus/basal nuclei. The caudate and putamen form dorsal striatum; globus pallidus, subthalamic nucleus and substantia nigra participate in motor circuits. The thalamus relays and modulates most sensory streams and important motor signals.

chapters.l: Meninges · liquor cerebrospinalis · sinus durae matris
chapters.r: Skull and spinal canal: layered coverings, ventricular cavities and dural venous channels
chapters.b: Middle meningeal artery supplies dura; venous sinuses drain cerebral veins to jugular system
chapters.n: Trigeminal and upper cervical sensory innervation to cranial dura; brain parenchyma itself lacks pain receptors
chapters.bl: Follow dura, arachnoid and pia; then CSF from choroid plexus to subarachnoid drainage.
chapters.sum: Cranial dura has periosteal and meningeal layers that separate at dural venous sinuses and create falx/tentorium folds. The arachnoid bridges across sulci; CSF occupies the subarachnoid space between arachnoid and pia, which closely follows brain contours. Choroid plexus secretes much CSF into ventricles: lateral → interventricular foramina → third → cerebral aqueduct → fourth → median/lateral apertures → subarachnoid cisterns. Arachnoid granulations drain much of it to dural sinuses, alongside other clearance routes. The subdural space is a potential pathologic space, not the normal CSF compartment.

chapters.r: Midbrain → pons → medulla; cerebellum dorsal to pons/medulla
chapters.b: Vertebrobasilar branches, PICA, AICA and superior cerebellar artery territories
chapters.n: Brainstem cranial nerve nuclei, ascending/descending tracts and cerebellar peduncles
chapters.bl: Locate brainstem levels, cranial-nerve nuclei, pyramids and cerebellar peduncles, cortex and nuclei.
chapters.sum: Midbrain, pons and medulla form the brainstem, carrying ascending sensation and descending motor commands while housing many cranial nerve nuclei and arousal/autonomic networks. Dorsal to pons and medulla, cerebellum compares intended and actual movement through cortex and deep nuclei. Inferior, middle and superior cerebellar peduncles connect it to medulla, pons and midbrain respectively; traffic direction is not identical in each peduncle. Purkinje cells inhibit deep nuclei; cerebellar dysfunction causes coordination deficits rather than classic isolated paralysis.

chapters.r: Distal to a terminal bronchiole within secondary pulmonary lobules
chapters.b: Pulmonary arterioles → alveolar capillaries → pulmonary venules; bronchial arteries supply conducting tissue
chapters.n: Autonomic fibers to airways/vessels; alveolar wall is not a skeletal-muscle structure
chapters.bl: From terminal bronchiole to alveolar sac, type I/II pneumocytes, macrophages and the air–blood barrier.
chapters.sum: A terminal bronchiole is the last purely conducting airway. Its distal respiratory bronchioles bear occasional alveoli and lead to alveolar ducts, sacs and alveoli. Thin type I pneumocytes cover most air-exchange surface; type II cells secrete surfactant and can contribute to epithelial repair. The air–blood barrier includes alveolar epithelium, thin interstitium/fused basement membranes and capillary endothelium. Alveolar macrophages provide immune surveillance; capillary red cells pass closely alongside exchange surfaces.

chapters.r: Liver parenchyma: portal tracts at lobule periphery and central venule inside
chapters.b: Portal venules and hepatic arterioles → sinusoids → central vein → hepatic veins
chapters.n: Autonomic fibers accompany portal vessels and biliary tree; hepatocyte plates are not motor nerves
chapters.bl: See portal triad, central vein, sinusoidal cells and the opposite directions of blood and bile.
chapters.sum: The classical hepatic lobule places a central vein in the middle and portal tracts at its margins. Portal venous and hepatic arterial blood mix in sinusoids and travel toward the central vein, while hepatocytes secrete bile into canaliculi that drain outward toward portal bile ducts. Fenestrated sinusoidal endothelium borders the space of Disse; Kupffer macrophages reside in/along sinusoids and stellate cells in the perisinusoidal space. The hepatic acinus maps perfusion zones: zone 1 periportal receives blood first; zone 3 near terminal hepatic venules is relatively most hypoxia-vulnerable.

chapters.r: Small bowel from luminal epithelium through mucosa, submucosa, muscularis and serosa
chapters.b: Mesenteric arterial branches → villus capillaries; lacteals carry dietary lipids
chapters.n: Myenteric and submucosal enteric plexuses modulated by vagal/sympathetic input
chapters.bl: Map villus–crypt renewal, epithelial cell types, capillaries and lacteals, plus two enteric nerve plexuses.
chapters.sum: The small-intestinal wall has mucosa (epithelium, lamina propria, muscularis mucosae), submucosa, muscularis externa (inner circular and outer longitudinal layers) and serosa/adventitia depending on site. Villi expand surface area and crypts house renewing stem cells, antimicrobial Paneth cells and secretory lineages. Enterocytes absorb nutrients; goblet cells secrete mucus; enteroendocrine cells release signals. The submucosal plexus regulates local secretion/flow, while the myenteric plexus between muscle layers coordinates motility. These locations are different from the intestinal lumen.

chapters.r: Head: 8 cranial bones around the brain and 14 facial bones supporting jaws, orbits and nose
chapters.b: External carotid branches supply much of face; internal carotid/ophthalmic contributions supply orbit and forehead
chapters.n: CN V carries most facial skin sensation; CN VII moves expression muscles; CN V3 moves major chewing muscles
chapters.bl: Name every one of the 14 facial and 8 cranial bones, with accurate visible labels and deeper views for hidden structures.
chapters.sum: An adult skull has 22 bones: 14 facial (six paired types and the unpaired vomer and mandible) and 8 cranial. The maxillae anchor upper teeth, the mandible is the mobile lower jaw, and the palatine bones lie deep at the back of the hard palate. Ethmoid contributes to the upper bony nasal septum but is counted as a cranial bone; the inferior nasal conchae are separate paired facial bones. A front view cannot reliably identify every deep or posterior bone; those entries use an unpinned sectional reference. The hyoid and the six ear ossicles belong in the wider 206-bone adult skeleton count but not the 22 skull bones.

chapters.r: Alveolar sockets of upper maxillae and lower mandible, within the oral cavity
chapters.b: Superior and inferior alveolar arterial branches serve tooth pulps and supporting tissues
chapters.n: CN V2 superior alveolar branches: upper teeth; CN V3 inferior alveolar branches: lower teeth
chapters.bl: Follow crown-to-root layers, 32 permanent and 20 primary tooth positions, class shapes, FDI/Universal numbers and dental sensory nerves.
chapters.sum: Dental anatomy links each named tooth position to a tooth class and a representative cross-section. The crown bears enamel over dentin; roots bear cementum and anchor in the jaw through the periodontal ligament. Pulp contains nerves and vessels that communicate through root canals and apical foramina. Incisors cut, canines grip, premolars crush, and molars grind, although roots and cusps vary. A full permanent arch has 32 positions including third molars; primary dentition has 20, without premolars. This chart uses Universal and FDI numbering while explicitly distinguishing patient right from viewer left. Upper dental sensation primarily follows maxillary CN V2 superior alveolar branches, and lower dental sensation mandibular CN V3 inferior alveolar branches; facial nerve CN VII moves expression muscles but does not supply pulp sensation. Plates are representative digital teaching illustrations, not a clinical scan, histology, or a unique rendering for every numbered tooth.

chapters.r: Whole-body reference position and conceptual section planes
chapters.b: Varies by organ and tissue; no single foundation-specific blood supply
chapters.n: Varies by structure; directional terms have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Learn patient right and left, body planes, directional terms and movements; the colored reference planes are labelled only where visibly shown.
chapters.sum: Anatomical terminology begins with the subject in anatomical position: upright, facing forward and palms anterior. Relative terms refer to the subject, not the observer. Median sagittal, coronal and transverse reference planes divide the body left-right, front-back and superior-inferior; parasagittal and oblique sections serve other views. Movements are defined about joints and their axes, with limb-specific terms including pronation, dorsiflexion and inversion. The translucent planes on this digitally rendered body are conceptual, not physical membranes. Imaging orientations must be confirmed for each modality.

chapters.r: Whole body; trunk cavities and abdominal surface maps
chapters.b: Varies by organ and tissue; no single foundation-specific blood supply
chapters.n: Varies by structure; directional terms have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Trace dorsal and ventral cavities, serous spaces and patient-oriented abdominal quadrants and regions.
chapters.sum: The cranial cavity and vertebral canal form the dorsal compartment. The ventral compartment includes the thorax and abdominopelvic cavity, divided by the diaphragm. Within the thorax, the pleural sacs surround the lungs and the mediastinum contains the heart and other midline structures; pleural and pericardial spaces are potential spaces, not hollow organ chambers. The peritoneum forms serous surfaces in the abdomen; kidneys lie retroperitoneally. Four quadrants cross at the umbilicus and nine regions supply different ways to describe abdominal surface location. The clickable charts represent patient right on the viewer’s left and never claim to pinpoint a deep organ on the body photograph.

chapters.r: Cell-to-tissue scale across organs; epithelial example shown on main plate
chapters.b: Varies by organ and tissue; no single foundation-specific blood supply
chapters.n: Varies by structure; directional terms have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Explore cell structure and the four tissue families with dedicated microscopic-scale teaching illustrations.
chapters.sum: Cells organize into tissues, and organs contain combinations of epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues. The main image illustrates a single layer of columnar epithelium above connective tissue; epithelium itself has no capillaries. Separate tissue-scale digital cutaways illustrate loose areolar connective tissue, skeletal muscle and a multipolar neuron. Cell organelles and some specialized tissue subtypes are described in text rather than falsely pinned on these images. These are computer-generated educational models, not histology slides, quantified microscopy or diagnostic samples.

chapters.r: Spermatozoa mature from seminiferous tubules through the epididymis
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: A separate sperm chapter: head, midpiece, flagellum, meiosis, Sertoli support and epididymal maturation.
chapters.sum: Sperm production begins in testicular seminiferous tubules: spermatogonia give rise to meiotic spermatocytes, haploid spermatids and then shaped spermatozoa through spermiogenesis. Sertoli cells support developing germ cells; Leydig cells produce testosterone. The head contains a haploid nucleus beneath an anterior acrosome, the midpiece contains mitochondria and the flagellum supports movement. Sperm leaving the testis mature in the epididymis and acquire fertilizing capacity after capacitation in the reproductive tract. The digital plate exaggerates dimensions for legibility and is not a diagnostic semen micrograph.

chapters.r: Ovarian follicle and infundibulum of uterine tube
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: A separate egg chapter: primary versus secondary oocyte, meiosis, zona pellucida, corona radiata and ovulation.
chapters.sum: An oocyte begins development before birth as a primary oocyte arrested in meiosis I. During a reproductive cycle, an LH surge triggers completion of meiosis I in a selected follicle; ovulation releases a secondary oocyte arrested in meiosis II, surrounded by zona pellucida and corona radiata. Meiosis II usually finishes only after sperm entry, creating the ovum and another polar body. The follicle becomes a progesterone-secreting corpus luteum. A secondary oocyte in this teaching cutaway has no large resting central nucleus; the small polar body is outside the oocyte membrane but inside the zona. This is a stylized microscopic-scale model, not an actual ovum photograph.

chapters.r: Usually ampulla of uterine tube, not the uterine cavity
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Follow sperm transit, capacitation, zona interaction, membrane fusion and formation of the diploid zygote.
chapters.sum: After intercourse, sperm travel through cervix and uterus toward a uterine tube; intercourse does not necessarily cause pregnancy. Fertilization normally occurs in the ampulla of the uterine tube, where a capacitated sperm contacts the secondary oocyte surrounded by corona radiata and zona pellucida. Acrosome-mediated events facilitate passage through the coat, followed by sperm–oocyte membrane fusion. The oocyte completes meiosis II, cortical changes reduce polyspermy, and maternal and paternal pronuclear material ultimately establishes a diploid zygote. The plate deliberately shows the earlier contact step only: it does not show pronuclei, embryo formation or a fertilization event inside the uterus.

chapters.r: Early conceptus moves from tube toward uterine cavity
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Trace the separate preimplantation chapter: zygote, cleavage, morula, blastocoel and hatching.
chapters.sum: After fertilization in a uterine tube, the zygote divides into blastomeres while moving toward the uterus. Early cleavage increases cell number without major increase in overall size inside the zona pellucida. Compaction forms a morula, then a fluid-filled blastocoel and two broad cell populations define the blastocyst: outer trophectoderm/trophoblast and an inner cell mass. Hatching from the zona precedes adhesion to endometrium. Timing varies; the illustration shows one blastocyst only, not a timed sequence or an implanted embryo.

chapters.r: Usually uterine endometrium near fundus or posterior wall
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Separate implantation stage: endometrial receptivity, hatching, trophoblast invasion and early hCG.
chapters.sum: A hatched blastocyst attaches to receptive endometrium around the end of the first post-fertilization week, with timing variable. Its trophoblast differentiates into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, which interact with maternal tissue and begin early placental development; the inner cell mass gives rise to embryo proper. hCG supports the corpus luteum and progesterone early in pregnancy. Implantation within the uterine lining is distinct from normal fertilization in the uterine tube. The generated microanatomy is a conceptual section, not a patient biopsy or a claim about exact days. Ectopic implantation requires clinical assessment.

chapters.r: Placenta attaches to uterine decidua; umbilical cord joins fetal surface
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Separate placenta chapter: chorionic villi, decidua, separated circulations, cord and membranes.
chapters.sum: The placenta joins fetal chorionic villi with a maternal decidual bed. Fetal blood travels in villous capillaries while maternal blood occupies surrounding intervillous spaces; the two circulations are normally separated by a placental barrier rather than directly mixing. The umbilical cord typically contains two arteries and one vein. The amnion surrounds the fluid-filled fetal environment; chorion contributes to the placental interface. Placental structure and transfer change over pregnancy. A computer-generated cross-section cannot measure oxygen transfer, diagnose placental disease or depict every stage. After birth, placenta delivery belongs to a distinct third labor stage.

chapters.r: Embryo proper develops inside amniotic environment after implantation
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Separate embryonic chapter: germ layers, neurulation, folding, early heart and limb buds before fetal growth.
chapters.sum: After implantation, the embryonic disc establishes ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm during gastrulation. Neurulation and body folding organize an early body plan, while early heart, gut, somites and limb buds form. In standard embryology the embryonic period of major organ formation covers approximately weeks 3–8 after fertilization, roughly two weeks less than corresponding obstetric gestational age; exact morphology varies. From the following developmental period, the term fetus emphasizes growth and maturation. The image is a stylized single early-developing human and is NOT a week-accurate clinical scan, histology image, or a reliable depiction of any specific day; no unidentifiable microscopic parts receive pins.

chapters.r: Developing fetus in amniotic sac within uterus
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Follow fetal growth, placenta, organs and first, second and third trimester landmarks without confusing pregnancy weeks and conception age.
chapters.sum: After early embryonic organ formation, the fetal period emphasizes growth and functional maturation until birth. Obstetric gestational age is counted from the first day of the last menstrual period (LMP), approximately two weeks longer than post-fertilization age in a typical cycle. Common trimester definitions are 0–13 weeks 6 days, 14–27 weeks 6 days, and 28 weeks to delivery by LMP. Three clearly labeled digital models give undated early-development, illustrative middle-pregnancy and illustrative later-pregnancy contexts; NONE can date a pregnancy, verify viability or measure a fetus. The images are not scans or photographs. Clinical fetal assessment requires appropriate prenatal care and actual imaging.

chapters.r: Uterus and cervix before complete dilation
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Separate first-stage birth chapter: uterine contractions, cervical effacement and dilation to complete opening.
chapters.sum: The first stage of labor begins when contractions produce progressive cervical change and ends at complete cervical dilation, approximately 10 cm. Effacement shortens and thins the cervix as it dilates. Latent and active phases vary; active labor is often defined around 6 cm, not a fixed timetable for every person. The NEW digital cutaway models a fetus before birth and a partially opening cervix. It is not an obstetric examination or an exact centimeter measurement. A second NONPREGNANT regional cervix image is provided separately for structural context. Fetal membranes may remain intact or rupture. Heavy bleeding, severe persistent pain or reduced fetal movement requires clinical assessment.

chapters.r: Maternal bony pelvis, pelvic floor and vaginal birth pathway
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Separate second-stage birth chapter: full dilation, fetal descent, rotation and delivery of the baby.
chapters.sum: The second stage begins at complete cervical dilation and ends at birth of the baby. In a typical vertex vaginal delivery, the presenting head descends and may flex and rotate to negotiate maternal pelvic dimensions, then extend beneath the pubic arch. The NEW digital cutaway illustrates head-down descent into the birth canal BEFORE full birth, not a photograph of delivery, final fetal station or an instructional maneuver. A separate nonpregnant pelvis illustration supplies skeletal context. Position, rate and birth route vary; cesarean delivery may be indicated. No patient-specific progress can be determined from these drawings.

chapters.r: Placenta detaches from uterine decidua after infant birth
chapters.b: Depends on testicular, ovarian, uterine and placental stage; see the named entries
chapters.n: Maternal pelvic autonomic and somatic pathways vary by structure; gametes have no nerve supply
chapters.bl: Separate third-stage birth chapter: placental separation, uterine contraction, membranes and postpartum bleeding awareness.
chapters.sum: The third stage begins immediately after the baby is born and ends when placenta and membranes are delivered. Uterine contraction reduces the attachment area and compresses maternal vessels to limit bleeding. The NEW post-birth teaching cutaway depicts a partially detaching placenta with an empty uterus; it is NOT a patient image or a photograph of a completely delivered placenta. A second older image separately shows the organ still attached during pregnancy and a third digital image depicts its villous exchange barrier BEFORE delivery. Clinicians assess completion and bleeding in real patients; heavy bleeding after birth is an emergency.

parts.d: The large vein draining the head, neck, upper limbs and thorax. It enters the upper part of the right atrium.
parts.f: Returns deoxygenated blood from everything above the diaphragm.
parts.c: Obstruction (SVC syndrome) causes facial and arm swelling with distended neck veins.

parts.d: The largest vein in the body. It collects blood from the abdomen, pelvis and lower limbs and enters the inferior part of the right atrium.
parts.f: Returns deoxygenated blood from below the diaphragm.
parts.c: Compression in late pregnancy reduces venous return and can cause supine hypotension.

parts.d: The largest artery in the body. It arises from the left ventricle, arches over the left main bronchus and descends through the thorax and abdomen.
parts.f: Distributes oxygenated blood to the entire systemic circulation.
parts.c: A tear in the wall (aortic dissection) causes sudden tearing chest or back pain — a surgical emergency.

parts.d: Leaves the right ventricle and divides into right and left pulmonary arteries. Uniquely, it carries deoxygenated blood.
parts.f: Carries blood from the right ventricle to the lungs for oxygenation.
parts.c: A clot lodging here (pulmonary embolism) causes breathlessness, pleuritic pain and hypoxia.

parts.d: Four veins — two from each lung — that carry freshly oxygenated blood into the left atrium.
parts.f: Return oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart.
parts.c: Ectopic electrical foci in the pulmonary vein ostia are the commonest trigger of atrial fibrillation.

parts.d: The thick middle layer of the heart wall, made of branching, interlinked cardiac muscle fibres joined by intercalated discs.
parts.f: Contracts to generate the pressure that ejects blood.
parts.c: Death of myocardium from a blocked coronary artery is a myocardial infarction; the dead tissue scars rather than regrows.

parts.d: Thin-walled receiving chamber for the superior and inferior venae cavae and the coronary sinus. Contains the fossa ovalis and the right auricle.
parts.f: Collects deoxygenated blood and passes it to the right ventricle through the tricuspid valve.
parts.c: Houses the SA node, so it initiates every normal heartbeat.

parts.d: The most posterior chamber, receiving the four pulmonary veins.
parts.f: Passes oxygenated blood to the left ventricle through the mitral valve.
parts.c: Enlargement can press on the oesophagus (dysphagia) or the recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness).

parts.d: Crescent-shaped chamber with a thinner wall than the left, lined by trabeculae carneae and containing the moderator band.
parts.f: Pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary valve into the pulmonary trunk.
parts.c: Fails first in pulmonary hypertension (cor pulmonale), causing raised jugular venous pressure and ankle oedema.

parts.d: The thickest-walled chamber — roughly three times the right ventricle — because it must drive blood around the whole body.
parts.f: Ejects oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta.
parts.c: Pressure overload (hypertension, aortic stenosis) causes concentric hypertrophy and later heart failure.

parts.d: The thin wall between the two atria. Its shallow depression, the fossa ovalis, marks where the foramen ovale closed after birth.
parts.f: Keeps the atrial circulations separate.
parts.c: A patent foramen ovale persists in ~25% of adults and can allow a paradoxical embolus to cause a stroke.

parts.d: Thick muscular wall between the ventricles, with a thin membranous part just below the aortic valve.
parts.f: Prevents mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood and carries the bundle branches.
parts.c: The membranous part is the commonest site of a ventricular septal defect, the most frequent congenital heart lesion.

parts.d: Three cusps (anterior, posterior, septal) between right atrium and right ventricle.
parts.f: Closes at ventricular systole to stop backflow into the right atrium.
parts.c: Regurgitation produces large "v" waves in the jugular venous pulse and a pulsatile liver.

parts.d: The bicuspid valve between left atrium and left ventricle, with anterior and posterior cusps.
parts.f: Closes at ventricular systole to stop backflow into the left atrium.
parts.c: Rheumatic fever most often narrows it (mitral stenosis), giving a mid-diastolic murmur and atrial fibrillation.

parts.d: Three semilunar cusps (right, left and non-coronary) at the root of the aorta. The right and left sinuses above the cusps give off the coronary arteries.
parts.f: Opens in systole, closes in diastole to prevent reflux into the left ventricle.
parts.c: Calcific aortic stenosis in the elderly causes angina, syncope and breathlessness.

parts.d: Three semilunar cusps at the junction of the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk.
parts.f: Prevents backflow from the pulmonary trunk into the right ventricle during diastole.
parts.c: Absent or stenotic in tetralogy of Fallot, contributing to right-to-left shunting.

parts.d: Fibrous "heart strings" running from the edges of the AV valve cusps to the papillary muscles.
parts.f: Tauten during systole so the cusps cannot prolapse into the atria.
parts.c: Rupture (e.g. after infarction or in endocarditis) causes sudden severe valve regurgitation.

parts.d: Conical muscles projecting from the ventricular walls; two in the left ventricle, three in the right.
parts.f: Contract with the ventricle to anchor the chordae tendineae.
parts.c: The posteromedial papillary muscle has a single blood supply and is the one most likely to rupture after infarction.

parts.d: Right and left coronary arteries arising from the aortic sinuses. The left divides into the anterior interventricular (LAD) and circumflex branches.
parts.f: Supply the myocardium itself — the heart fills during diastole but perfuses itself only then.
parts.c: Atherosclerotic narrowing here causes angina; acute occlusion causes myocardial infarction. The LAD is the "widow-maker".

parts.d: A crescent of specialised pacemaker cells in the right atrial wall at the entrance of the SVC. Fires at ~60–100/min without any nervous input.
parts.f: Sets the heart rate — the natural pacemaker.
parts.c: Sick sinus syndrome causes bradycardia and pauses, often needing a permanent pacemaker.

parts.d: Pacemaker tissue in the inferior interatrial septum, near the coronary sinus and the septal cusp of the tricuspid valve.
parts.f: Delays the impulse ~0.1 s so the atria finish emptying before the ventricles contract.
parts.c: The only normal electrical connection between atria and ventricles; block here causes heart block.

parts.d: The bundle of His crosses the fibrous skeleton, then splits into right and left bundle branches that run down the interventricular septum to the Purkinje fibres.
parts.f: Conducts the impulse rapidly to both ventricles so they contract almost simultaneously, from apex upwards.
parts.c: Branch blocks widen the QRS complex on the ECG; the left bundle branch block masks infarction patterns.

parts.d: A 10–12 cm tube held open by 16–20 C-shaped hyaline cartilage rings, open posteriorly where the trachealis muscle lies. Lined by ciliated pseudostratified columnar epithelium with goblet cells.
parts.f: Conducts, warms, humidifies and filters inspired air.
parts.c: Foreign bodies more often enter the right main bronchus because it is wider, shorter and more vertical.

parts.d: The trachea divides at the carina (T4/T5) into right and left main bronchi, which divide into lobar then segmental bronchi. Cartilage plates replace rings as the airways narrow.
parts.f: Distribute air to each lobe and bronchopulmonary segment.
parts.c: Each segmental bronchus supplies a bronchopulmonary segment that can be surgically removed on its own.

parts.d: Airways under 1 mm with no cartilage and relatively more smooth muscle, ending in terminal then respiratory bronchioles.
parts.f: Regulate airflow resistance and deliver air to the alveolar ducts.
parts.c: Smooth-muscle spasm of the bronchioles is the main problem in asthma; smooth muscle is also the target of salbutamol.

parts.d: Superior, middle and inferior lobes separated by the oblique and horizontal fissures. Shorter than the left because the liver sits below, but wider and heavier.
parts.f: Gas exchange across ~150 million alveoli.
parts.c: The right middle lobe is prone to collapse (middle-lobe syndrome) because its bronchus is narrow and surrounded by nodes.

parts.d: Superior and inferior lobes separated by the oblique fissure only. Narrower than the right because the heart bulges to the left.
parts.f: Gas exchange; the lingula of the superior lobe is the equivalent of the right middle lobe.
parts.c: A left upper-lobe mass can compress the recurrent laryngeal nerve, causing hoarseness.

parts.d: Deep invaginations of visceral pleura. The oblique fissure runs in both lungs (T4 posteriorly to the 6th rib anteriorly); the horizontal fissure is right-sided only.
parts.f: Allow the lobes to slide against each other and define surgical planes.
parts.c: Fluid collects in the fissures on a chest radiograph as a "phantom tumour" in heart failure.

parts.d: A concave impression on the anterior border of the left lung that cradles the heart; the tongue-like projection below it is the lingula.
parts.f: Makes room for the heart and left ventricular apex.
parts.c: The bare area of pericardium behind this notch allows pericardiocentesis without crossing the pleura.

parts.d: The wedge-shaped entry point on the mediastinal surface: main bronchus, pulmonary artery, pulmonary veins, bronchial vessels, lymphatics and nerves.
parts.f: The lung's root — everything enters and leaves here.
parts.c: Hilar lymph node enlargement is a classic sign of sarcoidosis and tuberculosis.

parts.d: Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the wall. Between them is a potential space with a film of serous fluid.
parts.f: Surface tension couples the lung to the chest wall so it expands with it, and the fluid lets the layers glide.
parts.c: Air entering the cavity collapses the lung — a pneumothorax. Fluid gives a pleural effusion with stony dullness on percussion.

parts.d: Carry deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle, branching alongside the bronchi into each segment.
parts.f: Bring the whole cardiac output to the alveolar capillaries.
parts.c: Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction shunts blood away from poorly ventilated regions — reversed globally in COPD, causing pulmonary hypertension.

parts.d: Four veins that collect oxygenated blood from the capillary plexus and drain into the left atrium.
parts.f: Return oxygenated blood to the systemic pump.
parts.c: They run in the interlobular septa — the opposite position to the pulmonary arteries.

parts.d: A dome-shaped musculotendinous sheet separating thorax from abdomen, with crura arising from the lumbar vertebrae and openings for the aorta (T12), oesophagus (T10) and IVC (T8).
parts.f: The main muscle of inspiration — contraction flattens the dome and enlarges the thorax.
parts.c: Supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3–C5): "C3, 4, 5 keeps the diaphragm alive". A high spinal cord injury above C3 stops spontaneous breathing.

parts.d: Thin-walled sacs of type I pneumocytes wrapped in capillaries; type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant and alveolar macrophages patrol the surface. Together they present ~70 m² of membrane only 0.5 µm thick.
parts.f: Diffusion of O₂ into blood and CO₂ out of it.
parts.c: Surfactant deficiency in premature infants causes respiratory distress syndrome. Emphysema destroys the walls, reducing surface area.

parts.d: Final nonalveolated conducting airway before respiratory zone.
parts.f: Delivers air to downstream acinus.
parts.c: Contains no cartilage plates or submucosal glands.

parts.d: First airway segment with alveoli interrupting its wall.
parts.f: Combines air conduction and some gas exchange.
parts.c: Marks proximal boundary of acinus.

parts.d: Distal passage whose walls are largely alveolar openings.
parts.f: Distributes air to multiple alveolar sacs.
parts.c: More extensively alveolated than respiratory bronchiole.

parts.d: Common terminal chamber opening into a cluster of alveoli.
parts.f: Shares airflow among terminal alveoli.
parts.c: Not synonymous with a single alveolus.

parts.d: Tiny airspace lined by specialized epithelium and surrounded by capillaries.
parts.f: Provides extensive diffusion surface.
parts.c: Destruction reduces gas-exchange area.

parts.d: Very thin squamous alveolar epithelial cell covering most alveolar surface.
parts.f: Minimizes gas diffusion distance.
parts.c: Damage can impair barrier integrity.

parts.d: Cuboidal cell with lamellar bodies, commonly at alveolar corners.
parts.f: Secretes surfactant and contributes to epithelial renewal.
parts.c: Immature surfactant production contributes to neonatal respiratory distress.

parts.d: Resident/mobile phagocyte in alveolar airspaces.
parts.f: Removes particulates and participates in host defense.
parts.c: Inflammation can recruit further macrophages.

parts.d: The largest part of the brain: two hemispheres of folded cortex over deep white matter, basal ganglia and the lateral ventricles.
parts.f: Voluntary movement, sensation, language, memory, personality and conscious thought.
parts.c: Its surface folding (gyri and sulci) triples cortical area; abnormal folding causes lissencephaly and epilepsy.

parts.d: Anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Contains the primary motor cortex, Broca's area (usually left) and the prefrontal cortex.
parts.f: Planning, judgement, personality, voluntary movement and expressive speech.
parts.c: Prefrontal damage (classically Phineas Gage) changes personality and impulse control while sparing memory and IQ.

parts.d: Behind the central sulcus, above the temporal lobe. Houses the primary somatosensory cortex in the postcentral gyrus.
parts.f: Processing of touch, pain, temperature, position sense and spatial awareness.
parts.c: Right-sided lesions cause hemispatial neglect — the patient ignores the whole left side of space.

parts.d: The posterior pole, bounded medially by the parieto-occipital sulcus, containing the primary visual cortex on the banks of the calcarine sulcus.
parts.f: Vision — the retinal image is mapped point-for-point on the calcarine cortex.
parts.c: A posterior cerebral artery stroke causes a congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing.

parts.d: Below the lateral sulcus, including the hippocampal formation and primary auditory cortex on the superior temporal gyrus.
parts.f: Hearing, memory formation, language comprehension (Wernicke's area) and emotion.
parts.c: The medial temporal lobe is the commonest focus of temporal-lobe epilepsy and the earliest region damaged in Alzheimer disease.

parts.d: The great C-shaped commissure of ~200 million myelinated fibres: rostrum, genu, body and splenium.
parts.f: Connects matching regions of the two hemispheres so they work as one brain.
parts.c: Surgically sectioned for intractable epilepsy, producing "split-brain" patients who cannot name an object felt in the left hand.

parts.d: C-shaped CSF cavity in each hemisphere with anterior, body, posterior and temporal horns, lined by ependyma with choroid plexus on the floor.
parts.f: Cushions the brain and circulates CSF produced by the choroid plexus.
parts.c: Obstruction of the interventricular foramen causes hydrocephalus and enlargement of the ventricle.

parts.d: Two ovals of grey matter flanking the third ventricle, subdivided into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups.
parts.f: The relay station: nearly all sensory information (except smell) is edited and sent on to the cortex. Also involved in arousal.
parts.c: A thalamic stroke can produce severe contralateral sensory loss and thalamic pain syndrome.

parts.d: Only 4 g, yet it controls the autonomic and endocrine systems: supraoptic, paraventricular, arcuate and suprachiasmatic nuclei.
parts.f: Temperature, thirst, hunger, circadian rhythm, and hormone release via the pituitary.
parts.c: Lesions cause diabetes insipidus, obesity or emaciation, and disruption of sleep-wake cycles.

parts.d: Sits in the sella turcica below the hypothalamus, joined by the infundibulum. Anterior lobe is glandular; posterior lobe is neural tissue.
parts.f: Secretes GH, TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH, prolactin, plus oxytocin and vasopressin released from the posterior lobe.
parts.c: A pituitary adenoma pressing upward on the optic chiasm causes bitemporal hemianopia — loss of the outer half of both visual fields.

parts.d: Tectum (superior and inferior colliculi) plus cerebral peduncles, with the cerebral aqueduct running through it.
parts.f: Visual and auditory reflexes, eye movements, and the dopamine-producing substantia nigra.
parts.c: Degeneration of the substantia nigra causes Parkinson disease: tremor, rigidity and bradykinesia.

parts.d: The bulging bridge anterior to the cerebellum, carrying transverse fibres into the middle cerebellar peduncles.
parts.f: Relays cortex to cerebellum; holds the pneumotaxic and apneustic centres that shape breathing, plus nuclei of cranial nerves V–VIII.
parts.c: Occlusion of the basilar artery can cause locked-in syndrome — full awareness with paralysis of everything except vertical eye movement.

parts.d: The lowest brainstem segment, continuous with the spinal cord at the foramen magnum. Contains the pyramids, olives and the floor of the fourth ventricle.
parts.f: Cardiac, vasomotor and respiratory centres; reflexes for vomiting, coughing and swallowing. The pyramidal decussation happens here.
parts.c: Because motor fibres cross at the medulla, a lesion above the decussation paralyses the opposite side of the body.

parts.d: Two hemispheres and a midline vermis, with a densely folded cortex, deep nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) and branching white matter — the arbor vitae.
parts.f: Compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects it: coordination, precision, timing, posture and motor learning.
parts.c: Damage causes ipsilateral ataxia, intention tremor, dysdiadochokinesia and a broad-based gait. Alcohol affects it first.

parts.d: A diamond-shaped cavity between the pons/medulla in front and the cerebellum behind, draining through the foramina of Luschka and Magendie.
parts.f: CSF passes from here into the subarachnoid space around brain and spinal cord.
parts.c: Blocked outflow causes obstructive hydrocephalus — a common presentation of posterior fossa tumours in children.

parts.d: Continues from the medulla at the foramen magnum and ends at L1/L2 as the conus medullaris, with the cauda equina below.
parts.f: Carries sensory information up and motor commands down, and runs reflex arcs independently of the brain.
parts.c: Transection above C3–C5 stops diaphragmatic breathing; at thoracic level it causes paraplegia with a sensory level.

parts.d: The folded ridges and grooves of the cortex. Grey matter (neuron cell bodies) is 2–4 mm thick on the surface; white matter (myelinated axons) lies beneath.
parts.f: Folding multiplies cortical surface area about threefold within the fixed volume of the skull.
parts.c: The pattern is individually unique and is disrupted in cortical dysplasias that cause focal epilepsy.

parts.d: Neuronal cell-body sheet folded into gyri and sulci.
parts.f: Integrates sensory, motor and association information.
parts.c: Regional cortical lesions give different deficits.

parts.d: Outer cranial dural layer adherent to inner skull.
parts.f: Forms tough outer covering and part of sinus walls.
parts.c: Spinal epidural space differs from cranial periosteal interface.

parts.d: Dorsal midbrain paired structure.
parts.f: Coordinates orienting eye/head movements to visual stimuli.
parts.c: Not the origin of the optic nerve.

parts.d: A tough transparent layer of collagenous tissue directly on the kidney surface, surrounded by perinephric fat.
parts.f: Protects the parenchyma and maintains its shape.
parts.c: It does not stretch: swelling inside the capsule in acute inflammation causes the dull loin pain of pyelonephritis.

parts.d: The outer 1 cm, containing all the renal corpuscles, the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, and cortical tissue dipping between pyramids as the renal columns.
parts.f: Site of blood filtration and most solute reabsorption.
parts.c: Thinning or scarring of the cortex on ultrasound indicates chronic kidney disease.

parts.d: 8–18 cone-shaped regions of medulla, striped by the straight loops of Henle, vasa recta and collecting ducts that run through them.
parts.f: Create and exploit the osmotic gradient that concentrates urine.
parts.c: Their striated appearance is lost in medullary cystic disease and in the scarring of chronic reflux nephropathy.

parts.d: The apex of each pyramid, pierced by dozens of duct openings (area cribrosa) that empty into a minor calyx.
parts.f: The final exit point for urine from the nephron system.
parts.c: Analgesic abuse, diabetes and sickle-cell disease can cause papillary necrosis, with sloughed tissue in the urine.

parts.d: Cup-like minor calyces (8–18) receive urine from papillae and join into 2–3 major calyces that funnel into the renal pelvis.
parts.f: Collect urine and conduct it to the pelvis; their smooth muscle helps propel it.
parts.c: This is where renal stones form and lodge, causing the colicky flank pain of renal colic.

parts.d: The funnel-shaped expansion of the upper ureter inside the hilum.
parts.f: Collects urine from the major calyces and channels it into the ureter.
parts.c: Dilatation of the pelvis (hydronephrosis) is the ultrasound sign of an obstructed outflow tract.

parts.d: A 25–30 cm muscular tube with an inner mucosa, muscular coat and outer adventitia, running retroperitoneally to the bladder.
parts.f: Propels urine to the bladder by peristaltic waves (1–5/min), not by gravity.
parts.c: Three natural narrowings — pelviureteric junction, pelvic brim and vesicoureteric junction — are where stones impact.

parts.d: The medial slit where structures enter and leave. Anterior to posterior: renal vein, renal artery, renal pelvis ("VAU").
parts.f: Gateway for vessels, nerves, lymphatics and the ureter.
parts.c: Surgeons use this fixed order when clamping the hilum during nephrectomy or transplant.

parts.d: A short, wide branch of the abdominal aorta at L1/L2 dividing into five segmental arteries — these are end-arteries with no anastomosis. Branching continues: interlobar → arcuate → interlobular → afferent arteriole.
parts.f: Delivers ~1.2 litres of blood per minute for filtration.
parts.c: Narrowing (renal artery stenosis) causes secondary hypertension through excess renin release.

parts.d: Leaves the hilum to drain into the inferior vena cava. The left renal vein is longer, passing between the aorta and the superior mesenteric artery and receiving the gonadal vein.
parts.f: Returns filtered blood to the systemic circulation.
parts.c: The left vein can be compressed between aorta and SMA ("nutcracker syndrome"), causing haematuria and left varicocele.

parts.d: A tuft of fenestrated capillaries invaginating a double-walled capsule. Between them, the filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, fused basement membrane and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms.
parts.f: Ultrafiltration of plasma — water and small solutes pass; cells and proteins do not.
parts.c: Damage to the barrier leaks protein (nephrotic syndrome) or blood (nephritic syndrome) into the urine.

parts.d: The longest, widest segment, lined by cells with a dense brush border of microvilli and many mitochondria.
parts.f: Reabsorbs ~65% of filtered water and sodium, and 100% of glucose and amino acids; secretes drugs and acids.
parts.c: SGLT2 inhibitors act on this tubule and can benefit selected patients with diabetes, heart failure or chronic kidney disease; use is a clinical decision.

parts.d: A hairpin with a thin descending limb (water-permeable) and a thick ascending limb (actively pumps out NaCl but is water-impermeable), dipping into the medulla.
parts.f: Countercurrent multiplication builds the medullary osmotic gradient that allows urine to be concentrated.
parts.c: Loop diuretics such as furosemide block the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter here and are the most powerful diuretics.

parts.d: Shorter than the proximal tubule, with fewer microvilli, and the site where the macula densa contacts its own glomerulus.
parts.f: Fine-tunes sodium, potassium, calcium and pH under aldosterone, PTH and vasopressin control.
parts.c: Thiazide diuretics act here; the macula densa senses sodium delivery and drives tubuloglomerular feedback.

parts.d: Receives filtrate from many nephrons and runs through the medulla to open on a papilla. Principal cells respond to vasopressin and aldosterone; intercalated cells handle acid.
parts.f: Determines final urine volume and concentration.
parts.c: Without vasopressin (diabetes insipidus) the duct stays water-impermeable and 10–20 L of dilute urine is passed daily.

parts.d: Brings arterial blood into glomerular capillary tuft.
parts.f: Regulates incoming glomerular pressure.
parts.c: Diameter influences filtration rate.

parts.d: Fenestrated capillary loops between afferent and efferent arterioles.
parts.f: Pass plasma water and small solutes toward Bowman space.
parts.c: Damage may permit albumin or red cells into urine.

parts.d: Vessel leaves glomerulus and feeds downstream capillary network.
parts.f: Maintains filtration pressure and supplies cortical/medullary beds.
parts.c: Unique arteriole between two capillary beds.

parts.d: Parietal squamous layer and visceral podocyte layer enclosing Bowman space.
parts.f: Collects primary filtrate from glomerulus.
parts.c: Filtrate flows from urinary pole to proximal tubule.

parts.d: Specialized basement membrane shared by capillary endothelium and podocytes.
parts.f: Contributes size/charge selectivity.
parts.c: Thickening or injury can alter permeability.

parts.d: The larger lobe, four to six times the volume of the left, occupying the right hypochondrium. Its diaphragmatic surface is smooth and convex.
parts.f: Carries most of the hepatic mass and function.
parts.c: Its inferior edge is what you palpate below the costal margin in hepatomegaly.

parts.d: Thinner and flatter, lying in the epigastrium and reaching across to the left. Separated from the right lobe on the diaphragmatic surface by the falciform ligament.
parts.f: Supplies the left half of the functional liver.
parts.c: In cirrhosis the left and caudate lobes often hypertrophy while the right lobe atrophies.

parts.d: A small lobe on the posterior surface between the IVC and the ligamentum venosum, draining directly into the IVC.
parts.f: Has independent vascular supply and biliary drainage.
parts.c: It hypertrophies in Budd–Chiari syndrome, and its size relative to the right lobe is a CT sign of cirrhosis.

parts.d: On the visceral surface between the gallbladder fossa and the fissure for the ligamentum teres.
parts.f: Functionally part of the left hemiliver.
parts.c: Together with the caudate lobe it defines the surgical anatomy of the portohepatic segments.

parts.d: A sickle-shaped fold of peritoneum attaching the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm; its free edge carries the ligamentum teres (obliterated umbilical vein).
parts.f: Anchors the liver and divides the anatomical lobes on the diaphragmatic surface.
parts.c: In portal hypertension the ligamentum teres can recanalise and cause a periumbilical caput medusae.

parts.d: A 7–10 cm pear-shaped sac on the visceral surface of the right lobe, with fundus, body and neck. Its wall concentrates bile up to tenfold.
parts.f: Stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum when fat arrives (CCK-mediated).
parts.c: Gallstones (cholelithiasis) cause biliary colic; a stone impacted in the neck gives acute cholecystitis with Murphy's sign.

parts.d: The spiral-valved duct joining the gallbladder neck to the common hepatic duct.
parts.f: Two-way channel: bile enters the gallbladder for storage and leaves it after a fatty meal.
parts.c: Its spiral valves of Heister make cannulation during ERCP tricky.

parts.d: Formed by union of common hepatic and cystic ducts; runs in the free edge of the lesser omentum, behind the first part of the duodenum and into the pancreatic head to the ampulla.
parts.f: Delivers bile to the duodenum for fat emulsification.
parts.c: A stone here causes obstructive jaundice, pale stools and dark urine; with infection, ascending cholangitis.

parts.d: Branch of the coeliac trunk (via the common hepatic), supplying oxygenated blood and running in the portal triad.
parts.f: Provides ~25% of hepatic blood flow but ~50% of its oxygen.
parts.c: It is the dominant supply to tumours, which is why chemoembolisation (TACE) via the hepatic artery works.

parts.d: Formed behind the pancreatic neck by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins; carries nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from gut, spleen and pancreas.
parts.f: Delivers 75% of hepatic blood and everything absorbed from the gut for first-pass processing.
parts.c: Portal hypertension (cirrhosis) causes oesophageal varices, splenomegaly and ascites.

parts.d: Three short veins (right, middle, left) draining the liver directly into the IVC at its superior surface.
parts.f: Return processed blood to the heart.
parts.c: Their obstruction defines Budd–Chiari syndrome: painful hepatomegaly, ascites and jaundice.

parts.d: Grooves a deep fossa on the posterior liver surface; the liver partly surrounds it.
parts.f: Carries hepatic outflow to the right atrium.
parts.c: Because the liver wraps it, major liver trauma can tear the IVC with catastrophic bleeding.

parts.d: Hexagonal units ~1 mm across: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, separated by sinusoids lined with endothelium and Kupffer macrophages; portal triads (artery, vein, bile duct) sit at the corners.
parts.f: Blood flows from triad to central vein while bile flows the opposite way, from canaliculi to the triad bile duct.
parts.c: Zone 3 (around the central vein) is most vulnerable to ischaemia and paracetamol toxicity; zone 1 to viral hepatitis.

parts.d: Small portal vein branch delivering nutrient-rich splanchnic blood to sinusoids.
parts.f: Feeds liver parenchyma.
parts.c: Portal obstruction can raise portal pressure.

parts.d: Terminal hepatic artery branch carrying oxygenated blood.
parts.f: Adds oxygen to sinusoidal flow and supplies biliary structures.
parts.c: Not the same as portal venous inflow.

parts.d: Cholangiocyte-lined duct traveling with arterial and portal venous branches.
parts.f: Receives bile from canalicular/ductular route.
parts.c: Duct injury causes cholestatic patterns.

parts.d: Connective-tissue region carrying portal venule, hepatic arteriole and bile duct plus nerves/lymphatics.
parts.f: Organizes inflow and bile outflow at lobular margin.
parts.c: Triad diagrams omit additional vessels/lymphatics.

parts.d: Terminal hepatic venule at center of classical lobule.
parts.f: Collects sinusoidal blood toward hepatic veins.
parts.c: Zone 3 near its side is vulnerable to low oxygen.

parts.d: Wide, discontinuous capillary channel between plates of hepatocytes.
parts.f: Allows blood–hepatocyte exchange en route to central vein.
parts.c: Fibrosis can impair sinusoidal exchange.

parts.d: Fenestrated endothelial layer lining hepatic sinusoids.
parts.f: Facilitates plasma exchange into space of Disse.
parts.c: Capillarization reduces permeability in disease.

parts.d: A 25 cm muscular tube from pharynx to stomach, passing through the diaphragm at T10.
parts.f: Propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower sphincter prevents reflux.
parts.c: Its lower third drains to the portal system via the left gastric vein — hence varices in portal hypertension.

parts.d: The dome above the oesophageal opening, usually filled with a gas bubble on erect films.
parts.f: Stores swallowed air and gives the stomach its reservoir.
parts.c: A fundal mass can be missed behind the gastric gas bubble on a plain radiograph.

parts.d: The main reservoir between fundus and antrum, lined by acid- and pepsin-secreting mucosa with rugae.
parts.f: Mixes food with acid and pepsin; intrinsic factor for B12 absorption is made here.
parts.c: Loss of parietal cells (autoimmune gastritis) causes pernicious anaemia through B12 malabsorption.

parts.d: The distal funnel ending in the thick pyloric sphincter.
parts.f: Grinds food and meters chyme into the duodenum; G cells here secrete gastrin.
parts.c: Chronic antral gastritis from Helicobacter pylori is the main route to peptic ulcer and gastric cancer.

parts.d: Longitudinal folds of gastric mucosa that flatten as the stomach distends.
parts.f: Allow expansion and channel the flow of chyme.
parts.c: Thickened rugae (Ménétrier disease) cause protein-losing gastropathy.

parts.d: A C-shaped 25 cm first part of the small bowel wrapping the pancreatic head; the ampulla opens on its second part.
parts.f: Neutralises acid with bicarbonate and mixes chyme with bile and pancreatic enzymes.
parts.c: Most peptic ulcers occur in the duodenal bulb; posterior ulcers can erode the gastroduodenal artery.

parts.d: The proximal two-fifths of the mobile small bowel, in the left upper quadrant, with tall circular folds and few Peyer's patches.
parts.f: The principal site of carbohydrate and protein absorption.
parts.c: Its rich vasa recta give it a deeper red colour and thicker wall than ileum at surgery.

parts.d: The distal three-fifths, in the right lower quadrant and pelvis, with Peyer's patches on the antimesenteric border.
parts.f: Absorbs bile salts and vitamin B12–intrinsic factor complex; delivers residue to the caecum.
parts.c: Crohn disease most often affects the terminal ileum, causing B12 deficiency and bile-salt diarrhoea.

parts.d: The blind first part of the colon in the right iliac fossa, with the worm-like appendix at its pole.
parts.f: Absorbs fluid; the appendix is a lymphoid organ and gut flora reservoir.
