parts.c: Appendicitis classically migrates from periumbilical pain to McBurney's point as the parietal peritoneum becomes inflamed.

parts.d: Retroperitoneal, from caecum to the hepatic flexure under the right lobe of liver.
parts.f: Absorbs water and electrolytes; moves residue proximally to distally.
parts.c: Right-sided cancers tend to bleed and cause iron-deficiency anaemia rather than obstruction.

parts.d: The mobile loop slung between hepatic and splenic flexures on the transverse mesocolon.
parts.f: Continues water absorption and storage.
parts.c: It is the commonest site of volvulus after the sigmoid, and of colonic obstruction from cancer.

parts.d: Retroperitoneal, from splenic flexure to the iliac fossa.
parts.f: Stores and transports faeces toward the sigmoid.
parts.c: The splenic flexure is a watershed zone (Griffiths' point) vulnerable to ischaemic colitis.

parts.d: The S-shaped mobile loop leading into the rectum, which follows the sacral curve to the anal canal.
parts.f: Stores faeces; rectal distension triggers the defecation reflex.
parts.c: The sigmoid is the commonest site of diverticular disease and of volvulus.

parts.d: Finger-like mucosal projections ~1 mm tall, each with a capillary network and a central lacteal, covered by enterocytes with a brush border of microvilli.
parts.f: Multiply the absorptive surface ~600-fold; sugars and amino acids enter blood, fat enters the lacteal.
parts.c: In coeliac disease, gluten-driven immunity flattens the villi, causing malabsorption and steatorrhoea.

parts.d: Fingerlike projection of small-intestinal mucosa with epithelial cover and lamina propria core.
parts.f: Expands absorptive surface.
parts.c: Typical colon lacks villi.

parts.d: Epithelial invagination between villus bases toward muscularis mucosae.
parts.f: Houses stem and secretory cell niches.
parts.c: Crypt loss can impair epithelial renewal.

parts.d: Absorptive columnar epithelial cell with apical microvilli.
parts.f: Takes up digested nutrients.
parts.c: Loss of brush-border surface impairs absorption.

parts.d: Dense apical microvilli on enterocytes, not the large villi themselves.
parts.f: Increases membrane area and supports digestive enzymes.
parts.c: Villus and microvillus are different scales.

parts.d: Mucin-producing epithelial cell scattered among enterocytes.
parts.f: Lubricates and helps protect mucosal surface.
parts.c: Cell proportions vary along intestine.

parts.d: Granule-rich cell near base of small-intestinal crypt.
parts.f: Produces antimicrobial molecules supporting stem-cell niche.
parts.c: Typical mature Paneth cells are much less common in normal colon.

parts.d: Transparent, avascular, five-layered dome at the front of the eye. Provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power.
parts.f: Bends and transmits light; its endothelium pumps water out to stay clear.
parts.c: Endothelial failure causes oedema and cloudy vision; reshaping the cornea (LASIK) corrects refractive error.

parts.d: The tough white outer coat of collagen, continuous with the cornea anteriorly and the dural sheath of the optic nerve posteriorly.
parts.f: Maintains the shape of the globe and anchors the extraocular muscles.
parts.c: Thins with age and in inflammation (scleritis, a painful red eye linked to autoimmune disease).

parts.d: The vascular middle layer between sclera and retina, densely packed with capillaries and melanin.
parts.f: Feeds the outer retina and absorbs stray light to sharpen the image.
parts.c: Its high blood flow makes it a common site for metastatic deposits and for uveitis.

parts.d: Ten-layered neural film: photoreceptors outermost (light must pass through the inner layers first), then bipolar and ganglion cells.
parts.f: Transduces light into nerve impulses.
parts.c: Retinal detachment is a surgical emergency — flashes, floaters and a curtain across the field.

parts.d: A 5.5 mm yellow-pigmented area at the posterior pole; its centre, the fovea, contains cones only and no vessels.
parts.f: High-acuity central vision for reading and faces.
parts.c: Age-related macular degeneration destroys the fovea and central vision while sparing peripheral sight.

parts.d: Where ganglion axons and the central retinal vessels pierce the sclera. It has no photoreceptors.
parts.f: Exit point of the optic nerve and entry of the central retinal artery.
parts.c: It is the physiological blind spot; swelling (papilloedema) signals raised intracranial pressure.

parts.d: About a million myelinated axons wrapped in meninges, running to the optic chiasm. It is brain tissue, not a peripheral nerve.
parts.f: Carries visual information to the lateral geniculate body and cortex.
parts.c: Optic neuritis can cause painful vision loss and has several causes, including demyelinating disease; new vision loss needs prompt assessment.

parts.d: A biconvex, avascular, elastic structure of crystallin proteins, suspended by zonular fibres from the ciliary body.
parts.f: Fine focus: relaxing the ciliary muscle tightens the zonule and flattens the lens for distance; contracting it bulges the lens for near.
parts.c: Loss of transparency is a cataract; loss of accommodation with age is presbyopia.

parts.d: The coloured diaphragm of smooth muscle (sphincter and dilator pupillae) in front of the lens.
parts.f: Controls pupil diameter and therefore light entry and depth of focus.
parts.c: Sphincter is parasympathetic (III), dilator sympathetic — hence Horner syndrome gives a small pupil and a fixed dilated pupil suggests III palsy.

parts.d: The central aperture of the iris — not a structure but a hole.
parts.f: Adjusts from ~2 mm in bright light to ~8 mm in the dark.
parts.c: An irregular or keyhole pupil suggests previous surgery or trauma; a relative afferent pupillary defect signals optic nerve disease.

parts.d: A ring of muscle and ciliary processes behind the iris; the processes secrete aqueous humour and the muscle controls lens shape through the zonular fibres.
parts.f: Accommodation and aqueous production.
parts.c: Aqueous drainage through the trabecular meshwork at the iridocorneal angle determines intraocular pressure — the target in glaucoma.

parts.d: The space between cornea and iris, filled with clear aqueous humour made by the ciliary processes and drained at the angle.
parts.f: Nourishes cornea and lens and maintains intraocular pressure.
parts.c: Blockage of drainage causes glaucoma: acute angle-closure is a painful red eye with a hard globe and haloes.

parts.d: A clear collagen-and-hyaluronan gel filling four-fifths of the globe, adherent at the disc, macula and ora serrata.
parts.f: Maintains globe shape and holds the retina in place.
parts.c: With age it liquefies and pulls away (posterior vitreous detachment), causing floaters and, if it tugs, retinal tears.

parts.d: Surface stratified nonkeratinizing epithelial layer.
parts.f: Barrier and smooth refractive surface.
parts.c: Abrasion causes pain because the cornea is richly innervated.

parts.d: Müller-cell endfeet make retinal inner boundary against vitreous.
parts.f: Supports vitreoretinal interface.
parts.c: Epiretinal traction can distort macula.

parts.d: Acellular anterior limiting layer beneath epithelium.
parts.f: Adds anterior structural support.
parts.c: Damage may scar rather than regenerate as normal layer.

parts.d: Unmyelinated ganglion axons converge toward optic disc.
parts.f: Conducts output to optic nerve.
parts.c: Glaucoma thins nerve fiber layer.

parts.d: Organized collagen lamellae form most of corneal thickness.
parts.f: Precise collagen arrangement maintains transparency.
parts.c: Edema disrupts transparency.

parts.d: Retinal ganglion somata whose axons become optic nerve.
parts.f: Final retinal output neurons.
parts.c: Ganglion-cell loss contributes to glaucomatous vision loss.

parts.d: Basement membrane of corneal endothelium.
parts.f: Supports endothelial monolayer.
parts.c: Can develop folds with corneal edema.

parts.d: A cartilaginous scoop: helix, antihelix, tragus, antitragus, concha and lobule.
parts.f: Collects sound and helps localise it, especially vertically.
parts.c: Its skin is a classic site for gouty tophi and for sun-related skin cancer.

parts.d: A 2.5 cm S-shaped canal, cartilaginous outer third and bony inner two-thirds, lined by skin with ceruminous glands.
parts.f: Conducts sound to the eardrum; cerumen traps dust and insects.
parts.c: Impacted wax and otitis externa (swimmer's ear) both cause conductive hearing loss and pain on pulling the pinna.

parts.d: A 9 × 10 mm cone of three layers, tilted so its umbo points medially; pars tensa below, pars flaccida above.
parts.f: Converts sound pressure into mechanical vibration of the malleus.
parts.c: A red bulging drum means otitis media; a pearly white mass behind it suggests cholesteatoma.

parts.d: The hammer: handle embedded in the eardrum, head articulating with the incus.
parts.f: First lever of the ossicular chain.
parts.c: Its handle is what you see as the cone-of-light landmark on otoscopy.

parts.d: The anvil, bridging malleus and stapes.
parts.f: Second lever; its long process is the most fragile part of the chain.
parts.c: Incudostapedial joint disruption is a common cause of conductive loss after head injury.

parts.d: The stirrup: the smallest bone in the body (~3 mm), its footplate closing the oval window.
parts.f: Delivers amplified vibration into the cochlear fluid.
parts.c: Otosclerosis fixes the footplate and causes conductive deafness, classically in young women; stapedotomy restores hearing.

parts.d: An air-filled cleft in the temporal bone containing the ossicles, two muscles (tensor tympani, stapedius) and the chorda tympani.
parts.f: Impedance matching between air and cochlear fluid.
parts.c: The stapedius reflex dampens loud sound; its paralysis causes hyperacusis in facial nerve palsy.

parts.d: A 3.5 cm tube to the nasopharynx, normally closed and opened by swallowing.
parts.f: Equalises middle-ear pressure and drains mucus.
parts.c: In children it is short and horizontal, which is why middle-ear infections follow colds so often.

parts.d: A 2.5-turn spiral containing the scala vestibuli, scala media and scala tympani, with the organ of Corti on the basilar membrane.
parts.f: Frequency analysis: base responds to high pitch, apex to low; hair cells release glutamate onto the cochlear nerve.
parts.c: Outer hair cells are killed by noise and aminoglycosides, causing sensorineural deafness. Cochlear implants bypass them.

parts.d: Two otolith organs whose hair cells carry crystals of calcium carbonate.
parts.f: Sense linear acceleration and head tilt — gravity sensing.
parts.c: Dislodged otoliths drifting into a semicircular canal cause BPPV, the commonest cause of positional vertigo.

parts.d: Three fluid-filled loops at right angles (horizontal, anterior, posterior), each with an ampulla containing a cupula.
parts.f: Detect angular acceleration of the head in three planes.
parts.c: Their mismatched input with vision and proprioception is what produces motion sickness and vertigo.

parts.d: Cochlear and vestibular divisions joining at the internal acoustic meatus, entering the brainstem at the cerebellopontine angle.
parts.f: Carries hearing and balance information to the cochlear and vestibular nuclei.
parts.c: A vestibular schwannoma at the cerebellopontine angle causes unilateral sensorineural loss, tinnitus and unsteadiness.

parts.d: Fibrocartilaginous ring anchoring the peripheral tympanic membrane in its sulcus.
parts.f: Fixes the membrane while its central portion vibrates.
parts.c: Posterior-superior quadrant requires care during ear procedures.

parts.d: Small slack superior portion of the tympanic membrane above the malleolar folds.
parts.f: Moves differently from the taut pars tensa.
parts.c: Retraction pockets here can precede cholesteatoma.

parts.d: Large tense fibrous part of the tympanic membrane attached to the malleus handle.
parts.f: Transmits sound vibration to the ossicles.
parts.c: Perforation can impair conductive hearing.

parts.d: Membrane-covered opening between stapes footplate and scala vestibuli.
parts.f: Transmits ossicular motion into cochlear fluid.
parts.c: Stapes fixation can cause conductive hearing loss.

parts.d: Flexible membrane at the basal cochlear scala tympani.
parts.f: Allows pressure displacement as the stapes drives cochlear fluid.
parts.c: Its position matters in cochlear surgery.

parts.d: Sensory epithelium on basilar membrane containing inner and outer hair cells.
parts.f: Transduces basilar-membrane motion into auditory nerve signals.
parts.c: Hair-cell damage causes sensorineural hearing loss.

parts.d: Graded elastic membrane separating scala media from scala tympani.
parts.f: Supports frequency-dependent cochlear vibration.
parts.c: Basal region responds strongly to high frequencies.

parts.d: Specialized vascular epithelium on lateral wall of cochlear duct.
parts.f: Maintains potassium-rich endolymph and its electrical potential.
parts.c: Disruption compromises hair-cell transduction.

parts.d: Otolith-bearing sensory patch in utricle oriented mainly for horizontal acceleration.
parts.f: Detects linear head acceleration and gravity component.
parts.c: Vestibular dysfunction can cause imbalance.

parts.d: Hair-cell sensory ridge in each semicircular-duct ampulla beneath cupula.
parts.f: Detects angular head acceleration.
parts.c: Testing canal function helps localize vestibular disease.

parts.d: The broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels.
parts.f: Houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct.
parts.c: A tumour here compresses the common bile duct, causing painless obstructive jaundice and a palpable gallbladder (Courvoisier's law).

parts.d: The short constriction in front of the portal vein's formation.
parts.f: Landmark separating head from body; the portal vein forms behind it.
parts.c: It is the transection line in a Whipple procedure and in distal pancreatectomy.

parts.d: The middle third crossing the aorta and vertebral body, behind the stomach in the lesser sac.
parts.f: Carries the duct and splenic vessels along its borders.
parts.c: It lies against the splenic vein — thrombosis of that vein from pancreatitis causes isolated gastric varices.

parts.d: The narrow left end reaching the splenic hilum between the layers of the splenorenal ligament.
parts.f: Contains a high density of islets.
parts.c: It is easily injured during splenectomy, causing a postoperative pancreatic fistula.

parts.d: Runs the length of the gland from tail to head, joining the common bile duct at the ampulla in the second part of duodenum.
parts.f: Delivers ~1.5 L of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice daily.
parts.c: A "double duct sign" (dilated pancreatic and bile ducts) on imaging suggests a head tumour.

parts.d: An inconstant second duct opening at the minor duodenal papilla above the main one.
parts.f: Provides alternative drainage, mainly of the head.
parts.c: Pancreas divisum — failure of the duct systems to fuse — drains most secretions through this narrow route and can cause recurrent pancreatitis.

parts.d: The common channel of bile and pancreatic ducts, guarded by the sphincter of Oddi at the major duodenal papilla.
parts.f: Gates the entry of bile and pancreatic juice into the duodenum.
parts.c: A gallstone impacted here causes both biliary colic and acute pancreatitis.

parts.d: 1–1.5 million microscopic clusters of alpha (glucagon), beta (insulin, amylin), delta (somatostatin) and PP cells, richly capillarised.
parts.f: Minute-to-minute control of blood glucose, plus intermediary metabolism.
parts.c: Autoimmune destruction of beta cells causes type 1 diabetes; resistance to insulin with beta-cell exhaustion causes type 2.

parts.d: Grape-like clusters of enzyme-packed cells draining into centroacinar cells and ductules.
parts.f: Secrete the pro-enzymes for digesting protein, fat and carbohydrate.
parts.c: Premature activation of trypsin inside acinar cells is the initiating event of acute pancreatitis.

parts.d: Hook-shaped pancreatic head extension passing posterior to superior mesenteric vessels.
parts.f: Completes deep head contour around the mesenteric root.
parts.c: A mass may involve mesenteric vessels.

parts.d: Anatomical interface where pancreatic head contacts the duodenal curve.
parts.f: Relates gland secretions to duodenal entry.
parts.c: Inflammation here can affect both organs.

parts.d: Small mucosal opening receiving the accessory pancreatic duct when patent.
parts.f: Provides an accessory pancreatic drainage route.
parts.c: Drainage pattern varies with duct fusion.

parts.d: Mucosal projection receiving ampulla or pancreatic and bile duct openings.
parts.f: Delivers bile and pancreatic juice to descending duodenum.
parts.c: Gallstones at this level may obstruct both ducts.

parts.d: Smooth-muscle complex surrounding terminal biliary and pancreatic outflow.
parts.f: Controls flow into duodenum and limits reflux.
parts.c: Dysfunction can mimic obstructive pain.

parts.d: Cluster of enzyme-secreting serous cells surrounding a small lumen.
parts.f: Releases digestive enzyme precursors into duct system.
parts.c: Acinar injury contributes to pancreatitis.

parts.d: Pale cells at acinus-to-intercalated-duct transition.
parts.f: Start ductal bicarbonate-rich secretion.
parts.c: They distinguish pancreatic from salivary acini histologically.

parts.d: Smallest exocrine duct receiving secretion from acinar lumen.
parts.f: Conveys and modifies pancreatic juice.
parts.c: Duct obstruction impairs exocrine drainage.

parts.d: Pancreatic islet endocrine cells concentrated variably within islets.
parts.f: Secrete insulin in response to glucose.
parts.c: Loss or dysfunction contributes to diabetes.

parts.d: Islet endocrine cells intermingled with other endocrine populations.
parts.f: Release glucagon during falling glucose.
parts.c: Glucagon raises hepatic glucose availability.

parts.d: Islet cells producing somatostatin.
parts.f: Modulate neighboring endocrine and exocrine secretion.
parts.c: Islet composition is not fixed across the gland.

parts.d: Periacinar and periductal mesenchymal cells activated by injury.
parts.f: Regulate extracellular matrix turnover.
parts.c: Persistent activation contributes to pancreatic fibrosis.

parts.d: A fibroelastic capsule sending trabeculae into the pulp, carrying the vessels.
parts.f: Structural framework and conduit for vessels.
parts.c: The capsule is thin and the pulp fragile — the spleen tears easily in blunt abdominal trauma and bleeds briskly.

parts.d: Splenic cords of Billroth and wide sinusoids lined by stave cells with slit-like gaps.
parts.f: Filters senescent and abnormal red cells; recycles iron; stores platelets and monocytes.
parts.c: In hereditary spherocytosis the rigid spheres are trapped here, causing haemolytic anaemia cured by splenectomy.

parts.d: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (T cells), follicles (B cells) and a marginal zone rich in macrophages.
parts.f: Immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules.
parts.c: Its loss explains why asplenic patients are vulnerable to pneumococcus, meningococcus and H. influenzae.

parts.d: Discontinuous, leaky channels whose endothelial slits force red cells to squeeze through.
parts.f: The mechanical filter: healthy deformable cells pass; rigid ones are eaten.
parts.c: Malaria parasites stiffen red cells, which is why the spleen enlarges in chronic infection.

parts.d: The notched medial border where splenic vessels enter and the tail of pancreas and stomach fundus relate.
parts.f: Vascular gateway; also the site of accessory spleens in ~15% of people.
parts.c: A missed accessory spleen can cause relapse of disease after splenectomy for ITP.

parts.d: A tortuous branch of the coeliac trunk running along the upper border of the pancreas.
parts.f: Supplies the spleen, pancreas (via branches) and part of the stomach.
parts.c: Its tortuosity makes it prone to aneurysm in pregnancy and portal hypertension.

parts.d: Drains the spleen and joins the superior mesenteric vein behind the pancreatic neck to form the portal vein.
parts.f: Returns filtered blood to the portal system.
parts.c: Its thrombosis causes left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension with isolated gastric varices.

parts.d: The pale core of an activated follicle where B cells proliferate and affinity-mature their antibodies.
parts.f: Produces high-affinity, memory B cells against blood-borne antigens.
parts.c: Vaccines against encapsulated organisms work partly by priming these centres before splenic loss.

parts.d: T-cell-rich white-pulp cylinder surrounding a central arteriole.
parts.f: Samples blood-borne antigens with nearby immune cells.
parts.c: Disrupted white pulp weakens adaptive responses.

parts.d: Lymphoid nodule adjacent to central arterioles in white pulp.
parts.f: Supports B-cell activation and antibody maturation.
parts.c: A germinal center appears after antigenic stimulation.

parts.d: Interface between white and red pulp with specialized macrophages and B cells.
parts.f: Traps circulating antigens, including encapsulated bacteria.
parts.c: Loss of splenic function increases sepsis risk.

parts.d: Cell-rich Billroth cords of red pulp between sinusoids.
parts.f: Filter circulating erythrocytes and platelets.
parts.c: Abnormal red-cell deformability leads to trapping.

parts.d: Gaps between elongated endothelial stave cells in splenic sinusoids.
parts.f: Allow deformable red cells to re-enter circulation.
parts.c: Rigid or senescent red cells may fail to pass.

parts.d: Arteriole coursing eccentrically through white pulp.
parts.f: Brings blood to immune surveillance regions.
parts.c: It is central to a follicle-associated sheath, not the whole spleen.

parts.d: Small branches departing splenic white pulp toward red pulp.
parts.f: Feed terminal capillaries and splenic cords.
parts.c: Their organization underlies blood filtration.

parts.d: Arterial branch traveling within a splenic connective-tissue trabecula.
parts.f: Distributes inflow deeper through parenchyma.
parts.c: Traumatic rupture can bleed briskly.

parts.d: Venous channel within trabecular connective tissue.
parts.f: Returns blood toward splenic vein at hilum.
parts.c: Distinct from sinusoidal microvessels.

parts.d: Phagocytes abundant in marginal zone and red pulp.
parts.f: Clear old erythrocytes and opsonized organisms.
parts.c: Asplenia impairs clearance of encapsulated pathogens.

parts.d: Lymphatic vessels largely associated with capsule and trabeculae.
parts.f: Drain tissue fluid toward pancreaticosplenic nodes.
parts.c: Splenic blood filtering differs from node lymph filtering.

parts.d: Peritoneal fold between stomach and spleen containing short gastric vessels.
parts.f: Suspends spleen and carries vessels to gastric fundus.
parts.c: Vessels may be injured during splenic mobilization.

parts.d: One of two lateral lobes, 5–8 cm long, lying against the trachea and oesophagus and covered by the pretracheal fascia.
parts.f: Secretes T3/T4 from its follicles.
parts.c: An enlarging lobe can compress the trachea (stridor) or the recurrent laryngeal nerve (hoarseness).

parts.d: The mirror-image lobe; asymmetry between lobes is common and usually benign.
parts.f: Secretes T3/T4.
parts.c: A dominant nodule in one lobe is investigated with ultrasound and, if suspicious, fine-needle cytology.

parts.d: The bridge crossing the 2nd–4th tracheal rings, joining the two lobes.
parts.f: Connects the lobes into a single gland.
parts.c: It is the landmark for emergency tracheostomy and cricothyroidotomy is performed above it.

parts.d: A tongue of thyroid tissue ascending toward the hyoid in ~50% of people, a remnant of the thyroglossal duct.
parts.f: Functionally ordinary thyroid tissue.
parts.c: If left behind at thyroidectomy it can hypertrophy and mimic a recurrent goitre or a midline neck mass.

parts.d: The gland wraps the airway; the cricoid cartilage and thyroid cartilage lie above.
parts.f: Anatomical landmark and the reason goitres cause compressive symptoms.
parts.c: Retrosternal extension of a goitre can be read on CT and may require sternotomy to remove.

parts.d: Superior thyroid (from external carotid) and inferior thyroid (from thyrocervical trunk), with rich anastomoses.
parts.f: Give the gland its extremely high blood flow per gram.
parts.c: The superior laryngeal nerve runs with the superior artery and the recurrent laryngeal with the inferior — both at risk in surgery.

parts.d: Spheres of follicular cells enclosing colloid (iodinated thyroglobulin). TSH stimulates iodide trapping, organification, coupling, and endocytosis of colloid to release T3/T4.
parts.f: Synthesis and storage of thyroid hormone — the only endocrine gland that stores its product extracellularly.
parts.c: In Graves disease, autoantibodies to the TSH receptor drive unregulated hormone release and goitre.

parts.d: Four small glands (occasionally 3–6) on the posterior surface, derived from the third and fourth pharyngeal pouches.
parts.f: PTH raises plasma calcium: bone resorption, renal retention and activation of vitamin D.
parts.c: Accidental removal or devascularisation at thyroidectomy causes hypocalcaemic tetany and a positive Chvostek sign.

parts.d: Simple cuboidal epithelial cell bordering a colloid-filled follicle.
parts.f: Synthesizes thyroglobulin and releases T3/T4 after processing.
parts.c: Cell height reflects activity but is not a stand-alone diagnosis.

parts.d: Extracellular storage material in follicular lumen.
parts.f: Stores iodinated precursor for thyroid hormones.
parts.c: Follicle appearance changes with stimulation.

parts.d: Endocrine cell between follicles or in follicular epithelium.
parts.f: Releases calcitonin.
parts.c: Medullary thyroid carcinoma arises from C-cell lineage.

parts.d: External carotid branch approaching upper thyroid pole.
parts.f: Supplies superior gland and adjacent tissues.
parts.c: External branch of superior laryngeal nerve is nearby.

parts.d: Thyrocervical trunk branch supplying posterior-inferior thyroid.
parts.f: Feeds gland and usually parathyroid region.
parts.c: Its relation to recurrent laryngeal nerve varies.

parts.d: Venous drainage from upper thyroid to internal jugular vein.
parts.f: Returns blood from superior thyroid pole.
parts.c: Veins need control in neck surgery.

parts.d: Short vein from lateral gland to internal jugular vein.
parts.f: Drains lateral thyroid surface.
parts.c: May be encountered early in gland mobilization.

parts.d: Variable veins from lower poles entering brachiocephalic venous system.
parts.f: Drain lower thyroid and isthmus region.
parts.c: Anterior tracheal venous plexus can bleed.

parts.d: Vagal branch ascending in tracheoesophageal groove toward larynx.
parts.f: Motor supply to most intrinsic laryngeal muscles.
parts.c: At risk near posterior thyroid and inferior thyroid artery.

parts.d: Superior laryngeal branch accompanying superior pole vascular region.
parts.f: Motor to cricothyroid for pitch adjustment.
parts.c: Injury can impair high-pitched phonation.

parts.d: Connective-tissue sheath closely adherent to thyroid parenchyma.
parts.f: Supports lobules and vascular entry.
parts.c: Surgical planes differ from outer pretracheal fascia.

parts.d: Dense posteromedial attachment of thyroid to cricoid and upper trachea.
parts.f: Anchors gland during swallowing.
parts.c: Recurrent laryngeal nerve runs close to this region.

parts.d: The superior part, pointing toward the pubic symphysis and connected to the urachus (median umbilical ligament).
parts.f: Expands upward into the abdomen as the bladder fills.
parts.c: A patent urachus can leak urine at the umbilicus in a newborn.

parts.d: Three layers of interlacing smooth muscle with the wall thickened into trabeculae when obstructed.
parts.f: Contraction empties the bladder; relaxation allows storage at low pressure.
parts.c: Chronic outlet obstruction (prostate) hypertrophies it into trabeculae and diverticula; overactivity causes urge incontinence.

parts.d: Stratified transitional epithelium with umbrella cells whose plaques make it impermeable to urine.
parts.f: A stretch-tolerant, urine-proof lining.
parts.c: Its instability to carcinogens (smoking, aniline dyes) makes transitional-cell carcinoma the classic bladder cancer.

parts.d: The smooth triangle bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; mucosa firmly bound to muscle.
parts.f: Funnel for emptying; its stretch receptors trigger the micturition reflex.
parts.c: The interureteric ridge between the orifices is the first landmark sought at cystoscopy.

parts.d: Slit-like openings of the ureters at the posterolateral corners of the trigone, with oblique intramural tunnels.
parts.f: One-way entry of urine; the tunnel acts as a flap valve.
parts.c: A short tunnel allows vesicoureteric reflux, a cause of childhood renal scarring.

parts.d: The inferior angle of the trigone where the bladder neck meets the urethra.
parts.f: Outlet guarded by the internal sphincter.
parts.c: Bladder neck sclerosis or prostate enlargement here causes obstructive voiding and retention.

parts.d: The internal sphincter is smooth muscle of the bladder neck (sympathetic); the external is skeletal muscle in the urogenital diaphragm (pudendal, voluntary).
parts.f: Maintain continence; the external sphincter is under conscious control.
parts.c: After spinal cord injury above S2 the bladder becomes reflexic with detrusor–sphincter dyssynergia.

parts.d: Female ~4 cm, male ~20 cm (prostatic, membranous, spongy parts).
parts.f: Conveys urine out of the body; in males, also semen.
parts.c: Catheterisation and instrumentation make it the commonest site of iatrogenic stricture, especially the male membranous urethra.

parts.d: The two muscular ducts pierce the posterolateral bladder wall obliquely.
parts.f: Deliver ureteric jets of urine every 10–30 seconds.
parts.c: The vesicoureteric junction is the third and commonest site of ureteric stone impaction.

parts.d: Distensible muscular reservoir between superior dome and base.
parts.f: Stores urine at low pressure until voiding.
parts.c: Overdistention can impair detrusor contraction.

parts.d: Posterior basal surface facing rectum in men and anterior vagina in women.
parts.f: Forms stable posterior surface as dome expands.
parts.c: Sex-specific adjacent anatomy matters in pelvic surgery.

parts.d: Oblique intramural path where ureter enters bladder wall.
parts.f: Compresses during filling to reduce vesicoureteral reflux.
parts.c: Short intramural course predisposes to reflux.

parts.d: Raised mucosal fold connecting the two ureteric openings.
parts.f: Marks upper margin of bladder trigone.
parts.c: Useful landmark during cystoscopy.

parts.d: Large superficial epithelial cells lining distensible urinary tract.
parts.f: Form an impermeable apical barrier as the bladder stretches.
parts.c: Loss of barrier can increase mucosal irritation.

parts.d: Connective tissue layer beneath urothelium containing vessels and nerves.
parts.f: Supports the bladder mucosa.
parts.c: Depth of tumor invasion is critical for staging.

parts.d: Folds of mucosa in an empty bladder outside the smooth trigone.
parts.f: Unfold as bladder fills.
parts.c: Trigone remains comparatively smooth.

parts.d: Patent proximal branches of umbilical artery from internal iliac artery.
parts.f: Supply superior bladder and distal ureter.
parts.c: Collateral pelvic vessels can affect operative bleeding.

parts.d: Network of veins around bladder draining toward internal iliac veins.
parts.f: Returns blood from bladder wall.
parts.c: Communicates with nearby pelvic venous plexuses.

parts.d: Fibrous postnatal remnant of urachus extending from bladder apex toward umbilicus.
parts.f: Tethers bladder dome anteriorly.
parts.c: Persistent urachal tissue may form a cyst or sinus.

parts.d: Loose connective tissue surrounding bladder in extraperitoneal space.
parts.f: Permits bladder filling and separates surgical planes.
parts.c: Inflammation may extend along extraperitoneal tissue.

parts.d: 15–20 layers of dead, flattened, keratin-filled corneocytes held by lipids — the "brick and mortar" barrier.
parts.f: Waterproofing and the main barrier to microbes and chemicals.
parts.c: Its thickness defines palms and soles; loss in burns allows catastrophic fluid and heat loss.

parts.d: The single basal row of dividing keratinocytes on the basement membrane, plus the prickle-cell layers above with desmosomes, melanocytes and Langerhans cells.
parts.f: Renews the epidermis; melanocytes transfer pigment; Langerhans cells present antigen.
parts.c: Basal cell carcinoma arises here at sun-exposed sites; melanoma from melanocytes.

parts.d: Papillary layer of loose connective tissue forming dermal papillae; reticular layer of dense irregular collagen and elastin.
parts.f: Strength, elasticity, sensation and the vascular supply of the epidermis.
parts.c: Split-thickness grafts take from the dermal remnants left in the wound bed; keloids are dermal over-scarring.

parts.d: Loose connective tissue and fat, with larger vessels and nerves and, in places, panniculus carnosus.
parts.f: Insulation, energy store, shock absorption and skin mobility.
parts.c: Subcutaneous insulin absorption varies with site and temperature because of this layer's blood flow.

parts.d: A keratinised shaft growing from a follicle that dips into dermis or fat, with a bulb around a dermal papilla and a bulge of stem cells.
parts.f: Protection, sensation and (in other mammals) insulation.
parts.c: Follicular stem cells re-epithelialise partial-thickness wounds; follicles are the target of alopecias.

parts.d: A band of smooth muscle from follicle to dermis, supplied by sympathetic fibres.
parts.f: Erects the hair (goose flesh) and helps express sebum.
parts.c: Its contraction in cold traps air for insulation — vestigial in humans.

parts.d: A holocrine gland of lipid-filled cells opening into the follicle above the arrector pili insertion.
parts.f: Sebum lubricates and waterproofs hair and skin and has mild antimicrobial action.
parts.c: Blocked, colonised glands are the lesion of acne vulgaris (Propionibacterium/Cutibacterium acnes).

parts.d: A coiled secretory coil deep in the dermis with a duct spiralling through the epidermis to a pore.
parts.f: Evaporative cooling — the main human thermoregulatory mechanism; also excretes salt, urea and lactate.
parts.c: Heat stroke follows when sweating fails; cystic fibrosis makes sweat abnormally salty (chloride test).

parts.d: A stacked, encapsulated ending in the dermal papillae of glabrous skin.
parts.f: Detects light touch and low-frequency vibration (rapidly adapting).
parts.c: Dense in fingertips and lips — the reason two-point discrimination is finest there.

parts.d: An onion-like encapsulated receptor in deep dermis and hypodermis.
parts.f: Senses deep pressure and high-frequency vibration.
parts.c: Its loss in leprosy and diabetes contributes to unnoticed injury and ulceration.

parts.d: A deep and a superficial plexus with capillary loops in each dermal papilla, plus glomus arteriovenous shunts in acral skin.
parts.f: Nutrition of the epidermis and control of heat loss by shunting blood.
parts.c: Opening the shunts flushes and cools; closing them in cold makes fingers pale — exaggerated in Raynaud phenomenon.

parts.d: Deep single proliferative keratinocyte layer adjoining basement membrane.
parts.f: Renews overlying epidermis.
parts.c: Basal-cell carcinoma derives from basal-type cells.

parts.d: Several layers of keratinocytes strongly joined by desmosomes.
parts.f: Provides mechanical cohesion.
parts.c: Desmosomal disruption causes epidermal blistering.

parts.d: Flattened keratinocytes with keratohyalin granules and lipid-releasing lamellar bodies.
parts.f: Builds the water-permeability barrier.
parts.c: Barrier injury increases transepidermal water loss.

parts.d: Thin translucent transition zone most apparent in glabrous palms and soles.
parts.f: Adds specialized layer in thick skin.
parts.c: Do not expect a distinct lucidum in ordinary thin hairy skin.

parts.d: Anchoring complex joining epidermis to dermis with hemidesmosomes and matrix.
parts.f: Resists separation and supports renewal.
parts.c: Plane of separation distinguishes blister disorders.

parts.d: Fingerlike papillary dermal projections interlocking with epidermal ridges.
parts.f: Increase attachment surface and house capillary loops.
parts.c: Rete ridge pattern varies by body site.

parts.d: Superficial loose connective tissue with capillaries and fine collagen.
parts.f: Nourishes avascular epidermis by diffusion.
parts.c: Superficial wounds may preserve deep appendages.

parts.d: Deeper dense irregular collagen-and-elastin connective tissue.
parts.f: Provides tensile strength and elasticity.
parts.c: Full-thickness injury through reticular dermis commonly scars.

parts.d: Adipose lobules and connective septa deep to the dermis.
parts.f: Insulation, cushioning and movable attachment.
parts.c: Not one of the histologic dermal layers.

parts.d: The slender upper horns receiving sensory afferents; laminae I–VI including the substantia gelatinosa.
parts.f: First synapse for pain, temperature and touch; gate control of nociception happens here.
parts.c: Loss of the spinothalamic decussation at a segment causes a segmental band of lost pain and temperature (syringomyelia).

parts.d: The broad lower horns containing the lower motor neuron cell bodies and Renshaw cells.
parts.f: Final common pathway: alpha motor neurons innervate skeletal muscle.
parts.c: Poliovirus and ALS destroy these cells, giving flaccid paralysis, wasting and fasciculation.

parts.d: Present only in T1–L2, holding preganglionic sympathetic neurons (and S2–S4 parasympathetic equivalents).
parts.f: Origin of the sympathetic outflow.
parts.c: Horner syndrome follows interruption of the T1 lateral horn or its pathway (e.g. Pancoast tumour).

parts.d: The ependyma-lined remnant of the neural tube lumen, continuous with the fourth ventricle.
parts.f: Circulates a trickle of CSF within the cord.
parts.c: Its dilatation defines syringomyelia, classically causing a cape-like loss of pain and temperature.

parts.d: Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus), lateral spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts.
parts.f: Highways for sensation upward and motor commands downward.
parts.c: B12 deficiency (subacute combined degeneration) damages dorsal columns and corticospinal tracts together.

parts.d: The tough outer sleeve, ending as the dural sac at S2 with the filum terminale beyond.
parts.f: Protects and forms the epidural and subarachnoid boundaries.
parts.c: Epidural anaesthesia deposits drug outside it; a dural puncture headache follows CSF leak from within.

parts.d: The web-like middle layer; the subarachnoid space beneath holds CSF and the cord's vessels.
parts.f: CSF cushion and nutrient exchange.
parts.c: Lumbar puncture samples CSF here below L2, where only the cauda equina floats.

parts.d: The delicate inner layer adherent to the cord, throwing out toothed lateral ligaments to the dura.
parts.f: Suspends the cord centrally in CSF.
parts.c: The ligaments are the surgical landmark between anterior and posterior roots.

parts.d: Sensory rootlets converging on the oval dorsal root ganglion of pseudo-unipolar cell bodies.
parts.f: Carries all afferent input from one dermatome.
parts.c: Shingles (zoster) reactivates in a ganglion, giving a dermatomal vesicular rash.

parts.d: Motor rootlets from the anterior horn joining the dorsal root at the intervertebral foramen.
parts.f: Carries motor and preganglionic autonomic fibres out.
parts.c: Root compression by a prolapsed disc causes radicular pain in the matching dermatome and myotome.

parts.d: The mixed nerve formed by union of the roots, dividing at once into dorsal and ventral rami.
parts.f: Supplies one segment of body wall and limb.
parts.c: 31 pairs: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal — cervical nerves are numbered above their vertebra.

parts.d: Deep longitudinal ventral groove of cord containing the anterior spinal arterial course.
parts.f: Separates right and left anterior funiculi.
parts.c: Helps orient cord cross-sections.

parts.d: Shallow dorsal midline groove separating posterior columns.
parts.f: Marks posterior sensory pathway division.
parts.c: A lesion here can affect dorsal-column modalities.

parts.d: Medial ascending dorsal-column tract carrying lower-body touch and proprioception.
parts.f: Projects to gracile nucleus in medulla.
parts.c: Posterior-column injury impairs vibration and joint-position sense.

parts.d: Lateral dorsal-column tract above about T6 carrying upper-body sensory input.
parts.f: Projects to cuneate nucleus in medulla.
parts.c: Absent below upper thoracic levels.

parts.d: Descending motor fibers in lateral funiculus after pyramidal decussation.
parts.f: Controls skilled voluntary movement, especially distal limbs.
parts.c: Damage produces ipsilateral upper-motor-neuron signs below cord lesion.

parts.d: Ascending axons carrying pain, temperature and crude touch after segmental crossing.
parts.f: Transmits nociceptive signals to higher centers.
parts.c: Cord hemisection produces contralateral pain-temperature loss below lesion.

parts.d: Single midline vessel supplying much of anterior two-thirds of cord.
parts.f: Perfuses anterior horns and many descending tracts.
parts.c: Infarction can spare dorsal-column sensation.

parts.d: Paired longitudinal vessels supplying dorsal cord regions.
parts.f: Support posterior columns and dorsal horns.
parts.c: Segmental arterial input varies by level.

parts.d: Tapered end of adult spinal cord, usually near L1–L2 vertebral level.
parts.f: Contains terminal sacral cord segments.
parts.c: Compression may cause saddle sensory and sphincter symptoms.

parts.d: Pial strand descending from conus to coccygeal anchoring tissues.
parts.f: Stabilizes caudal cord within dural sac.
parts.c: A thickened tethering filum can restrict cord movement.

parts.d: Bundle of descending lumbar, sacral and coccygeal nerve roots below conus.
parts.f: Conveys motor, sensory and autonomic fibers to lower body.
parts.c: Compression is a neurosurgical emergency.

parts.d: 250–300 lobules of coiled seminiferous tubules (total ~250 m) with Sertoli cells and developing germ cells, wrapped in tunica albuginea.
parts.f: Spermatogenesis and testosterone production.
parts.c: Undescended testis (cryptorchidism) raises infertility and germ-cell tumour risk; torsion is a 6-hour surgical emergency.

parts.d: A 6 m coiled duct (head, body, tail) applied to the posterior border of the testis.
parts.f: Sperm maturation, motility acquisition and storage (up to weeks).
parts.c: A common site of infection (epididymitis) and of obstruction after vasectomy or infection.

parts.d: A thick-walled 45 cm muscular duct from the epididymal tail, through the inguinal canal into the pelvis.
parts.f: Propels sperm by powerful peristalsis at emission.
parts.c: Vasectomy divides it for contraception; sperm granulomas may form at the cut ends.

parts.d: A coiled sac behind the bladder whose duct joins the vas to form the ejaculatory duct.
parts.f: Adds ~60% of semen volume: fructose, prostaglandins and clotting proteins.
parts.c: Its fructose is the energy source for sperm and a marker of ejaculatory duct patency.

parts.d: A walnut-sized fibromuscular gland around the urethra below the bladder, with peripheral, central and transition zones.
parts.f: Secretes citrate, zinc and PSA that liquefy the seminal coagulum.
parts.c: Benign hyperplasia of the transition zone obstructs voiding; most cancers arise in the peripheral zone (felt on DRE).

parts.d: Pea-sized glands (of Cowper) in the deep perineal pouch opening into the spongy urethra.
parts.f: Secrete pre-ejaculate mucus that lubricates and neutralises urethral acidity.
parts.c: Pre-ejaculate can carry sperm, which is why withdrawal is unreliable contraception.

parts.d: Prostatic, membranous and spongy (penile) parts, ~20 cm long.
parts.f: Common channel for urine and semen.
parts.c: Strictures commonly follow catheterisation or gonococcal infection at the bulbar urethra.

parts.d: Two corpora cavernosa and one corpus spongiosum enclosing the urethra, ending in the glans.
parts.f: Erection by parasympathetic NO-mediated vasodilatation and venous occlusion; ejaculation by sympathetic emission plus somatic expulsion.
parts.c: PDE5 inhibitors potentiate the NO–cGMP pathway; priapism over 4 hours threatens the corpora.

parts.d: Skin and dartos muscle housing the testes, with the pampiniform venous plexus acting as a counter-current cooler.
parts.f: Keeps spermatogenesis at ~34 °C.
parts.c: Pampiniform varices (varicocele, usually left) cause a "bag of worms" and impaired fertility.

parts.d: Sits above the prostate; the vas and ureters pass behind it.
parts.f: Urinary reservoir sharing the urethral outlet.
parts.c: An enlarged prostate elevates its floor, seen as a raised "J" of the ureteric orifices at cystoscopy.

parts.d: Serous covering with visceral and parietal layers.
parts.f: Allows mobile testis within scrotum.
parts.c: Fluid accumulation in the cavity forms a hydrocele.

parts.d: Smooth-muscle outlet superior to prostate.
parts.f: Closes during emission to limit retrograde ejaculation.
parts.c: Bladder-neck dysfunction may affect voiding.

parts.d: Two dorsal longitudinal erectile cylinders that unite in shaft and separate proximally as crura.
parts.f: Primary rigid erectile compartment.
parts.c: Fibrous tunica helps compress emissary venous outflow.

parts.d: Dense white capsule under tunica vaginalis.
parts.f: Partitions testis into lobules via septa.
parts.c: Traumatic rupture may require urgent evaluation.

parts.d: Zone surrounding proximal prostatic urethra.
parts.f: Contains glandular ducts and fibromuscular tissue.
parts.c: Common origin of benign prostatic enlargement.

parts.d: Single ventral erectile column surrounding spongy urethra.
parts.f: Engorges without compressing urethral lumen closed.
parts.c: Its distal expansion is the glans penis.

parts.d: Posterior thickening of albuginea containing rete testis.
parts.f: Organizes lobules and duct outflow.
parts.c: Important landmark in testicular ultrasound.

parts.d: Posterior-lateral zone palpable through rectum.
parts.f: Produces prostatic secretions.
parts.c: Most prostatic cancers arise in this zone.

parts.d: Smooth-muscle and connective-tissue struts bordering interconnected blood sinusoids.
parts.f: Relaxation permits filling of cavernous lacunae.
parts.c: Vascular dysfunction can impair rigidity.

parts.d: Septa divide testis into lobules containing seminiferous tubules.
parts.f: Compartmentalize sperm production.
parts.c: Germ-cell tumors often distort intratesticular architecture.

parts.d: The domed fundus above the tubal openings and the tapering body, of smooth muscle (myometrium) lined by endometrium.
parts.f: Houses and nourishes a pregnancy; the myometrium generates labour.
parts.c: Fibroids (leiomyomas) arise in the myometrium and cause heavy bleeding and pressure symptoms.

parts.d: A functional layer of glands and stroma that proliferates under oestrogen and becomes secretory under progesterone, plus a permanent basal layer.
parts.f: Site of implantation; sheds each cycle if no embryo implants.
parts.c: Ectopic endometrium (endometriosis) causes cyclical pain and infertility; unopposed oestrogen drives hyperplasia and carcinoma.

parts.d: The fibrous neck projecting into the vagina, with an endocervical canal of mucus-secreting columnar epithelium and a squamous ectocervix.
parts.f: Keeps pregnancy in and microbes out; dilates 10 cm in labour.
parts.c: The squamocolumnar junction is where cervical cancer begins — the target of smear tests and HPV vaccination.

parts.d: A fibromuscular canal lined by glycogen-rich stratified squamous epithelium, angled back over the levator plate.
parts.f: Birth canal, menstrual outlet and copulatory organ; lactobacilli keep pH ~4.
parts.c: The acidic pH protects against infection; antibiotics and oestrogen loss can allow candidiasis.

parts.d: A 10 cm ciliated duct with interstitial, isthmic, ampullary and infundibular parts.
parts.f: Captures the oocyte, is the site of fertilisation (ampulla) and transports the embryo by ciliary beat and peristalsis.
parts.c: Damage from infection (PID) or surgery is the main cause of ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility.

parts.d: Finger-like projections around the tubal opening, one (fimbria ovarica) attached to the ovary.
parts.f: Sweep the oocyte into the tube at ovulation.
parts.c: Fimbrial epithelium is now recognised as the origin of many "ovarian" high-grade serous cancers.

parts.d: An almond of stroma holding the follicle pool, covered by germinal epithelium and suspended by the mesovarium.
parts.f: Ovulation and secretion of oestradiol, progesterone and inhibin.
parts.c: Polycystic ovaries show peripheral follicles with anovulation; epithelial tumours are the silent gynaecological cancer.

parts.d: Primordial → primary → antral → dominant (Graafian) follicle; after ovulation the remnant becomes the progesterone-secreting corpus luteum, then corpus albicans.
parts.f: Produces the oocyte and the cycle's hormones.
parts.c: A follicle that fails to rupture forms a follicular cyst; a persistent luteum forms a corpus luteum cyst.

parts.d: Peritoneal folds (broad, round, ovarian, suspensory) carrying the tubes, vessels and ureters.
parts.f: Suspend the uterus and convey its vessels.
parts.c: The ureter runs under the uterine artery ("water under the bridge") — the classic injury point in hysterectomy.

parts.d: Dome above the two tubal openings.
parts.f: Expands in pregnancy; fundal position is an obstetric landmark.
parts.c: Fundal height is a rough gestational growth marker.

parts.d: Part of cervix visible at the vaginal vault.
parts.f: Covered by nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium.
parts.c: Visual examination and directed biopsy sample this surface.

parts.d: Outer ovarian zone with follicles at several stages.
parts.f: Houses the oocyte reserve.
parts.c: Cortical tissue is considered in fertility-preserving surgery.

parts.d: Potential space whose walls normally lie against one another.
parts.f: Passage for menstrual flow, intercourse and birth.
parts.c: Distensibility varies; do not interpret the lumen as a permanently open tube.

parts.d: Fatty pad over pubic symphysis.
parts.f: Cushions pubic bone.
parts.c: Normal hair pattern and contour vary widely.

parts.d: Main muscular region between fundus and isthmus.
parts.f: Houses uterine cavity and contracts during labor.
parts.c: Fibroids often arise here and may distort the cavity.

parts.d: Canal linking internal to external os.
parts.f: Conducts sperm and menstrual flow; glandular mucus changes cyclically.
parts.c: Stenosis may obstruct sampling or menstrual outflow.

parts.d: Central vascular stromal zone.
parts.f: Supports vessels, nerves and the hilum.
parts.c: Ovarian pedicle bleeding arises at the hilum.

parts.d: Shorter wall adjoining bladder base and urethra.
parts.f: Provides anterior pelvic support.
parts.c: Anterior compartment weakness may be associated with cystocele.

parts.d: Outer skin folds containing fat and connective tissue.
parts.f: Protect the vestibule and inner folds.
parts.c: Vulvar lymph largely drains to superficial inguinal nodes.

parts.d: Upper lateral junctions where uterine tubes enter.
parts.f: Communicate with intramural tube segments.
parts.c: Interstitial ectopic pregnancy arises near the cornu.

parts.d: Control centre housed in the skull, glowing through the translucent scalp.
parts.f: Integrates sensation, movement, thought, memory and autonomic drive.
parts.c: Stroke risk rises with age — remember FAST: face, arms, speech, time.

parts.d: Butterfly-shaped gland on the front of the neck.
parts.f: Sets metabolic rate via T3/T4 under TSH control.
parts.c: Hypothyroidism causes fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance.

parts.d: Paired thoracic organs flanking the heart.
parts.f: Gas exchange across ~300 million alveoli.
parts.c: Smoking destroys alveolar walls → emphysema.

parts.d: Muscular pump in the mediastinum, a little left of midline.
parts.f: Drives about 5 L of blood per minute through two circuits.
parts.c: Coronary blockage causes myocardial infarction.

parts.d: Largest internal organ, right upper quadrant.
parts.f: Metabolism, detoxification, bile, plasma proteins.
parts.c: Cirrhosis scars the parenchyma (alcohol, hepatitis).

parts.d: J-shaped reservoir under the diaphragm, left side.
parts.f: Acid–pepsin digestion; intrinsic factor for B12.
parts.c: H. pylori is the commonest cause of peptic ulcer.

parts.d: Small and large intestine coiling through the abdomen.
parts.f: Absorbs nutrients, water, electrolytes; hosts the microbiome.
parts.c: Obstruction and appendicitis present as acute pain.

parts.d: Pelvic reservoir behind the pubic symphysis.
parts.f: Stores urine; stretch triggers the micturition reflex.
parts.c: Frequency + dysuria usually mean infection.

parts.d: External organ of urination and copulation.
parts.f: Erectile tissue engorges; delivers semen.
parts.c: Erectile dysfunction is an early vascular warning sign.

parts.d: Paired gonads in the scrotum, outside the body cavity.
parts.f: Spermatogenesis and testosterone production.
parts.c: Undescended testis raises malignancy risk.

parts.d: Paired retroperitoneal organs on either side of the upper lumbar spine.
parts.f: Filter plasma and regulate fluid, electrolytes and blood pressure.
parts.c: The right kidney commonly sits slightly lower than the left.

parts.d: Elongated gland behind the stomach from duodenum toward spleen.
parts.f: Produces digestive enzymes and endocrine hormones.
parts.c: Deep retroperitoneal relationships matter in abdominal imaging.

parts.d: Immune organ in the left upper abdomen below the diaphragm.
parts.f: Filters blood and supports immune responses.
parts.c: Blunt left-sided trauma can damage this vascular organ.

parts.d: Small endocrine glands positioned above each kidney.
parts.f: Secrete corticosteroids and catecholamines.
parts.c: Their deep position cannot be verified from the surface figure.

parts.d: Gland below the bladder surrounding the proximal urethra.
parts.f: Adds secretions to semen.
parts.c: The prostate is not a visible surface organ.

parts.d: Paired glands behind the bladder and above the prostate.
parts.f: Supply fluid contributing to semen.
parts.c: Adjacent anatomy is better studied in a focused male pelvic plate.

parts.d: Long coiled duct lying along the posterior side of each testis.
parts.f: Allows sperm maturation and storage.
parts.c: Scrotal position does not reveal the individual microscopic duct coils.

parts.d: Dome-shaped muscle separating thoracic and abdominal cavities.
parts.f: Principal muscle for quiet inspiration.
parts.c: Only a cross-section can show its full internal attachment pattern.

parts.d: Central nervous tissue inside the vertebral canal.
parts.f: Relays sensory and motor signals to and from the brain.
parts.c: A whole-body surface figure cannot resolve spinal tracts.

parts.d: Largest arterial trunk descends from the heart into the abdomen.
parts.f: Supplies oxygenated blood through its branches.
parts.c: Deep arterial branches require dedicated vascular diagrams.

parts.d: Control centre housed in the skull, glowing through the translucent scalp.
parts.f: Integrates sensation, movement, thought, memory and autonomic drive.
parts.c: Stroke risk rises with age — remember FAST: face, arms, speech, time.

parts.f: Sets metabolic rate via T3/T4 under TSH control.
parts.c: Hypothyroidism causes fatigue, weight gain and cold intolerance.

parts.d: Pelvic reservoir behind the pubic symphysis.
parts.f: Stores urine; stretch triggers the micturition reflex.
parts.c: Frequency + dysuria usually mean infection.

parts.d: Glandular tissue over the pectoral muscles.
parts.f: Milk production in lobules under prolactin control.
parts.c: New lump + skin change needs imaging.

parts.d: Muscular pear-shaped organ of the pelvis.
parts.f: Houses and nourishes a developing fetus; menstrual cycle.
parts.c: Fibroids cause heavy bleeding — benign but common.

parts.d: Paired gonads either side of the uterus.
parts.f: Ovulation; oestrogen and progesterone secretion.
parts.c: Persistent bloating — rule out ovarian cancer.

parts.d: Paired retroperitoneal organs beside the upper lumbar spine.
parts.f: Filter plasma and regulate fluid, electrolytes and blood pressure.
parts.c: Both kidneys belong in the body overview regardless of sex.

parts.d: Elongated gland behind the stomach from duodenum toward spleen.
parts.f: Provides digestive enzymes and endocrine hormones.
parts.c: Not separately discernible on this whole-body illustration.

parts.d: Vascular immune organ in the left upper abdomen.
parts.f: Filters blood and supports immune responses.
parts.c: A focused organ plate provides clearer boundaries.

parts.d: Endocrine glands positioned on the superior aspects of the kidneys.
parts.f: Release corticosteroids and catecholamines.
parts.c: Their deep position cannot be localized on a surface view.

parts.d: Lower part of the uterus projecting into the upper vagina.
parts.f: Connects uterine cavity with the vaginal canal.
parts.c: The transformation zone requires dedicated cervical study, not a surface label.

parts.d: Paired tubes extend from the uterine horns toward the ovaries.
parts.f: Carry the oocyte; fertilization commonly occurs in the ampulla.
parts.c: Internal tubal details are not visible on a body silhouette.

parts.d: Muscular canal from the cervix to the vaginal opening.
parts.f: Forms an outlet for menstrual flow and a birth canal.
parts.c: The vagina is internal; the vulva names external genital structures.

parts.d: Dome-shaped muscle separating thorax and abdomen.
parts.f: Principal muscle for quiet inspiration.
parts.c: Individual muscle attachments require a deeper plate.

parts.d: Central nervous tissue within the vertebral canal.
parts.f: Relays motor, sensory and autonomic signals.
parts.c: Spinal tracts are microscopic and cannot be resolved on this overview.

parts.d: Cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem inside the cranial vault.
parts.f: Integration, consciousness, motor planning and autonomic control.
parts.c: Head injury scales from concussion to diffuse axonal injury.

parts.d: Hindbrain structure behind the brainstem.
parts.f: Coordination, balance and motor learning.
parts.c: Lesion → intention tremor and ataxia on the same side.

parts.d: Midbrain, pons and medulla connecting cord to brain.
parts.f: Vital centres: respiration, heart rate, consciousness.
parts.c: Brainstem death is legal death in most jurisdictions.

parts.d: 31-segment cord from foramen magnum to L1–L2.
parts.f: Two-way tracts plus segmental reflex circuits.
parts.c: Cord transection level predicts deficit pattern precisely.

parts.d: Nerve network in the posterior triangle of the neck.
parts.f: Neck muscles and skin; phrenic nerve to diaphragm.
parts.c: C3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive — injury above C4 stops breathing.

parts.d: Roots-trunks-divisions-cords-branches behind the clavicle.
parts.f: All motor and sensory supply of the upper limb.
parts.c: Erb's palsy (C5-6) from birth traction: waiter's-tip hand.

parts.d: Ventral rami running in subcostal grooves.
parts.f: Chest-wall muscles and segmental skin band.
parts.c: Shingles follows one intercostal dermatome.

parts.d: Network within psoas major.
parts.f: Anterior thigh and medial leg supply.
parts.c: Femoral nerve block anaesthetises the anterior thigh.

parts.d: Plexus on the piriformis wall of the pelvis.
parts.f: Gluteal region, perineum and the sciatic nerve.
parts.c: Sciatica radiates along its branches down the leg.

parts.d: Largest nerve in the body (L4–S3).
parts.f: Hamstrings and all muscles below the knee.
parts.c: Wrong gluteal injection site can injure it — use upper outer quadrant.

parts.d: L2–L4 branch under the inguinal ligament.
parts.f: Quadriceps power and anterior-thigh sensation.
parts.c: Loss → buckling knee and absent knee jerk.

parts.d: Chain of ganglia from skull base to coccyx.
parts.f: Fight-or-flight: heart up, gut down, pupils wide.
parts.c: Horner's syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis.

parts.d: Longest cranial nerve, neck to pelvis.
parts.f: Parasympathetic brake on heart, lungs and gut.
parts.c: Vagal stimulation terminates SVT — the Valsalva trick.

parts.d: Sensory cell-body cluster on each dorsal root.
parts.f: Houses pseudounipolar sensory neurons.
parts.c: Varicella hides here and re-emerges as shingles.

parts.d: Neuronal cell-body sheet folded into gyri and sulci.
parts.f: Integrates sensory, motor and association information.
parts.c: Regional cortical lesions give different deficits.

parts.d: Rostral brainstem around cerebral aqueduct between diencephalon and pons.
parts.f: Hosts III/IV-related nuclei and visual/auditory orienting circuits.
parts.c: Midbrain lesions can combine ocular and long-tract signs.

parts.d: Five spinal nerve ventral rami build the typical plexus; not the intrathecal dorsal/ventral rootlets.
parts.f: Provide segmental motor and sensory fibers to upper limb.
parts.c: Anatomy can be prefixed C4–C8 or postfixed C6–T2.

parts.d: Superficial neuropil-rich layer below pia, with relatively few neuronal somata.
parts.f: Supports horizontal intracortical connections.
parts.c: Six-layer plan is a template, not identical in every area.

parts.d: Dorsal midbrain paired structure.
parts.f: Coordinates orienting eye/head movements to visual stimuli.
parts.c: Not the origin of the optic nerve.

parts.d: Roots and trunks pass between anterior and middle scalene muscles.
parts.f: Conveys plexus out of neck.
parts.c: Site of interscalene regional anesthesia.

parts.d: Parasympathetic fibers from sacral levels S2–S4 travel to pelvic autonomic plexuses.
parts.f: Reach bladder, rectal and reproductive pelvic organ targets.
parts.c: Do not confuse these autonomic fibers with somatic pudendal branches.

parts.d: Paired networks on the lateral walls of the rectum combine sympathetic and parasympathetic fibers.
parts.f: Distribute autonomic pathways to pelvic organs.
parts.c: Operations near these plexuses can affect urinary or sexual function.

parts.d: Descending autonomic connections between the superior and inferior hypogastric plexuses.
parts.f: Convey predominantly sympathetic pathways into the pelvis.
parts.c: Do not equate them with the somatic pudendal nerve.

parts.d: Paired somatic S2–S4 nerve passes through the pudendal canal toward the perineum.

parts.d: Fibrous seams joining frontal to parietal, and right to left parietal bones.
parts.f: Stabilize the cranial vault.
parts.c: Sutures are not additional counted bones.

parts.d: Part of the tooth covered by enamel, even if gingiva later covers a small portion. The clinical crown is the portion exposed in the mouth.
parts.f: Offers a cutting or grinding surface depending on tooth class.
parts.c: Do not confuse anatomical crown with clinical crown.

parts.d: Highly mineralized outer cover of the crown, shown white above the gum; enamel does not normally cover the root.
parts.f: Protects deeper dentin from wear and acid, though it can demineralize.
parts.c: Once mature enamel is lost, it does not regrow as an intact enamel layer.

parts.d: Yellowish tissue beneath crown enamel and root cementum; surrounds pulp throughout the tooth.
parts.f: Supports the crown and houses dentinal tubules.
parts.c: Exposed dentin can be sensitive and is more vulnerable than enamel.

parts.d: Scalloped interface between the crown enamel shell and underlying dentin.
parts.f: Bonds two different mineralized tissues and transfers forces.
parts.c: This interface is a boundary, not a separate layer visible in every digital plate.

parts.d: Central space in the crown holding vascular, neural and connective dental pulp; its roof lies under occlusal dentin.
parts.f: Supports tooth vitality, defense and dentin formation.
parts.c: Deep caries can inflame pulp; a digital cutaway cannot diagnose pulp disease.

parts.d: Small coronal projections of the pulp chamber toward the cusp tips, variable with tooth type and age.
parts.f: Bring living pulp close to coronal dentin.
parts.c: Young permanent teeth often have more prominent pulp horns; do not pin them without a clear boundary.

parts.d: Portion anchored below the crown in an alveolar socket; molar roots may be multiple but number and canal shape vary.
parts.f: Anchors the tooth through periodontal ligament and cementum.
parts.c: A generic two-root cutaway cannot represent the root anatomy of every tooth.

parts.d: Narrow continuation of the pulp space inside each root, opening toward its apex.
parts.f: Conveys pulpal nerve and blood supply through the root.
parts.c: Extra canals and variation matter in clinical endodontics; this illustration is only a model.

parts.d: Tiny opening near a root tip where neurovascular tissues enter or leave the canal.
parts.f: Connects root pulp with tissues outside the tooth.
parts.c: Not all accessory foramina can be identified on this rendering.

parts.d: Thin mineralized covering of root dentin below the cervical region, not a white enamel coat.
parts.f: Provides attachment for periodontal ligament fibers.
parts.c: It is too thin to accurately mark as an individual pixel band in this model.

parts.d: Fibrous interface between root cementum and the alveolar socket wall.
parts.f: Suspends the tooth and helps absorb chewing forces.
parts.c: A widened periodontal space on a radiograph needs clinical interpretation.

parts.d: Jawbone forming the root socket around the periodontal ligament; the trabecular texture is shown beside roots.
parts.f: Supports roots and remodels with function.
parts.c: Alveolar bone is part of the maxilla or mandible, not another tooth layer.

parts.d: Pink gum tissue encircling the neck of the tooth and covering the alveolar process.
parts.f: Forms a protective soft-tissue collar around the tooth.
parts.c: Inflammation and recession need an actual dental examination, not this model.

parts.d: Cervical transition where crown enamel meets root cementum near the gingival margin.
parts.f: Separates anatomical crown from root.
parts.c: The visible gum line is not always at the anatomical cementoenamel junction.

parts.d: Cusp-bearing chewing surface of posterior teeth such as premolars and molars.
parts.f: Crushes and grinds food in contact with opposing teeth.
parts.c: An incisor has an incisal edge rather than a broad posterior occlusal table.

parts.d: Raised occlusal peaks separated by developmental grooves; arrangement differs by maxillary or mandibular molar and by tooth.
parts.f: Distribute chewing contacts across a broad posterior crown.
parts.c: Do not use this particular cutaway to count cusps of another molar.

parts.d: Region where the two depicted roots diverge below the crown; not present in single-root teeth.
parts.f: Separates root surfaces in a multi-root tooth.
parts.c: Periodontal disease can expose furcations, especially around molars.

parts.d: Mesial faces the midline of the dental arch; distal faces away from it. They are relative tooth surfaces, not fixed left/right labels.
parts.f: Define contact relationships between neighboring teeth.
parts.c: Avoid swapping mesial and distal when changing the jaw or side.

parts.d: Facial surface faces lip or cheek; lingual faces tongue (called palatal on the upper arch).
parts.f: Orient individual teeth in the dental arch.
parts.c: Naming tooth surfaces is separate from numbering a tooth.

parts.d: Posterior, often middle, and anterior superior alveolar branches of the maxillary division supply upper teeth; their branching varies.
parts.f: Carry pulpal and periodontal sensory fibers from maxillary teeth.
parts.c: The middle superior alveolar nerve is variable and may be absent; no individual V2 branch is identifiable on the generic tooth image.

parts.d: Mandibular division branch entering the mandibular foramen and canal; dental branches serve lower teeth.
parts.f: Carries sensory fibers from mandibular teeth; its terminal mental branch supplies chin and lower lip.
parts.c: CN VII facial motor branches do not supply pulpal sensation to the teeth.

parts.d: Small red and yellow vessels/fibers travel through the jaw near the root tips into the pulp canals.
parts.f: Maintain pulp blood supply and relay tooth sensation.
parts.c: The digital model depicts a general path, not a precise named nerve or artery.

parts.d: The usual primary dentition has 20 teeth; the conventional full permanent dentition has 32 including third molars.
parts.f: Primary teeth support chewing, speech and the developing dental arches.
parts.c: Congenitally absent, unerupted and removed third molars make individual adult counts variable.

parts.d: Universal 1–32 names permanent teeth and A–T primary teeth in US practice; two-digit FDI identifies quadrant and position internationally.
parts.f: Lets students locate a tooth unambiguously before describing its anatomy.
parts.c: The chart is viewed facing the patient: the patient’s right appears at the viewer’s left.
