parts.f: Provides a consistent reference for locations and movements.
parts.c: Prone or supine patients retain anatomical left and right.

parts.d: Right and left always refer to the subject; on an anterior image, patient right usually appears on the viewer’s left.
parts.f: Prevents reversal when describing a structure or reading a map.
parts.c: Check image-view conventions before labeling a side on a scan.

parts.d: Vertical plane through the midline dividing the body into equal right and left halves. The translucent sheet is a conceptual aid.
parts.f: Defines exact midline relationships.
parts.c: Do not confuse sagittal with a front-versus-back coronal section.

parts.d: Any sagittal plane parallel to but displaced from the midline, yielding unequal left and right portions.
parts.f: Locates off-center section views.
parts.c: An off-center sagittal CT or MRI is not a median image.

parts.d: Vertical plane dividing anterior and posterior portions; shown by a translucent sheet, not a real tissue boundary.
parts.f: Organizes front-to-back relationships.
parts.c: Coronal scans can show both kidneys and the spine on one slice.

parts.d: Plane perpendicular to the long axis of an upright body, dividing superior and inferior portions.
parts.f: Explains cross-sections and many CT/MRI slices.
parts.c: Image display orientation must be checked rather than guessed.

parts.d: A section angled relative to standard sagittal, coronal and transverse planes.
parts.f: Follows a structure that does not lie in a cardinal plane.
parts.c: Oblique imaging can change apparent shape and size.

parts.d: Anterior points toward the front of the body; posterior toward the back, in anatomical position.
parts.f: Describes depth along the front-to-back axis.
parts.c: The sternum is anterior to the heart; the spine is posterior to it.

parts.d: Superior indicates nearer the head; inferior nearer the feet when the body is in standard anatomical position.
parts.f: Orders structures along the long axis of the body.
parts.c: The diaphragm lies inferior to the lungs.

parts.d: Medial is closer to the median plane; lateral is farther toward a side.
parts.f: Compares transverse location without depending on the viewer.
parts.c: The thumb is lateral in anatomical position.

parts.d: Proximal is nearer a limb’s attachment to the trunk; distal farther away along the limb.
parts.f: Describes relative position along a limb.
parts.c: The elbow is proximal to the wrist.

parts.d: Superficial is closer to the external body surface; deep is farther within.
parts.f: Separates skin, muscle, bone and deeper organs.
parts.c: Deep does not mean the structure is always visible in an illustration.

parts.d: Ipsilateral structures lie on the same side; contralateral structures lie on opposite sides of the body.
parts.f: Describes side-to-side clinical relationships.
parts.c: A left brain motor pathway usually controls contralateral limb muscles.

parts.d: Flexion generally decreases the angle between articulating segments; extension generally increases it. Direction can differ by joint.
parts.f: Describes common sagittal-plane motions at limb joints.
parts.c: At the knee, flexion bends the leg posteriorly; use joint-specific terminology.

parts.d: Abduction moves away from the body’s median plane; adduction moves toward it, with hand and foot digits referenced to their own axes.
parts.f: Describes movement in the frontal plane at many joints.
parts.c: Finger abduction uses the middle finger as its reference axis.

parts.d: A limb rotates about its long axis toward or away from the body midline; joint position and axis must be specified.
parts.f: Describes shoulder and hip rotations.
parts.c: Do not equate axial rotation with limb abduction.

parts.d: Combined sequence of flexion, abduction, extension and adduction that traces a cone with the distal segment.
parts.f: Integrates movement around a multiaxial joint.
parts.c: It is a combination of motions, not a separately spinning bone.

parts.d: Forearm pronation rotates the radius across the ulna to turn the palm posteriorly in anatomical position; supination restores the palm anteriorly.
parts.f: Orientates the hand while radius and ulna move at radioulnar joints.
parts.c: Elbow flexion changes apparent palm orientation in space, not the definition.

parts.d: Dorsiflexion brings the dorsum of the foot toward the leg; plantarflexion points the foot downward.
parts.f: Describes ankle motion during gait.
parts.c: These terms apply at the ankle, not to inversion at the subtalar complex.

parts.d: Inversion turns the sole toward the midline; eversion turns it outward, across the hindfoot and midfoot joints.
parts.f: Describes sole orientation on uneven ground.
parts.c: Do not confuse inversion with internal rotation at the hip.

parts.d: Thumb moves across the palm so its pad approaches a finger pad; reposition is the return movement.
parts.f: Enables precision pinch and grasp.
parts.c: Median-nerve injury can impair thumb opposition.

parts.d: Externally palpable landmarks such as the clavicle, sternum and iliac crest orient deeper structures.
parts.f: Connects real surface examination with three-dimensional anatomy.
parts.c: A visible skin mark is not proof of a deep organ’s exact boundary.

parts.d: A cross-sectional image depicts a slice; a radiographic projection superimposes structures along the X-ray beam.
parts.f: Prevents confusing slice depth with an overlaid projection.
parts.c: Never map an unseen internal structure to an arbitrary pixel on this plane model.

parts.d: People differ in organ, vessel, muscle and nerve branching; the schematic reference stance is not a patient-specific map.
parts.f: Encourages cautious interpretation of generic teaching illustrations.
parts.c: Atypical anatomy needs appropriate clinical assessment when relevant.

parts.d: Posterior continuous compartment composed of cranial and vertebral cavities, with brain and spinal cord inside.
parts.f: Protects central nervous tissue.
parts.c: A deep nerve root is not automatically inside the peritoneal cavity.

parts.d: Intracranial space enclosed by cranial bones, containing brain, meninges, vessels and cerebrospinal-fluid spaces.
parts.f: Shields the brain and supports intracranial structures.
parts.c: Intracranial pressure is clinically important after injury.

parts.d: Canal within the vertebral column containing spinal cord, meninges, nerve roots and their surroundings.
parts.f: Protects neural tissue while permitting spinal roots to exit.
parts.c: Cord commonly ends near L1–L2 in adults, though level varies.

parts.d: Anterior body compartment conventionally divided by the diaphragm into thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities.
parts.f: Contains major viscera with room for organ movement.
parts.c: It is a teaching subdivision, not one unbroken serous sac.

parts.d: Within the chest wall above the diaphragm; includes the two pleural cavities and mediastinum.
parts.f: Houses lungs, heart and major vessels.
parts.c: A lung is not inside the mediastinum.

parts.d: Thin potential spaces between visceral and parietal pleura surrounding each lung separately.
parts.f: Permit low-friction lung movement.
parts.c: Air or fluid in a pleural space can impair lung expansion.

parts.d: Central thoracic compartment between the two pleural sacs, from sternum to vertebral column.
parts.f: Contains heart, great vessels, trachea and esophagus.
parts.c: The heart is in the middle mediastinum within the pericardial sac.

parts.d: Potential space between visceral and parietal serous pericardium around the heart.
parts.f: Reduces friction as the heart beats.
parts.c: Excess fluid may restrict cardiac filling.

parts.d: Musculotendinous partition between thoracic and abdominopelvic cavities, with passageways for major structures.
parts.f: Principal muscle of quiet inspiration.
parts.c: Diaphragmatic hernia can allow abdominal contents to enter thorax.

parts.d: Upper portion of abdominopelvic compartment below the diaphragm, containing much of the digestive tract and associated organs.
parts.f: Accommodates abdominal organs and their motion.
parts.c: Kidneys lie posteriorly and retroperitoneally, not inside the peritoneal sac.

parts.d: Lower portion of the abdominopelvic compartment within the bony pelvis, containing bladder, rectum and internal reproductive organs.
parts.f: Supports pelvic viscera and their neural/vascular routes.
parts.c: Its boundary with the abdomen is an anatomical convention, not a watertight wall.

parts.d: Parietal peritoneum lines abdominal wall; visceral peritoneum covers many abdominal organs; the cavity between is normally a potential space.
parts.f: Provides sliding surfaces and forms mesenteries.
parts.c: Retroperitoneal organs lie behind parietal peritoneum.

parts.d: Space posterior to the parietal peritoneum, where kidneys and parts of duodenum and pancreas are located.
parts.f: Separates posterior structures from intraperitoneal viscera.
parts.c: Not all abdominal organs share the same peritoneal relationship.

parts.d: Patient-right, above a horizontal umbilical line; often includes much of the liver and gallbladder.
parts.f: Provides a rapid clinical location shorthand.
parts.c: A quadrant is not a diagnosis or exact organ outline.

parts.d: Patient-left, above the umbilicus; includes stomach and spleen regions.
parts.f: Provides location shorthand for upper-left abdominal findings.
parts.c: Abdominal organ position varies with filling and individual anatomy.

parts.d: Patient-right, below the umbilicus; includes the cecal and appendiceal region in typical anatomy.
parts.f: Locates lower-right examination findings.
parts.c: Appendix position varies; pain site alone does not confirm a diagnosis.

parts.d: Patient-left, below the umbilicus; includes sigmoid-colon region in typical anatomy.
parts.f: Locates lower-left examination findings.
parts.c: Cross-midline pain cannot be assigned to one organ from the chart.

parts.d: Upper right of the nine abdominal regions, beneath the right costal margin.
parts.f: Refines location compared with four broad quadrants.
parts.c: Right is the patient’s right, shown on the viewer’s left in the frontal chart.

parts.d: Central upper abdomen between right and left hypochondriac regions.
parts.f: Names a midline upper-abdominal surface region.
parts.c: A surface region is not identical to the underlying stomach boundary.

parts.d: Upper left of the nine abdominal regions beneath the left costal margin.
parts.f: Orients the upper-left abdominal surface.
parts.c: Underlying organs may project across several regions.

parts.d: Right middle abdominal region, lateral to the umbilical region.
parts.f: Names a lateral mid-abdominal location.
parts.c: Do not confuse surface lumbar region with the retroperitoneal kidney itself.

parts.d: Central middle abdominal region around the navel.
parts.f: Provides a reproducible surface-location term.
parts.c: The umbilicus is a surface landmark, not the location of every central visceral structure.

parts.d: Left middle region lateral to the umbilical region.
parts.f: Names a left lateral mid-abdominal surface region.
parts.c: The colon position varies with body habitus and filling.

parts.d: Lower right of nine regions, adjacent to right iliac fossa.
parts.f: Localizes lower-right surface anatomy.
parts.c: An inguinal region is not a single hernia diagnosis.

parts.d: Lower central abdominal region above pubis.
parts.f: Localizes lower midline surface findings.
parts.c: Bladder fullness can change organ projection into this region.

parts.d: Lower left of nine regions, adjacent to left iliac fossa.
parts.f: Localizes lower-left surface findings.
parts.c: The sigmoid colon may cross regional boundaries.

parts.d: Palpable anterior midline breastbone used as a thoracic orientation landmark.
parts.f: Orients ribs and anterior chest examination.
parts.c: A skin-level point does not identify a deep vessel precisely.

parts.d: Palpable superior margin of each iliac bone at the lateral waist.
parts.f: Orients pelvic and lumbar surface anatomy.
parts.c: Its height and palpable projection vary with posture and body habitus.

parts.d: A cell is a membrane-bound living unit with internal components that perform metabolism and communication.
parts.f: Combines organelles to maintain tissue function.
parts.c: A cutaway is a stylized model, not a universal cell portrait.

parts.d: Lipid bilayer with embedded proteins separates cell interior from extracellular fluid.
parts.f: Regulates exchange, signaling and cellular identity.
parts.c: Its molecular bilayer cannot be directly resolved on a gross organ plate.

parts.d: Cytoplasm includes cytosol and organelles outside the nucleus; cytosol is the fluid component.
parts.f: Hosts much of cellular metabolism.
parts.c: Do not treat the two terms as exact synonyms.

parts.d: Membrane-enclosed compartment holding most nuclear DNA in many human cell types.
parts.f: Coordinates gene expression and cell division.
parts.c: Mature red blood cells lack a nucleus; visible ovals on this plate are idealized epithelial nuclei.

parts.d: Double-membrane organelles that generate much cellular ATP through oxidative phosphorylation.
parts.f: Provide energy for many cellular activities.
parts.c: Mitochondrial shapes on this digital cell model are illustrative, not microscopy.

parts.d: Ribosomes translate messenger RNA; those bound to rough endoplasmic reticulum make many secreted and membrane proteins.
parts.f: Supports protein synthesis and processing.
parts.c: Ribosome dots on this teaching model are not individually identifiable microscopy.

parts.d: Stacked membrane compartments that modify and sort proteins and lipids.
parts.f: Directs cargo toward secretion, membrane or lysosomal pathways.
parts.c: The colored Golgi-like stack is a digital teaching aid, not a clinical specimen.

parts.d: Noncellular network of fibrous proteins and hydrated ground substance outside connective-tissue cells.
parts.f: Supports tissues and influences cell signaling.
parts.c: Its composition varies between areolar tissue, cartilage, tendon and bone.

parts.d: Close-packed cell sheets cover body surfaces, line passages and form much glandular tissue; the image depicts one simple columnar example.
parts.f: Provides selective barrier, absorption, transport and secretion.
parts.c: This is a digital teaching cutaway, not a patient histology slide or a picture of every epithelium.

parts.d: The free epithelial cell surface faces a lumen or environment, while the basal side faces the underlying support.
parts.f: Allows directional absorption, secretion and barrier function.
parts.c: Apical microvilli on the plate are schematic and cannot classify a specimen alone.

parts.d: Specialized extracellular layer beneath epithelial cells, shown as a fine strip above vascular connective tissue.
parts.f: Anchors and organizes the epithelial sheet.
parts.c: Basement membrane in tissue sections often includes more than the basal lamina alone.

parts.d: Simple epithelium has one cell layer; stratified epithelium has multiple layers. This plate depicts a simple arrangement.
parts.f: Relates layer number to transport or protective roles.
parts.c: Pseudostratified epithelium appears layered but every cell contacts the basal lamina.

parts.d: Cells are dispersed in an extracellular matrix; the companion plate illustrates loose areolar connective tissue.
parts.f: Supports and integrates tissues, with many specialized forms.
parts.c: Bone, cartilage and blood are distinct connective-tissue forms, not the same as areolar tissue.

parts.d: Spindle-shaped cells synthesize components of connective extracellular matrix, including collagen.
parts.f: Maintains and remodels connective tissue.
parts.c: Digital cell shapes alone cannot substitute for a histologic diagnosis.

parts.d: Protein fibers provide tensile support; loose areolar tissue contains scattered wavy bundles.
parts.f: Resists stretch and mechanical load.
parts.c: Fiber amount and type change with tissue and disease.

parts.d: Small vessel in supporting connective tissue carries blood near, not into, the epithelial sheet.
parts.f: Supplies nutrients that diffuse toward avascular epithelium.
parts.c: This schematic is not a scale-accurate microvascular map.

parts.d: Excitable cells shorten and produce force; skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle are three distinct types.
parts.f: Supports movement, circulation and organ wall function.
parts.c: The accompanying striated plate depicts skeletal muscle only.

parts.d: Long multinucleated, striated contractile cell with peripheral nuclei in normal skeletal muscle.
parts.f: Produces voluntary skeletal movement.
parts.c: The illustrated longitudinal section should not be confused with branching cardiac muscle.

parts.d: Thin connective-tissue layer surrounding each individual skeletal muscle fiber.
parts.f: Supports small vessels and transmits contractile forces.
parts.c: Perimysium instead surrounds bundles of fibers.

parts.d: Striated, typically branched cardiomyocytes join through intercalated discs in the heart.
parts.f: Generates coordinated cardiac pumping.
parts.c: This illustration is a stylized cardiac example, not a diagnostic histology slide.

parts.d: Nonstriated spindle-shaped contractile cells occur in walls of many hollow organs and vessels.
parts.f: Controls lumen diameter and organ-wall motion.
parts.c: This plate is a stylized smooth-muscle example, not diagnostic histology.

parts.d: Neurons and supporting glia form excitable networks in central and peripheral nervous systems.
parts.f: Detects, processes and transmits information.
parts.c: Illustrated neuron and myelin are teaching-scale models, not micrographs.

parts.d: Soma houses cell machinery and receives signals through branching dendrites; form varies with neuron class.
parts.f: Integrates synaptic inputs.
parts.c: A multipolar example cannot represent all neuronal morphologies.

parts.d: Single main output process carries electrical impulses away from a neuron’s initial segment; it may have collaterals.
parts.f: Communicates toward synaptic targets.
parts.c: The illustrated path is conceptual, not a clinical nerve map.

parts.d: Repeated myelin segments electrically insulate portions of some axons, leaving short gaps called nodes of Ranvier.
parts.f: Supports rapid saltatory conduction.
parts.c: Not every axon is myelinated and different glia myelinate CNS and PNS axons.

parts.d: Astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, microglia and Schwann cells have different CNS or PNS roles.
parts.f: Support neurons, homeostasis and myelin formation.
parts.c: The small background cells here are generic, not separately identifiable glial subtypes.

parts.d: Epithelial, connective, muscle and nervous tissue are the four broad human tissue families.
parts.f: Provides a framework for reading tissue architecture.
parts.c: An organ usually contains more than one tissue type.

parts.d: Histology examines prepared tissue sections with microscopy; these four generated images are stylized educational cutaways.
parts.f: Distinguishes tissue concepts from diagnostic specimens.
parts.c: Never diagnose disease or claim real staining or magnification from these images.

parts.d: Flattened cell head contains compact haploid paternal DNA and an anterior cap; the picture is enlarged, not to biological scale.
parts.f: Delivers genetic material at fertilization.
parts.c: Shape alone on this teaching image cannot establish fertility.

parts.d: Enzyme-containing cap over the anterior head; actual molecular reactions cannot be observed in this model.
parts.f: Participates in penetration of the oocyte coverings after capacitation.
parts.c: Acrosome reaction occurs at contact with oocyte investments, not during testicular meiosis.

parts.d: Condensed chromatin within the head contains one set of chromosomes following meiosis.
parts.f: Contributes paternal nuclear genetic material.
parts.c: Not all chromosome changes are visible by ordinary shape inspection.

parts.d: Short connecting piece between head and midpiece carries centriolar structures.
parts.f: Connects the head to the motile tail apparatus.
parts.c: Tiny details are not independently resolved in the digital plate.

parts.d: Thicker proximal flagellar segment has mitochondria arranged around the axonemal core.
parts.f: Provides local energy supply for swimming.
parts.c: The model is schematic and does not measure mitochondrial function.

parts.d: Single long motile tail with principal and end pieces propelled by an internal axoneme.
parts.f: Drives sperm through fluid; tract transport also involves other mechanisms.
parts.c: One sperm has one flagellum in this reference model.

parts.d: Microtubule-based motile core runs along the flagellum; its molecular pattern requires appropriate microscopy.
parts.f: Converts motor-protein action to bending movement.
parts.c: Never pinpoint the microscopic axoneme on the whole-cell plate.

parts.d: Diploid precursor near the seminiferous tubule basement membrane enters the production lineage.
parts.f: Replenishes and supplies germ cells.
parts.c: This cell is not separately visible on the sperm-only image.

parts.d: Diploid cell that enters meiosis I within the seminiferous epithelium.
parts.f: Undergoes homologous chromosome separation.
parts.c: Not a mature motile spermatozoon.

parts.d: Short-lived haploid cell produced by meiosis I and proceeding through meiosis II.
parts.f: Produces spermatids after the second meiotic division.
parts.c: Specific cell stages need microscopy and cannot be pinned on a whole sperm.

parts.d: Haploid round precursor differentiates without another division during spermiogenesis.
parts.f: Forms the shaped head and tail.
parts.c: Spermatids are not identical in morphology to ejaculated mature sperm.

parts.d: Remodels the spermatid: chromatin condenses, acrosome forms and flagellum grows.
parts.f: Converts a round germ cell into a sperm-shaped cell.
parts.c: Do not confuse cellular shaping with meiotic reduction.

parts.d: Somatic support cell spans seminiferous tubules, nourishes germ cells and contributes to a blood-testis barrier.
parts.f: Supports germ cell development and releases inhibin B.
parts.c: The isolated sperm image does not show Sertoli cells.

parts.d: Interstitial testicular endocrine cell responds to luteinizing hormone and produces testosterone.
parts.f: Supports spermatogenesis indirectly through hormonal signaling.
parts.c: Does not become a sperm cell.

parts.d: Coiled testicular tubule houses stratified developing germ cells and Sertoli cells.
parts.f: Site of sperm production.
parts.c: A single drawn sperm is not a histologic section through a tubule.

parts.d: Highly coiled duct alongside testis where sperm undergo functional maturation and storage.
parts.f: Conditions sperm motility before ejaculation.
parts.c: Production begins in testis, not in epididymis.

parts.d: Muscular duct moves sperm from epididymis toward ejaculatory ducts during emission.
parts.f: Transports stored sperm.
parts.c: Contributes no new sperm nuclei after meiosis.

parts.d: Post-ejaculatory functional changes in sperm membrane and motility occur in the reproductive tract.
parts.f: Prepares sperm for interaction with oocyte coverings.
parts.c: Capacitation is not the same as the acrosome reaction.

parts.d: Secretions from seminal vesicles, prostate and other glands mix with sperm during ejaculation.
parts.f: Provides transport medium and biochemical support.
parts.c: A semen analysis requires clinical sampling, not inference from this plate.

parts.d: Normal cells differ in appearance, and only laboratory-standard methods can assess morphology or motility.
parts.f: Prevents treating one reference drawing as every gamete.
parts.c: A generic render cannot diagnose infertility.

parts.d: Female fetal germ cell proliferates before birth; primary oocytes arise during fetal ovarian development.
parts.f: Provides precursor pool for later follicles.
parts.c: The adult ovarian plate does not depict embryonic ovarian cells.

parts.d: Diploid meiotic cell arrested in prophase I inside an ovarian follicle before the ovulatory cycle.
parts.f: Preserves a germ cell until a later cycle recruits the follicle.
parts.c: Not the same stage as the secondary oocyte depicted on the main plate.

parts.d: LH-associated resumption of meiosis I forms a secondary oocyte and the first polar body.
parts.f: Reduces chromosome set before ovulation.
parts.c: Chronology varies and does not guarantee later fertilization.

parts.d: Large haploid-stage cell released at ovulation, arrested in metaphase II until fertilization.
parts.f: Contributes maternal genetic material when fertilization occurs.
parts.c: The illustrated cytoplasm is not a distinct mature nucleus.

parts.d: Extracellular glycoprotein layer immediately outside oocyte cell membrane and inside corona radiata.
parts.f: Supports sperm recognition and protects the developing conceptus early.
parts.c: It is not the oocyte nucleus or an ovarian follicle wall.

parts.d: Layer of granulosa-derived cells closely surrounds zona pellucida after ovulation.
parts.f: Provides support around the released oocyte.
parts.c: The individual cells in the digital cutaway are illustrative, not a diagnostic slide.

parts.d: Small meiotic by-product sits in perivitelline space between the oocyte membrane and zona pellucida.
parts.f: Reflects unequal cytoplasmic division during oogenesis.
parts.c: Do not confuse it with a second oocyte or early embryo.

parts.d: Narrow space between oocyte membrane and zona pellucida, where a polar body may lie.
parts.f: Separates cell surface from extracellular coat.
parts.c: A drawing may exaggerate this very small gap.

parts.d: Oolemma surrounds the oocyte cytoplasm beneath the zona pellucida.
parts.f: Participates in sperm–oocyte membrane interaction.
parts.c: The zona and membrane are distinct boundaries.

parts.d: Ooplasm contains maternal organelles and factors needed for early divisions.
parts.f: Supports the earliest conceptus before substantial placental exchange.
parts.c: A secondary oocyte is not shown with a large interphase nucleus.

parts.d: Meiotic apparatus lies near cell periphery in the unfertilized secondary oocyte.
parts.f: Positions chromosomes for completion of meiosis II.
parts.c: Tiny spindle details cannot be reliably pinned on this stylized image.

parts.d: Cells within ovarian follicles surround the oocyte and later contribute to corpus luteum.
parts.f: Provide growth support and steroid-related signaling.
parts.c: Corona cells are follicular derivatives, not sperm cells.

parts.d: Outer follicular cells participate in androgen substrate production for granulosa estrogen synthesis.
parts.f: Support ovarian follicle steroidogenesis.
parts.c: Not identifiable on the isolated oocyte image.

parts.d: Fluid-filled follicular space develops in growing antral follicles around the oocyte complex.
parts.f: Accompanies follicle maturation.
parts.c: This space is not the cavity inside the ovulated oocyte.

parts.d: Selected follicle grows and responds to gonadotropins ahead of ovulation in a typical cycle.
parts.f: Supports final oocyte maturation and release.
parts.c: Cycles differ; follicles may not all mature on day 14.

parts.d: Rise in luteinizing hormone triggers final oocyte maturation and ovulatory processes.
parts.f: Coordinates meiosis I completion and follicular rupture.
parts.c: A calendar date does not directly prove an LH surge.

parts.d: Follicle ruptures and releases secondary oocyte with surrounding cells from the ovary.
parts.f: Makes a secondary oocyte available to the uterine tube.
parts.c: Ovulation is not fertilization and not implantation.

parts.d: Finger-like fringe and funnel-shaped tubal opening are near the ovary.
parts.f: Aid capture of ovulated oocyte; cilia and muscular activity support transport.
parts.c: The tube and ovary are close but not a permanently fused pipe.

parts.d: Postovulatory follicular structure produces progesterone and estrogen; hCG can sustain it in early pregnancy.
parts.f: Supports secretory endometrium.
parts.c: Not a fertilized egg or an early placenta.

parts.d: Following sperm entry, the secondary oocyte completes meiosis II and extrudes another polar body.
parts.f: Contributes mature maternal haploid pronuclear material.
parts.c: Without fertilization, meiosis II generally remains incomplete.

parts.d: Semen is commonly deposited in vagina with sperm entering cervical mucus under favorable conditions.
parts.f: Begins sperm transit toward uterine tubes.
parts.c: Intercourse timing, contraception and fertility vary; no pregnancy is guaranteed.

parts.d: Cervical secretion varies across cycle and affects sperm passage toward uterus.
parts.f: Acts as a changing selective gateway.
parts.c: A cervical photograph alone cannot determine conception.

parts.d: Sperm passing cervix cross uterine cavity en route to a tube.
parts.f: Connects lower reproductive tract to usual fertilization site.
parts.c: The uterus is not the typical site of normal fertilization.

parts.d: Distal wider segment of uterine tube near ovary is the most common site of normal sperm–oocyte encounter.
parts.f: Provides site for fertilization and early conceptus transit.
parts.c: Tubal implantation is ectopic and needs medical assessment.

parts.d: Ovulated secondary oocyte is surrounded by a zona pellucida and corona radiata.
parts.f: Supplies maternal haploid material when fertilization succeeds.
parts.c: It is arrested in meiosis II until sperm entry.

parts.d: Tract conditions modify sperm membrane and movement after ejaculation.
parts.f: Enables effective interaction with oocyte investments.
parts.c: A mature-looking tail on a drawing does not prove capacitation.

parts.d: Sperm traverse the surrounding granulosa-derived corona radiata before reaching the zona.
parts.f: Brings sperm to extracellular zona coat.
parts.c: Only an illustrative contact location is shown on this plate.

parts.d: Sperm contact oocyte extracellular zona layer and undergo molecular interactions required for entry.
parts.f: Precedes membrane fusion.
parts.c: A sperm touching the zona in an image is not proof fertilization occurred.

parts.d: Membrane and enzyme release from the sperm head facilitates passage through zona pellucida.
parts.f: Helps sperm reach oocyte plasma membrane.
parts.c: This molecular event cannot be identified on the large digital plate.

parts.d: Sperm and oocyte plasma membranes fuse after passage through outer coats.
parts.f: Introduces paternal genetic material into oocyte.
parts.c: This stage is later than the single sperm–zona contact depicted.

parts.d: Oocyte cortical granules alter surrounding coat following sperm fusion.
parts.f: Helps limit polyspermy.
parts.c: Do not represent this process as a visible colored ring on the static contact image.

parts.d: Sperm entry stimulates the secondary oocyte to complete the second meiotic division.
parts.f: Generates mature maternal haploid contribution and a polar body.
parts.c: It does not finish during ordinary ovulation without fertilization.

parts.d: Haploid maternal nuclear material reorganizes following meiosis II.
parts.f: Participates in establishing the zygote genome.
parts.c: The earlier contact plate does not depict pronuclei. The nearby postfusion plate does not resolve an individual pronucleus.

parts.d: Sperm chromatin decondenses to form paternal pronuclear material.
parts.f: Contributes the paternal chromosome set.
parts.c: A sperm head outside the zona is not yet a paternal pronucleus. The nearby postfusion plate does not resolve an individual pronucleus.

parts.d: New single-celled conceptus arises after union of maternal and paternal genetic material.
parts.f: Begins the cellular development of an individual conceptus.
parts.c: A zygote must still divide, reach uterus and implant for an ongoing pregnancy.

parts.d: Dizygotic twins arise from two oocytes fertilized separately; monozygotic twins arise from one early conceptus that divides.
parts.f: Clarifies different routes to twin pregnancy.
parts.c: The single-oocyte plate does not depict twins.

parts.d: Fertilization in a tube is normal; implantation within a tube is not.
parts.f: Separates normal fertilization location from abnormal implantation site.
parts.c: Severe pain or bleeding in a possible pregnancy requires urgent clinical evaluation.

parts.d: Epithelial cilia and tubal muscle activity help move gametes and early conceptus toward uterus.
parts.f: Connects tubal fertilization to uterine implantation.
parts.c: The contact illustration cannot measure tubal transport.

parts.d: Fertilization age counts from conception; obstetric gestational age usually counts from last menstrual period, roughly two weeks earlier.
parts.f: Prevents misreading embryo and fetal weeks.
parts.c: Ovulation timing differs, so the two-week offset is an approximation.

parts.d: Sperm survival, ovulation, tubal transport and many biological factors affect the chance of fertilization.
parts.f: Sets realistic expectations for the sequential study path.
parts.c: A diagram cannot diagnose the cause of infertility.

parts.d: Diploid one-cell conceptus results after fertilization of one oocyte by one sperm.
parts.f: Begins early development.
parts.c: A zygote has not yet implanted and is not a fetus.

parts.d: The zygote divides into two blastomeres without the usual cell growth between divisions.
parts.f: Begins increase in cell number.
parts.c: Exact day of the first division is variable.

parts.d: Each early daughter cell forms as the conceptus cleaves in its surrounding zona.
parts.f: Builds the multicellular early conceptus.
parts.c: One blastomere alone is not the same as a mature embryo.

parts.d: Additional cleavage creates a small group of blastomeres still enclosed by zona.
parts.f: Extends early proliferation.
parts.c: This single blastocyst plate does not show a four-cell stage.

parts.d: Further divisions make smaller blastomeres as the early conceptus approaches compaction.
parts.f: Sets up more extensive cell-to-cell contact.
parts.c: Do not count blastocyst cells to infer a precise day.

parts.d: Extracellular glycoprotein envelope persists around early cleavage stages.

faqs.q: How many chambers does the heart have?
faqs.a: The heart has two upper receiving chambers, the right and left atria, and two lower pumping chambers, the right and left ventricles. The right ventricle sends blood to the lungs; the left sends it to the body.

faqs.q: What route does blood take through the heart?
faqs.a: Blood returns from the body to the right atrium, passes the tricuspid valve to the right ventricle, then crosses the pulmonary valve to the lungs. Oxygenated blood returns to the left atrium, passes the mitral valve to the left ventricle and leaves through the aortic valve.

faqs.q: Why is the left ventricular wall thicker?
faqs.a: The left ventricle must generate greater pressure to move blood through the systemic circulation. Its myocardium is therefore thicker than that of the right ventricle, which pumps into the lower-pressure pulmonary circulation.

faqs.q: Do coronary arteries carry blood through the heart chambers?
faqs.a: No. Coronary arteries branch near the aortic root and supply the heart muscle itself. The blood passing through the chambers does not directly nourish the full thickness of the myocardium.

faqs.q: How do heart valves keep blood moving forward?
faqs.a: Tricuspid and mitral valves guard the atrioventricular openings; pulmonary and aortic valves guard ventricular outflow. They open and close in response to pressure changes, limiting backward flow rather than actively pumping blood.

faqs.q: What are the lobes of the right and left lungs?
faqs.a: The right lung usually has superior, middle and inferior lobes; the left has superior and inferior lobes with a cardiac notch. Fissures divide the lobes, though normal anatomy can vary.

faqs.q: Where does air go after the bronchi?
faqs.a: Air passes from progressively smaller bronchi to bronchioles, then through the respiratory zone toward alveoli. Exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide occurs across the very thin alveolar–capillary barrier.

faqs.q: What is a Type I pneumocyte?
faqs.a: A Type I pneumocyte is a very thin squamous cell forming much of the alveolar gas-exchange surface. It can be recognized on the separate microscopic-scale teaching illustration, not on the whole-lung image.

faqs.q: What does a Type II pneumocyte do?
faqs.a: A Type II pneumocyte is a plumper alveolar cell that secretes pulmonary surfactant, which helps reduce surface tension. It also contributes to maintenance and repair of the alveolar lining.

faqs.q: Is the enlarged alveolar image an actual microscope slide?
faqs.a: No. It is a digital educational illustration that shows the thin Type I lining next to a plumper Type II cell. It is not histology or a literal magnification of the macroscopic lung image.

faqs.q: What are the main parts of the brain?
faqs.a: The cerebrum supports complex thought, sensation and voluntary movement; the cerebellum coordinates movement; and the brainstem connects the brain to the spinal cord and helps regulate essential functions.

faqs.q: What protects the brain inside the skull?
faqs.a: The skull, three meningeal layers and cerebrospinal fluid provide physical protection. Blood vessels supply its metabolically active tissue.

faqs.q: What is the frontal lobe?
faqs.a: Anterior to the central sulcus and above the lateral sulcus. Contains the primary motor cortex, Broca's area (usually left) and the prefrontal cortex. Function: Planning, judgement, personality, voluntary movement and expressive speech.

faqs.q: Where is the thalamus located?
faqs.a: Two ovals of grey matter flanking the third ventricle, subdivided into anterior, medial and lateral nuclear groups. Function: The relay station: nearly all sensory information (except smell) is edited and sent on to the cortex. Also involved in arousal.

faqs.q: What is the function of the cerebellum?
faqs.a: Function: Compares intended movement with actual movement and corrects it: coordination, precision, timing, posture and motor learning. Two hemispheres and a midline vermis, with a densely folded cortex, deep nuclei (dentate, emboliform, globose, fastigial) and branching white matter — the arbor vitae.

faqs.q: What do the kidneys do?
faqs.a: Kidneys filter blood, return most water and useful solutes to circulation, and excrete wastes in urine. They also help regulate electrolytes, blood pressure and acid-base balance.

faqs.q: How does urine travel from the kidney to the bladder?
faqs.a: Filtrate passes through nephron tubules into collecting ducts, then through calyces and the renal pelvis. A ureter carries the resulting urine to the bladder.

faqs.q: What is the renal cortex?
faqs.a: The outer 1 cm, containing all the renal corpuscles, the proximal and distal convoluted tubules, and cortical tissue dipping between pyramids as the renal columns. Function: Site of blood filtration and most solute reabsorption.

faqs.q: Where is the glomerulus & Bowman's capsule located?
faqs.a: A tuft of fenestrated capillaries invaginating a double-walled capsule. Between them, the filtration barrier: fenestrated endothelium, fused basement membrane and podocyte foot processes with slit diaphragms. Function: Ultrafiltration of plasma — water and small solutes pass; cells and proteins do not.

faqs.q: What is the function of the loop of Henle?
faqs.a: Function: Countercurrent multiplication builds the medullary osmotic gradient that allows urine to be concentrated. A hairpin with a thin descending limb (water-permeable) and a thick ascending limb (actively pumps out NaCl but is water-impermeable), dipping into the medulla.

faqs.q: What are the main functions of the liver?
faqs.a: The liver processes nutrients, makes bile and many blood proteins, stores glycogen and participates in drug and toxin metabolism. Its blood arrives from both the portal vein and hepatic artery.

faqs.q: Where is the liver located?
faqs.a: Most of the liver lies beneath the diaphragm in the right upper abdomen, with a smaller part extending across the midline.

faqs.q: What is the gallbladder?
faqs.a: A 7–10 cm pear-shaped sac on the visceral surface of the right lobe, with fundus, body and neck. Its wall concentrates bile up to tenfold. Function: Stores and concentrates bile, releasing it into the duodenum when fat arrives (CCK-mediated).

faqs.q: Where is the hepatic portal vein located?
faqs.a: Formed behind the pancreatic neck by the splenic and superior mesenteric veins; carries nutrient-rich, deoxygenated blood from gut, spleen and pancreas. Function: Delivers 75% of hepatic blood and everything absorbed from the gut for first-pass processing.

faqs.q: What is the function of the hepatic lobule & sinusoids?
faqs.a: Function: Blood flows from triad to central vein while bile flows the opposite way, from canaliculi to the triad bile duct. Hexagonal units ~1 mm across: plates of hepatocytes radiating from a central vein, separated by sinusoids lined with endothelium and Kupffer macrophages; portal triads (artery, vein, bile duct) sit at the corners.

faqs.q: What happens to food in the stomach and intestines?
faqs.a: The stomach stores and mixes food with acid and enzymes. The small intestine completes much digestion and absorbs nutrients; the large intestine absorbs water and forms stool.

faqs.q: How long is the route through the digestive tract?
faqs.a: Food moves from oesophagus to stomach, small intestine and large intestine before leaving through the rectum and anal canal. Length varies between people and measurement methods.

faqs.q: What is the oesophagus?
faqs.a: A 25 cm muscular tube from pharynx to stomach, passing through the diaphragm at T10. Function: Propels the bolus by peristalsis; the lower sphincter prevents reflux.

faqs.q: Where is the body of stomach located?
faqs.a: The main reservoir between fundus and antrum, lined by acid- and pepsin-secreting mucosa with rugae. Function: Mixes food with acid and pepsin; intrinsic factor for B12 absorption is made here.

faqs.q: What is the function of the rugae?
faqs.a: Function: Allow expansion and channel the flow of chyme. Longitudinal folds of gastric mucosa that flatten as the stomach distends.

faqs.q: How does the eye focus light on the retina?
faqs.a: The cornea provides much of the eye's focusing power, while the lens changes shape for near and far vision. Light is converted into neural signals by retinal photoreceptors.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the retina and the optic nerve?
faqs.a: The retina is the light-sensitive neural tissue lining the back of the eye. Its ganglion-cell axons bundle together to form the optic nerve.

faqs.q: What is the cornea?
faqs.a: Transparent, avascular, five-layered dome at the front of the eye. Provides about two-thirds of the eye's refractive power. Function: Bends and transmits light; its endothelium pumps water out to stay clear.

faqs.q: Where is the retina located?
faqs.a: Ten-layered neural film: photoreceptors outermost (light must pass through the inner layers first), then bipolar and ganglion cells. Function: Transduces light into nerve impulses.

faqs.q: What is the function of the macula & fovea?
faqs.a: Function: High-acuity central vision for reading and faces. A 5.5 mm yellow-pigmented area at the posterior pole; its centre, the fovea, contains cones only and no vessels.

faqs.q: How do the outer, middle and inner ear work together?
faqs.a: The outer ear collects sound, the eardrum and three middle-ear bones transmit vibration, and the cochlea in the inner ear converts movement into nerve signals.

faqs.q: Which part of the ear helps with balance?
faqs.a: The vestibular organs of the inner ear, including the semicircular canals and otolith organs, detect head rotation and linear movement.

faqs.q: What is the tympanic membrane?
faqs.a: A 9 × 10 mm cone of three layers, tilted so its umbo points medially; pars tensa below, pars flaccida above. Function: Converts sound pressure into mechanical vibration of the malleus.

faqs.q: Where is the stapes located?
faqs.a: The stirrup: the smallest bone in the body (~3 mm), its footplate closing the oval window. Function: Delivers amplified vibration into the cochlear fluid.

faqs.q: What is the function of the vestibule (utricle & saccule)?
faqs.a: Function: Sense linear acceleration and head tilt — gravity sensing. Two otolith organs whose hair cells carry crystals of calcium carbonate.

faqs.q: What does the pancreas do?
faqs.a: Its exocrine tissue releases digestive enzymes into the small intestine. Endocrine islets release hormones such as insulin and glucagon into the blood.

faqs.q: Where is the pancreas located?
faqs.a: It lies behind the stomach across the upper abdomen. Its head sits near the duodenum, while its tail reaches toward the spleen.

faqs.q: Where is the head of the pancreas?
faqs.a: The broad end nestled in the C-loop of the duodenum, with the uncinate process hooking behind the superior mesenteric vessels. Function: Houses much of the exocrine tissue and the terminal duct.

faqs.q: Where is the main pancreatic duct located?
faqs.a: Runs the length of the gland from tail to head, joining the common bile duct at the ampulla in the second part of duodenum. Function: Delivers ~1.5 L of enzyme- and bicarbonate-rich juice daily.

faqs.q: What is the function of the acinar cells & ductules?
faqs.a: Function: Secrete the pro-enzymes for digesting protein, fat and carbohydrate. Grape-like clusters of enzyme-packed cells draining into centroacinar cells and ductules.

faqs.q: What is the spleen's function?
faqs.a: The spleen filters blood, removes aging red blood cells and helps immune cells respond to blood-borne material. Its red and white pulp perform different tasks.

faqs.q: Can you feel a normal spleen?
faqs.a: A normal adult spleen is usually protected beneath the left lower ribs and is not readily felt on examination; enlargement is a medical finding, not something this atlas can diagnose.

faqs.q: What is the capsule & trabeculae?
faqs.a: A fibroelastic capsule sending trabeculae into the pulp, carrying the vessels. Function: Structural framework and conduit for vessels.

faqs.q: Where is the white pulp located?
faqs.a: Periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (T cells), follicles (B cells) and a marginal zone rich in macrophages. Function: Immune surveillance of blood: antibody and opsonin production, especially against capsules.

faqs.q: What is the function of the hilum?
faqs.a: Function: Vascular gateway; also the site of accessory spleens in ~15% of people. The notched medial border where splenic vessels enter and the tail of pancreas and stomach fundus relate.

faqs.q: Where is the thyroid gland located?
faqs.a: The thyroid has two lateral lobes joined by an isthmus in the front of the neck, close to the larynx and upper trachea.

faqs.q: What do thyroid follicles make?
faqs.a: Follicular cells use iodine and stored thyroglobulin in colloid to produce thyroid hormones. Nearby parafollicular cells produce calcitonin.

faqs.q: What is the isthmus?
faqs.a: The bridge crossing the 2nd–4th tracheal rings, joining the two lobes. Function: Connects the lobes into a single gland.

faqs.q: Where is the trachea & larynx located?
faqs.a: The gland wraps the airway; the cricoid cartilage and thyroid cartilage lie above. Function: Anatomical landmark and the reason goitres cause compressive symptoms.

faqs.q: What is the function of the follicle & colloid?
faqs.a: Function: Synthesis and storage of thyroid hormone — the only endocrine gland that stores its product extracellularly. Spheres of follicular cells enclosing colloid (iodinated thyroglobulin). TSH stimulates iodide trapping, organification, coupling, and endocytosis of colloid to release T3/T4.

faqs.q: How does the urinary bladder store and release urine?
faqs.a: A stretchable urothelial lining and detrusor muscle allow filling. During urination, coordinated detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation empty the bladder.

faqs.q: What is the trigone of the bladder?
faqs.a: The trigone is a triangular region on the internal bladder floor between the two ureteric openings and the internal urethral opening.

faqs.q: What is the detrusor muscle?
faqs.a: Three layers of interlacing smooth muscle with the wall thickened into trabeculae when obstructed. Function: Contraction empties the bladder; relaxation allows storage at low pressure.

faqs.q: Where is the urothelium located?
faqs.a: Stratified transitional epithelium with umbrella cells whose plaques make it impermeable to urine. Function: A stretch-tolerant, urine-proof lining.

faqs.q: What is the function of the trigone?
faqs.a: Function: Funnel for emptying; its stretch receptors trigger the micturition reflex. The smooth triangle bounded by the two ureteric orifices and the internal urethral orifice; mucosa firmly bound to muscle.

faqs.q: What are the main layers of the skin?
faqs.a: The epidermis is the outer epithelial barrier; the vascular dermis contains connective tissue, vessels and nerves. Subcutaneous tissue lies beneath the skin and varies by region.

faqs.q: How does skin help protect the body?
faqs.a: The keratinized epidermal surface limits water loss and helps block external injury and microbes, while deeper tissue supports sensation, repair and temperature regulation.

faqs.q: What is the stratum corneum?
faqs.a: 15–20 layers of dead, flattened, keratin-filled corneocytes held by lipids — the "brick and mortar" barrier. Function: Waterproofing and the main barrier to microbes and chemicals.

faqs.q: Where is the dermis (papillary & reticular) located?
faqs.a: Papillary layer of loose connective tissue forming dermal papillae; reticular layer of dense irregular collagen and elastin. Function: Strength, elasticity, sensation and the vascular supply of the epidermis.

faqs.q: What is the function of the hair shaft & follicle?
faqs.a: Function: Protection, sensation and (in other mammals) insulation. A keratinised shaft growing from a follicle that dips into dermis or fat, with a bulb around a dermal papilla and a bulge of stem cells.

faqs.q: Where does the spinal cord end in adults?
faqs.a: The spinal cord usually tapers to the conus medullaris near the L1-L2 vertebral level in adults; nerve roots continue below it as the cauda equina.

faqs.q: What is the difference between gray and white matter in the spinal cord?
faqs.a: Central gray matter contains neuronal cell bodies and local circuits; surrounding white matter carries ascending sensory and descending motor pathways.

faqs.q: What is the posterior (dorsal) horn?
faqs.a: The slender upper horns receiving sensory afferents; laminae I–VI including the substantia gelatinosa. Function: First synapse for pain, temperature and touch; gate control of nociception happens here.

faqs.q: Where is the lateral horn located?
faqs.a: Present only in T1–L2, holding preganglionic sympathetic neurons (and S2–S4 parasympathetic equivalents). Function: Origin of the sympathetic outflow.

faqs.q: What is the function of the white funiculi & tracts?
faqs.a: Function: Highways for sensation upward and motor commands downward. Dorsal columns (fasciculus gracilis & cuneatus), lateral spinothalamic and corticospinal tracts, and spinocerebellar tracts.

faqs.q: How is sperm produced and transported?
faqs.a: Sperm develop in seminiferous tubules of the testes, mature in the epididymis and pass through the vas deferens and ejaculatory ducts into the urethra.

faqs.q: What do the prostate and seminal vesicles contribute?
faqs.a: The seminal vesicles and prostate add fluids to semen. Their ducts join the sperm outflow route near the prostate before ejaculation.

faqs.q: What is the testis & seminiferous tubules?
faqs.a: 250–300 lobules of coiled seminiferous tubules (total ~250 m) with Sertoli cells and developing germ cells, wrapped in tunica albuginea. Function: Spermatogenesis and testosterone production.

faqs.q: Where is the vas deferens located?
faqs.a: A thick-walled 45 cm muscular duct from the epididymal tail, through the inguinal canal into the pelvis. Function: Propels sperm by powerful peristalsis at emission.

faqs.q: What is the function of the prostate?
faqs.a: Function: Secretes citrate, zinc and PSA that liquefy the seminal coagulum. A walnut-sized fibromuscular gland around the urethra below the bladder, with peripheral, central and transition zones.

faqs.q: What organs are included in the female reproductive system?
faqs.a: The system includes ovaries, uterine tubes, uterus, cervix, vagina and external genital structures. Each has distinct roles in cycles, reproduction and pelvic support.

faqs.q: Where does fertilization usually occur?
faqs.a: Fertilization most often occurs in the ampulla of a uterine tube. The resulting early embryo travels toward the uterine cavity.

faqs.q: What is the fundus & body?
faqs.a: The domed fundus above the tubal openings and the tapering body, of smooth muscle (myometrium) lined by endometrium. Function: Houses and nourishes a pregnancy; the myometrium generates labour.

faqs.q: Where is the cervix located?
faqs.a: The fibrous neck projecting into the vagina, with an endocervical canal of mucus-secreting columnar epithelium and a squamous ectocervix. Function: Keeps pregnancy in and microbes out; dilates 10 cm in labour.

faqs.q: What is the function of the uterine tube?
faqs.a: Function: Captures the oocyte, is the site of fertilisation (ampulla) and transports the embryo by ciliary beat and peristalsis. A 10 cm ciliated duct with interstitial, isthmic, ampullary and infundibular parts.

faqs.q: Where are the main organs in the male body?
faqs.a: The brain is in the skull; lungs and heart occupy the chest; liver, stomach, intestines and kidneys occupy the abdomen; and pelvic organs include bladder and reproductive structures.

faqs.q: Does a male body map show every deep structure?
faqs.a: No. The overview is an orientation map; its chapter links provide deeper tissue, vascular, skeletal and nerve details not separately visible on one full-body plate.

faqs.q: Where is the brain shown on the male body map?
faqs.a: Control centre housed in the skull, glowing through the translucent scalp. Function: Integrates sensation, movement, thought, memory and autonomic drive.

faqs.q: Where are the lungs in the male body map?
faqs.a: Paired thoracic organs flanking the heart. Function: Gas exchange across ~300 million alveoli.

faqs.q: What does the liver do in the male body?
faqs.a: Function: Metabolism, detoxification, bile, plasma proteins. Largest internal organ, right upper quadrant.

faqs.q: Where are the main organs in the female body?
faqs.a: The brain lies in the skull; lungs and heart in the chest; digestive and urinary organs in the abdomen; and uterus, tubes and ovaries in the pelvis.

faqs.q: Does a female body map show every deep structure?
faqs.a: No. It is a regional orientation view. Detailed chapters explain deeper pelvic supports, breast tissue, nerves and microscopic layers that a single image cannot resolve.

faqs.q: Where is the brain shown on the female body map?
faqs.a: Control centre housed in the skull, glowing through the translucent scalp. Function: Integrates sensation, movement, thought, memory and autonomic drive.

faqs.q: Where are the lungs in the female body map?
faqs.a: Paired thoracic organs flanking the heart. Function: Gas exchange across ~300 million alveoli.

faqs.q: What does the liver do in the female body?
faqs.a: Function: Metabolism, detoxification, bile, plasma proteins. Largest internal organ, right upper quadrant.

faqs.q: What are the main divisions of the nervous system?
faqs.a: The central nervous system consists of brain and spinal cord. Peripheral nerves and ganglia connect it to the rest of the body; autonomic circuits regulate many involuntary functions.

faqs.q: How do nerves carry information between the body and brain?
faqs.a: Sensory pathways bring information toward the central nervous system, and motor pathways send commands outward. Spinal and cranial nerves also support reflexes and organ control.

faqs.q: What is the brain?
faqs.a: Cerebrum, cerebellum and brainstem inside the cranial vault. Function: Integration, consciousness, motor planning and autonomic control.

faqs.q: Where is the brainstem located?
faqs.a: Midbrain, pons and medulla connecting cord to brain. Function: Vital centres: respiration, heart rate, consciousness.

faqs.q: What is the function of the cervical plexus?
faqs.a: Function: Neck muscles and skin; phrenic nerve to diaphragm. Nerve network in the posterior triangle of the neck.

faqs.q: Is the male nervous system built differently from the female nervous system?
faqs.a: The main brain, spinal cord and peripheral nerve plan is shared. A male-focused pelvic view highlights branches serving the prostate, penis and scrotum rather than implying separate male brain or spinal pathways.

faqs.q: Which nerves contribute to penile erection?
faqs.a: Autonomic cavernous nerves arising from the prostatic plexus influence penile smooth muscle and blood flow. Somatic sensation from the penis is carried largely through the dorsal nerve of the penis, a pudendal branch.

faqs.q: What is the pudendal nerve in the male pelvis?
faqs.a: The pudendal nerve derives from sacral segments S2–S4 and supplies much of the perineum. Its branches include the inferior rectal, perineal and dorsal penile nerves; these are distinct from pelvic autonomic nerves.

faqs.q: How do pelvic splanchnic nerves differ from hypogastric nerves?
faqs.a: Pelvic splanchnic nerves carry sacral parasympathetic fibers from S2–S4 into pelvic plexuses. Hypogastric nerves convey predominantly sympathetic pathways from higher plexuses; both contribute to pelvic organ innervation.

faqs.q: Can the full-body male nerve picture show individual cavernous nerves?
faqs.a: No. It is an orientation image for major nervous-system routes. Cavernous and prostatic plexus branches are described as unpinned study structures rather than falsely marked on a whole-body plate.

faqs.q: Is the female nervous system built differently from the male nervous system?
faqs.a: The central and most peripheral pathways share the same basic organization. A female-focused pelvic view discusses branches serving the uterus, vagina, clitoris and vulva without implying a separate female brain or spinal cord.

faqs.q: What carries sensation from the clitoral glans?
faqs.a: The dorsal nerve of the clitoris, a terminal branch of the pudendal nerve, conveys much of the somatic sensation. Autonomic nerves influence erectile tissues but should not be confused with that sensory pathway.

faqs.q: Which nerves supply the vulva and lower vagina?
faqs.a: Pudendal branches supply much of the posterior vulva and lower vaginal region. The anterior labia also receive contributions from ilioinguinal and genitofemoral branches, so a single nerve label cannot cover the entire area.

faqs.q: What is the uterovaginal plexus?
faqs.a: It is an autonomic network associated with the cervix and upper vagina that carries branches toward the uterus and upper vagina. It is anatomically distinct from the superficial pudendal branches of the perineum.

faqs.q: Does the full-body female nerve plate identify tiny pelvic branches?
faqs.a: No. The full-body plate is for orientation to larger pathways. Tiny pelvic autonomic and sensory branches are explained in study entries without pretending they can be seen or precisely localized on this image.

faqs.q: How many cranial nerves are there?
faqs.a: There are 12 paired cranial nerves, numbered I through XII. Their functions include smell, vision, eye movement, facial sensation, hearing, swallowing and tongue movement.

faqs.q: Which cranial nerve controls facial expression?
faqs.a: The facial nerve, cranial nerve VII, supplies most muscles of facial expression. The trigeminal nerve, cranial nerve V, carries most facial skin sensation.

faqs.q: What is the olfactory nerve (CN I)?
faqs.a: Sensory filaments from nasal epithelium to bulb. Function: Smell.

faqs.q: Where does the oculomotor nerve (CN III) originate?
faqs.a: Midbrain nerve to four eye muscles + lid + pupil. Function: Eye elevation/adduction, lid lift, pupil constriction.

faqs.q: What does the trigeminal nerve (CN V) do?
faqs.a: Function: Face sensation + muscles of mastication. Three divisions: ophthalmic, maxillary, mandibular.

faqs.q: What is the difference between sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves?
faqs.a: Both are autonomic pathways. Sympathetic activity often prepares organs for exertion; parasympathetic pathways support many resting functions. Their effects depend on the organ and receptor.

faqs.q: Where are autonomic ganglia located?
faqs.a: Sympathetic ganglia lie in chains beside the spine or in prevertebral groups; many parasympathetic ganglia lie near or within their target organs.

faqs.q: What is the sympathetic trunk?
faqs.a: Paired chain from neck to sacrum beside vertebrae. Function: Mass fight-or-flight discharge.

faqs.q: Where is the coeliac ganglion & plexus located?
faqs.a: Largest prevertebral relay at T12/L1, around coeliac trunk. Function: Foregut sympathetic supply.

faqs.q: What is the function of the inferior mesenteric ganglion?
faqs.a: Function: Hindgut and pelvic sympathetic supply. Relay at IMA origin.

faqs.q: What structures make up breast tissue?
faqs.a: Breast tissue includes glandular lobules, a branching duct network, connective-tissue support, fat, vessels and nerves. Ducts open at the nipple.

faqs.q: Are breast lobules and milk ducts the same thing?
faqs.a: No. Lobules contain milk-producing units; ducts transport secretions toward the nipple. Both are embedded in supporting connective and fatty tissue.

faqs.q: What are the lobules (glandular)?
faqs.a: Secretory alveolar clusters at duct ends. Function: Milk production under prolactin.

faqs.q: Where is the lactiferous ducts located?
faqs.a: 15–20 branching channels to the nipple. Function: Transport milk.

faqs.q: What is the function of the axillary lymph nodes?
faqs.a: Function: Immune surveillance of the breast. 75% of breast lymph drains here.

faqs.q: Why is the adult human skeleton usually counted as 206 bones?
faqs.a: The conventional adult count includes bones that have fused during development and six middle-ear ossicles. Individual counts can differ because accessory bones, variable sesamoids and fusion patterns vary among people.

faqs.q: What belongs to the axial skeleton?
faqs.a: The axial skeleton contains the skull, vertebral column and thoracic cage. It supports the head and trunk and helps protect the brain, spinal cord, heart and lungs.

faqs.q: What belongs to the appendicular skeleton?
faqs.a: The shoulder and pelvic girdles, arms and legs form the appendicular skeleton. These bones provide attachment and leverage for movement and connect the limbs to the axial framework.

faqs.q: What is the difference between compact and spongy bone?
faqs.a: Compact bone forms a dense outer layer; spongy bone contains a lattice of trabeculae inside many bones. Both are living tissues, and marrow occupies spaces within bones.

faqs.q: Where is blood cell production found in adult bones?
faqs.a: Red marrow produces blood cell precursors in selected adult bones, especially axial bones and the proximal ends of some long bones. Yellow marrow is richer in fat and has different activity.

faqs.q: How do skeletal muscles move joints?
faqs.a: Skeletal muscle fibers contract and transmit force through tendons or other attachments. When a muscle crosses a joint, its contraction can pull the attached bones; opposing muscles help control the movement.

faqs.q: Are all human muscles listed among the overview cards?
faqs.a: No. The overview cards introduce major regions, while the linked full-body muscle and tendon atlas contains hundreds of named records. A single fixed count of muscles varies with naming and counting conventions.

faqs.q: Where can I find posterior muscles such as the triceps and hamstrings?
faqs.a: The full-body muscle atlas groups them by arm and thigh region, including deeper layers and sex-specific pelvic floor views. The front-oriented overview image alone cannot identify posterior fibers.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a tendon and a ligament?
faqs.a: A tendon transfers muscular force to an attachment, commonly a bone; a ligament connects bones across a joint. Both consist largely of dense collagenous connective tissue but have different mechanical roles.

faqs.q: Is the diaphragm a skeletal muscle?
faqs.a: Yes. The diaphragm is a dome-shaped skeletal muscle separating the thoracic and abdominal cavities and is the primary muscle used during quiet inspiration. Its central tendon is an attachment region, not a separate muscle.

faqs.q: What does the lymphatic system do?
faqs.a: It returns excess interstitial fluid to the bloodstream, transports absorbed fats from the intestine and supports immune surveillance through nodes and lymphoid organs.

faqs.q: Where does lymph drain back into the blood?
faqs.a: Large lymphatic ducts empty near the junctions of the internal jugular and subclavian veins. The thoracic duct drains most of the body.

faqs.q: What is the cervical nodes?
faqs.a: Chains along jugular and spine. Function: Drain head and neck.

faqs.q: Where is the inguinal nodes located?
faqs.a: Horizontal + vertical groups in the groin. Function: Drain leg, perineum and lower abdominal wall.

faqs.q: What is the function of the thymus?
faqs.a: Function: T-cell maturation in childhood. Bilobed school for T cells, behind sternum.

faqs.q: What is the difference between arteries and veins?
faqs.a: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins return it. The distinction is direction of flow, not oxygen level: pulmonary arteries carry less-oxygenated blood.

faqs.q: What is the aorta's role in circulation?
faqs.a: The aorta receives blood from the left ventricle and supplies the systemic arterial tree through branches serving the head, trunk and limbs.

faqs.q: What is the aortic arch?
faqs.a: Curve giving brachiocephalic, left carotid, left subclavian. Function: Distributes to head and arms.

faqs.q: Where is the subclavian artery located?
faqs.a: Under clavicle to axillary artery. Function: Arm supply; gives vertebral to brain.

faqs.q: What is the function of the descending aorta?
faqs.a: Function: Segmental branches to wall and viscera. Thoracic then abdominal aorta.

faqs.q: What organs make up the endocrine system?
faqs.a: The endocrine system includes hormone-producing structures such as the pituitary, thyroid, parathyroids, adrenals and pancreatic islets, with other organs also contributing hormones.

faqs.q: How do endocrine glands differ from exocrine glands?
faqs.a: Endocrine tissue releases hormones into the blood. Exocrine glands deliver products through ducts to a surface or lumen, as pancreatic acini do for digestion.

faqs.q: What is the pituitary gland?
faqs.a: Pea-sized master gland in the sella turcica. Function: Releases ACTH, TSH, GH, LH/FSH, prolactin, ADH/oxytocin store.

faqs.q: Where in the neck is the thyroid gland located?
faqs.a: Butterfly gland on the trachea. Function: T3/T4 metabolic rate; calcitonin.

faqs.q: What is the function of the adrenal glands?
faqs.a: Function: Cortisol, aldosterone, adrenaline. Caps on each kidney: cortex + medulla.

faqs.q: What holds a joint together?
faqs.a: A joint may be supported by a capsule, ligaments, tendons and nearby muscles. Exact stabilizers vary between joints; the knee also has menisci and cruciate ligaments.

faqs.q: What do the ACL and PCL do in the knee?
faqs.a: The anterior and posterior cruciate ligaments resist different directions of tibial translation and help stabilize the knee during movement.

faqs.q: What is the anterior cruciate ligament?
faqs.a: From lateral femoral condyle to anterior tibial plateau. Function: Blocks anterior tibial translation; pivots in rotation.

faqs.q: Where is the posterior cruciate ligament located?
faqs.a: Medial femoral condyle to posterior tibia. Function: Blocks posterior tibial slide (dashboard injury).

faqs.q: What is the function of the menisci (medial & lateral)?
faqs.a: Function: Load sharing, shock absorption, joint lubrication. Fibrocartilage crescents on the tibial plateau.

faqs.q: Why can the shoulder move so freely?
faqs.a: The shallow glenoid cavity permits a wide range of movement. The labrum, capsule, rotator cuff and surrounding muscles help stabilize the humeral head.

faqs.q: Which muscles form the rotator cuff?
faqs.a: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor and subscapularis form the rotator cuff around the glenohumeral joint.

faqs.q: What is the supraspinatus tendon?
faqs.a: Over the top of the humeral head. Function: Initiates abduction (first 15°).

faqs.q: Where is the teres minor tendon located?
faqs.a: Below infraspinatus. Function: External rotation + capsule tension.

faqs.q: What is the function of the glenoid labrum?
faqs.a: Function: Adds ~50% of glenoid depth. Fibrocartilage rim deepening the socket.

faqs.q: What is the path of air through the upper airway?
faqs.a: Air enters the nose or mouth, passes through the pharynx and larynx, then moves down the trachea toward the bronchi.

faqs.q: What does the epiglottis do during swallowing?
faqs.a: The epiglottis is one structure involved in protecting the laryngeal entrance during swallowing; coordinated movement of the larynx and vocal folds also matters.

faqs.q: What is the nasal cavity & conchae?
faqs.a: Three conchae turbo-charge the surface area. Function: Warms, humidifies and filters inspired air.

faqs.q: Where is the nasopharynx & adenoid located?
faqs.a: Posterior nasal chamber with lymphoid adenoid. Function: Air passage; immune sampling in childhood.

faqs.q: What is the function of the epiglottis?
faqs.a: Function: Flips to cover the larynx during swallowing. Elastic leaf above the larynx.

faqs.q: What is the difference between red and yellow bone marrow?
faqs.a: Red marrow supports blood-cell production. Yellow marrow contains more fat; distribution changes with age and differs across skeletal sites.

faqs.q: Where are blood cells made in adults?
faqs.a: Most adult blood-cell production occurs in red marrow of axial bones and selected proximal long-bone regions.

faqs.q: What is the red marrow?
faqs.a: Spongy bone of vertebrae, pelvis, sternum, epiphyses. Function: Haematopoiesis: all blood cell lines.

faqs.q: Where is the trabecular (spongy) bone located?
faqs.a: Latticework of struts along stress lines. Function: Strength at low weight; houses red marrow.

faqs.q: What is the function of the endosteum & osteoblasts?
faqs.a: Function: Remodelling: osteoblasts build, osteoclasts eat. Cellular lining of all internal bone surfaces.

faqs.q: Which organs are located in the male pelvis?
faqs.a: The male pelvis contains bladder, prostate and rectum, along with parts of the urethra, reproductive ducts, pelvic vessels and nerves.

faqs.q: What is the pelvic floor's role in men?
faqs.a: Pelvic-floor muscles support pelvic organs and contribute to continence. Their relationship to the urethra and perineal structures is important in regional anatomy.

faqs.q: Where is the urinary bladder in the male pelvis?
faqs.a: Reservoir behind the pubis. Function: Stores urine; trigone is its smooth base.

faqs.q: Where is the prostatic & membranous urethra located?
faqs.a: Urethra traversing prostate and perineum. Function: Conduit for urine and semen; sphincters here.

faqs.q: What is the function of the rectum?
faqs.a: Function: Stores stool before defecation. Terminal 12–15 cm with three valves.

faqs.q: Which organs are located in the female pelvis?
faqs.a: The female pelvis contains bladder, uterus, cervix, vagina and rectum, with ovaries and uterine tubes toward the lateral pelvic regions.

faqs.q: What supports the uterus and pelvic organs?
faqs.a: Pelvic-floor muscles and connective-tissue attachments provide key support. The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold, not the sole load-bearing support.

faqs.q: Where is the urinary bladder in the female pelvis?
faqs.a: Reservoir behind the pubic symphysis. Function: Stores urine.

faqs.q: Where is the vagina located?
faqs.a: Muscular canal from cervix to vestibule. Function: Intercourse, menstrual flow, birth canal.

faqs.q: What is the function of the vesico- & recto-uterine pouches?
faqs.a: Function: Allow organ movement; collect free fluid. Peritoneal recesses front and back of uterus.

faqs.q: What are the layers of the uterine wall?
faqs.a: The uterus has an inner endometrium, muscular myometrium and outer serosal or connective covering depending on the region.

faqs.q: What happens to the endometrium during the menstrual cycle?
faqs.a: The endometrium responds to changing ovarian hormones. Its functional layer grows and changes during the cycle and is shed if pregnancy does not occur.

faqs.q: What is the fundus?
faqs.a: Dome above the two tubal openings. Function: Expands in pregnancy; fundal position is an obstetric landmark.

faqs.q: Where are the uterine cornua located?
faqs.a: Upper lateral junctions where uterine tubes enter. Function: Communicate with intramural tube segments.

faqs.q: What is the function of the endometrium — functionalis?
faqs.a: Function: Proliferates under estrogen and becomes secretory under progesterone. Superficial cyclic glandular layer; sheds with menses.

faqs.q: What is the cervical transformation zone?
faqs.a: It is the region where squamous epithelium of the ectocervix and columnar epithelium of the endocervix meet and change over time.

faqs.q: Why is the transformation zone important in cervical screening?
faqs.a: Many cervical precancerous changes arise near the squamocolumnar junction. Screening samples this region, but this atlas does not interpret individual test results.

faqs.q: What is the ectocervix?
faqs.a: Part of cervix visible at the vaginal vault. Function: Covered by nonkeratinizing stratified squamous epithelium.

faqs.q: Where is the endocervical columnar epithelium located?
faqs.a: Mucus-secreting simple columnar lining of the canal. Function: Produces cervical mucus under hormonal regulation.

faqs.q: What is the function of the squamocolumnar junction?
faqs.a: Function: Migrates with age, hormones and pregnancy. Border where glandular and squamous epithelia meet.

faqs.q: Where does an egg go after ovulation?
faqs.a: After release from an ovarian follicle, the oocyte is taken up near the fimbriae and usually enters the uterine tube before moving toward the uterus.

faqs.q: Which part of the fallopian tube is the usual site of fertilization?
faqs.a: The ampulla, a wider segment of the uterine tube, is the most common site of fertilization.

faqs.q: What is the ovarian cortex?
faqs.a: Outer ovarian zone with follicles at several stages. Function: Houses the oocyte reserve.

faqs.q: Where are the primordial follicles located?
faqs.a: Small oocyte with flat granulosa cells in outer cortex. Function: Dormant ovarian reserve pool.

faqs.q: What is the function of the dominant antral follicle?
faqs.a: Function: Releases a secondary oocyte after the LH surge. Large fluid-filled preovulatory follicle.

faqs.q: What are the layers of the vaginal wall?
faqs.a: The vaginal wall contains a mucosal lining, a muscular layer and outer connective tissue. Its folds and tissue properties vary with age and hormonal state.

faqs.q: Where are the vaginal fornices?
faqs.a: Fornices are recesses around the cervix at the upper end of the vagina; the posterior fornix lies behind the cervix.

faqs.q: What is the vaginal lumen?
faqs.a: Potential space whose walls normally lie against one another. Function: Passage for menstrual flow, intercourse and birth.

faqs.q: Where is the posterior vaginal wall located?
faqs.a: Wall lying anterior to rectum, longer near posterior fornix. Function: Supports the posterior compartment.

faqs.q: What is the function of the vaginal muscularis?
faqs.a: Function: Allows distension and elastic return. Circular and longitudinal smooth-muscle bundles.

faqs.q: What structures are included in the vulva?
faqs.a: The vulva is the external genital region: mons pubis, labia majora and minora, clitoral structures and the vestibule with urethral and vaginal openings. Some deeper glands, vessels and nerves are described separately.

faqs.q: Are the vulva and vagina the same structure?
faqs.a: No. The vulva refers to external genital anatomy; the vagina is an internal muscular canal extending from the cervix to the vaginal opening. The opening lies within the vulvar vestibule.

faqs.q: How are the urethral and vaginal openings positioned?
faqs.a: The external urethral opening is typically inferior to the clitoral glans and superior to the vaginal opening within the vestibule. Their appearance varies normally, so a teaching illustration is not a diagnostic reference.

faqs.q: What do the labia minora do?
faqs.a: The labia minora are inner hairless folds that border the vestibule and join anteriorly near the clitoral hood. Their size, color and asymmetry vary normally between people.

faqs.q: Can the surface image show Bartholin glands or the clitoral crura?
faqs.a: No. The greater vestibular glands and most clitoral erectile structures lie below the surface. Their locations are described as deep study notes, not marked as visible on the external surface illustration.

faqs.q: What is the difference between the broad ligament and pelvic support ligaments?
faqs.a: The broad ligament is a peritoneal fold. Cardinal and uterosacral connective tissues, together with pelvic-floor muscles, contribute substantially to uterine support.

faqs.q: Why is the ureter important in pelvic surgery anatomy?
faqs.a: The ureter travels near the uterine artery and cervix. Understanding their relationship helps explain why surgical planes require careful identification.

faqs.q: What is the broad ligament?
faqs.a: Double peritoneal sheet draped over uterus, tubes and associated structures. Function: Supports relationships but is not the main mechanical uterine support.

faqs.q: Where is the mesosalpinx located?
faqs.a: Broad ligament portion related to uterine tube. Function: Supports tube and its vessels.

faqs.q: What is the function of the round ligament?
faqs.a: Function: Helps maintain anteversion; not principal apical support. Band from uterine cornu through inguinal canal to labium majus.

faqs.q: Where are sperm made in the testis?
faqs.a: Sperm develop within seminiferous tubules. Supporting Sertoli cells and hormone-producing interstitial Leydig cells occupy different microscopic compartments.

faqs.q: How do sperm leave the testis?
faqs.a: They move from seminiferous tubules through a collecting network and efferent ductules into the epididymis, where maturation and storage continue.

faqs.q: What is the tunica vaginalis?
faqs.a: Serous covering with visceral and parietal layers. Function: Allows mobile testis within scrotum.

faqs.q: Where is the mediastinum testis located?
faqs.a: Posterior thickening of albuginea containing rete testis. Function: Organizes lobules and duct outflow.

faqs.q: What is the function of the seminiferous tubules?
faqs.a: Function: Spermatogenesis. Coiled tubules lined by developing germ cells and Sertoli cells.

faqs.q: Where is the prostate located?
faqs.a: The prostate sits below the bladder and surrounds the first part of the urethra. Ducts from the reproductive tract open into the prostatic urethra.
